articles.title: Japan is reaching for the sword again
articles.body:
Japan is reaching for the sword again
In recent months, there’s been a distinct sense of ‘historical déjà vu’ – from Germany’s interest in long-range missiles to the development of hypersonic missile technologies in Japan. The first question that comes to mind is whether revanchism is emerging more than 80 years after the defeat of the fascists and militarists in WWII. However, this question is quite complicated, so for now, we will focus on a more practical issue: Japan’s military-technical buildup. Below, we will attempt to assess the significance of this shift in Japan’s strike capabilities and understand the direction in which the country is heading.
By the end of the 20th century, Japan had become one of the strongest and most loyal allies of the US in the Pacific region. The Japan Self-Defense Forces are equipped with American aircraft, missiles, interceptors, and other weapons. Japan is the first and to date the only country in the world to manufacture Patriot surface-to-air missiles under license, and it is the first foreign recipient of Tomahawk subsonic cruise missiles.
On July 29, 2026, the first test launches of Tomahawk cruise missiles were conducted in the Pacific Ocean from the Kongo-class guided-missile destroyer JS Chokai, equipped with the Aegis system. These tests mark the beginning of the Japanese Navy’s adoption of American long-range cruise missiles. The program to acquire these missiles is quite ambitious: Japan plans to equip four additional Aegis-capable destroyers – JS Kirishima, JS Haguro, JS Myoko, and JS Atago—with these state-of-the-art missiles, with the long-term goal of upgrading all other destroyers of this class. In total, the acquisition of 400 missiles (Block IV and Block V variants) is planned by the end of the 2027 fiscal year. This arsenal significantly alters the capabilities of the Japanese Navy, given that such cruise missiles can strike targets at ranges of up to 1,600 km. Furthermore, this is merely an interim solution pending the adoption of domestically developed missiles with similar or superior specifications.
Japan is currently working on several missile projects, with a particular focus on hypersonic technologies. Japan has already concluded an agreement with Australia to conduct joint tests at Australian missile ranges, which offer the necessary facilities for testing long-range missiles; the development of several strike missile projects is scheduled to begin in 2027.
One of the major initiatives is the project to develop a submarine-launched hypersonic missile capable of striking land-based targets. The missile is expected to be versatile, capable of being deployed from both Japanese Navy submarines and surface ships. Japan justifies the deployment of such missiles on submarines by citing the need for retaliatory strike capabilities in the event of an external attack. Naturally, Japan is pointing to the growing capabilities of China’s navy and missile forces. For its part, China is also actively enhancing its capabilities in light of a possible confrontation with the US and Japan.
While the hypersonic missile project is currently in the preliminary design phase, it draws upon Japan’s existing experience in developing various types of missiles and submarine-based vertical launch systems, as well as ambitious programs to build new missile-equipped vessels and, eventually, nuclear-powered submarines. In 2023, the Japanese Ministry of Defense signed a contract with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries for the development of a submarine-launched guided missile; a separate official program launched that same year is focused on developing an indigenous hypersonic guided missile; the work is set to continue through 2031. These programs are essentially aimed at creating preliminary designs for future missiles and developing hypersonic technologies in general; however, following the research phase, Japan will move on to developing specific missile models. The potential for this already exists.
What about launch platforms? Currently, the Japanese Navy operates several Aegis-equipped destroyers and non-nuclear submarines; they could carry a limited number of missiles. However, this would not be sufficient for mass deployment.
In 2027, the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force is set to commission the lead ASEV-class destroyer into service. Though the destroyer is modestly designated as a “missile defense ship,” it is in reality a guided-missile cruiser. It will measure approximately 189 meters in length and 25 meters in beam, with a standard displacement of around 12,000 tons. This makes it significantly larger than the current Maya-class destroyers or even US Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruisers. Each vessel will carry 128 modular vertical launch system (VLS) cells capable of housing Standard Missile shipborne guided missiles, anti-ship missiles, and strike missiles – ranging from the Tomahawk to future domestically-developed hypersonic missiles. Plans currently call for the construction of two such ships. The speed of construction is impressive: one ship is set to be built in three years. This will be the most heavily armed missile-carrying warship in the Pacific.
And what about nuclear-powered submarines? Recently, Japan’s Ministry of Defense officially included nuclear-powered submarines in its defense posture review, paving the way for Tokyo to assess the feasibility of building such vessels alongside its conventional fleet. Strict restrictions on the military use of nuclear energy had previously been in place in Japan, but in regard to submarines, this particular constraint is now being quietly lifted.
Naturally, such a move would logically expand Japan’s underwater operations in the Western Pacific; from a shipbuilding perspective, Japan certainly has the capacity for it. Nuclear propulsion would allow Japanese submarines to remain submerged for virtually unlimited periods, effectively neutralizing potential Chinese undersea superiority. The US would, of course, be Japan’s primary industrial partner in this endeavor, though the UK or France could also share their expertise in nuclear submarine construction. Following Japan’s lead, South Korea is also considering the development of nuclear submarines. While Japan blames China, South Korea cites the threat of North Korea. In both cases, it looks like the arms industry lobby is actively seeking an outlet for its manufacturing capacity.
But that’s not all – there is also the aviation sector. Alongside the UK and Italy, Japan is participating in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet. The program aims to finalize the aircraft’s requirements and technical specifications by the end of 2027. Furthermore, the Excalibur flying test laboratory and the demonstrator aircraft are scheduled to begin testing by the end of 2027. These efforts are critically important for Japan, as it decides which joint initiative to participate in and whether it should launch its own program to develop a next-generation fighter jet
Therefore, by the 2040s-2050s, the capabilities of the Japanese armed forces could change beyond recognition. Japan could possess nuclear-powered submarines, a missile-armed fleet, a modern air force, ground-launched and subsonic long-range hypersonic and cruise missiles.
Finally, experts believe that, if necessary, Japan could quickly produce nuclear weapons. This would take only a few months. The country possesses a highly developed nuclear industry and nuclear energy sector – with stockpiles of plutonium and other materials, as well as all the requisite technologies. Japan also has nuclear weapons delivery systems at its disposal. In short, all the prerequisites are in place, though strict constitutional constraints currently remain in effect. However, if one threshold is crossed and the decision to build nuclear submarines is made, one might expect this nuclear trend to continue in the direction of classified research and weapons development. A highly advanced nation like Japan could develop nuclear weapons quickly and covertly.
That’s the ‘samurai sword’ slowly but surely emerging from the East. How should we react to it? Sound the alarm and deploy weapons, or call for peace and dispatch ballet troupes? Perhaps, both. Let’s hope that we’ll never have to use the weapons, but be prepared just in case; as for ballet, it’s always a good idea.

articles.title: Europeans warn of rising Russian sabotage but see no imminent NATO attack
articles.body:
Europeans warn of rising Russian sabotage but see no imminent NATO attack
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 23 - Russia is intensifying sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid attacks across Europe to undermine support for Ukraine, European ministers said, while dismissing concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO.
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, officials from countries on NATO's eastern flank said Moscow was increasingly using drone incursions, cyberattacks, sabotage and other covert operations to sow fear, test Western resolve and weaken backing for Kyiv.
"Europe faces a fast proliferation of sabotage attacks and airspace violations," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters. "Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine."
European governments increasingly see Russia's most immediate threat not as a conventional military attack, but as a campaign of covert and deniable actions aimed at unsettling Ukraine's allies and eroding Western unity as the war drags on.
Kallas said Russia appeared willing to take greater risks and argued the answer was to increase pressure on Moscow through tougher sanctions, including measures targeting its "shadow fleet" and military-industrial complex.
"Russia's economy is one of its weakest parts, and we need to increase the pressure on it so that they would stop this war," she said.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said such activity was no longer merely a threat.
"They're not just threats; they're actual attacks," Sikorski told Reuters, citing arson, explosions, drone incursions and what Warsaw says was a deliberate cruise missile violation of its territory.
The Polish Army Operational Command said on Wednesday a Russian military Mi-8 helicopter made a brief incursion into its airspace from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
"Our F-16s are scrambled up almost every day now because you just never know when these drones or missiles that approach might not actually be possible," he said.
Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told Reuters Bucharest had seen more than 100 incursions by drones or drone fragments onto its territory as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure near the Danube and Black Sea.
"We do not have data to indicate we're targeted directly, but that doesn't change the responsibility of Russia for the risk it creates," she said.
Romania has responded by closing Russia's consulate in Constanta and coordinating diplomatic measures with European allies, she added.
The Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries or plotting any confrontation.
NO IMMINENT NATO ATTACK
Despite the incidents, ministers drew a distinction between Russia's covert campaign and the prospect of a direct attack on NATO territory.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Reuters alarmist predictions of an imminent Russian assault on the alliance were misplaced.
"We don’t see that Russia is able and even preparing for some kind of active military aggression against NATO or the European countries," he said, arguing Moscow lacked the capabilities for such an operation while its forces remained heavily engaged in Ukraine.
He said Moscow's campaign was designed primarily to create fear and divisions within Western societies.
"This is mainly meant for creating fear, fear of escalation, to divide us, to play with our unity," Tsahkna said. "The main message is: Don't let Putin play with the fear of escalation," he said, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said allied intelligence pointed to a risk that Russia could seek to broaden pressure on NATO countries through attacks on critical infrastructure and other forms of hybrid activity.
"There are some considerations on the Russian side to escalate horizontally, so to say, or geographically," Budrys told Reuters.
The ministers said the best way to counter such tactics was through unity, deterrence and continued support for Ukraine, particularly ahead of winter, when Russia is expected to intensify attacks on energy infrastructure.
Budrys warned that "the cold will be weaponized by Russia" and urged European countries to provide more assistance, arguing support remained patchy across the bloc.
Several ministers argued that firm responses had already shown results. Tsahkna pointed to the sharp reduction in serious Russian airspace violations on NATO's eastern flank following a strong allied reaction to previous incidents.
"Putin is carefully watching," he said. "We have lots of leverage, but we just need to have self-confidence and be clear about our language." REUTERS

articles.title: Trump to meet China’s Xi as Congress mulls bill banning artificial superintelligence – US politics live
articles.body:
Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
Bernie Sanders introduces bill to “ban artificial superintelligence”
Bernie Sanders, the left-wing independent Senator from Vermont who has quickly become one of the loudest AI-skeptical voices in US politics, announced on Wednesday new legislation that would, in his words, “ban artificial superintelligence.”
“The leading experts are clear: AI is rapidly escaping our control,” Sanders wrote in a post to social media announcing the bill. “Congress must act NOW. Today I’m introducing legislation to permanently ban artificial superintelligence and pause advanced AI until clear safety rules are in place.”
The Associated Press reported earlier this morning that the legislation – backed in the House of Representatives by Texas Democrat Greg Cesar – would pause the development of frontier AI until a new “Department of Artificial Intelligence” could establish guardrails around the industry.
It would also ban, in perpetuity, “artificial superintelligence,” a category that includes AI systems that exceed the limits of human intelligence or have “sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” per AP.
Maine Democrats seize on pay-for-play donation allegations against Collins
The allegations, first reported in a ProPublica story yesterday, were the latest development in an already chaotic Maine Senate race: that Maine GOP senator Susan Collins’ campaign had accepted large donations from a defense contractor in return for Collins steering government funds to the company.
A day later, Maine Democrats are centering those allegations as they seek to win Collins’ seat in the November midterm elections.
“I cannot stress enough today the seriousness of these allegations,” Devon Murphy-Anderson, executive director of the Maine Democratic Party, said at a party press conference called to highlight the investigation.
Collins, Murphy-Anderson said, had “sold us out yet again, and gotten bailed out of trouble by the President of the United States. It is not the first time she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure it is one of the last.”
Collins’s team has fiercly denied the allegations, which emerged from an FBI investigation into Martin Kao, former executive of the defense contractor Navakek. Kao, who detailed the alleged scheme to the FBI, has since been convicted and sentenced to prison on unrelated charges.
ProPublica reports that the FBI has been investigating Collins as part of a wide-ranging probe into members of Congress, but that the inquiry died as part of the Trump administration’s restructuring of the FBI.
Troy Jackson, Collins’ opponent for her Maine Senate seat in November, has also seized on the corruption allegations, implying that Collins has been deferential to Trump because his FBI helped kill the probe into her conduct. (Jackson was chosen by the Maine Democrats to replace their previous nominee, one-time progressive darling Graham Platner, after allegations of sexual assault led him to terminate his campaign.)
“This is corruption of the highest order,” Jackson wrote in a post to social media. “Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then Donald Trump helped her cover it up.”
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.
Rodriguez took the reins in Venezuela after the US raided her country’s capital of Caracas and seized Maduro, the toppled autocrat, in the dead of night. Since then, she’s been pliant to US interests and brokered a deal that would see a vast share of her country’s oil wealth into US coffers.
During remarks to reporters, Rubio said that the US was working to “create the groundwork and rebuild the institutions necessary to have free and fair elections in Venezuela.”
But he caveated that free and fair elections would have to wait until Venezuela was in the shape to support an “enduring Republic,” and that its first elected leader could not inherit “a complete catastrophe, economic and social.”
The conditions for such a democratic transition, per Rubio, include rebuilding Venezuela’s independent media, creating the infrastructure for a trustworthy electoral process, and bringing back opposition political parties exiled abroad. Here Rubio name dropped María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who had maintained close tied with Trump before the administration ultimately backed Rodriguez.
Speaking to reporters at the UN, Rubio alludes to regime change in Cuba
Addressing reporters at the United Nations, Marco Rubio reiterated, in so many words, that the Trump administration is seeking to replace the current Cuban leadership, and did not rule out the use of force to achieve that goal.
“The Cuban Revolution has failed. It has failed for sixty-something years, it’s a failure now,” Rubio said. “The question is what replaces it.”
He continued: “We’re open to measures moving forward that begin that process of change.”
Pressed on whether the Trump administration would try to repeat its tactics in Venezuela – where it raided the country in the dead of night, arrested former autocrat Nicolas Maduro, and ushered in a more US-friendly leader to replace him – Rubio equivocated, but did not rule out the possibility.
“If there is a threat to the national security of the United States, the president has both the power and the obligation to address it,” Rubio said. “That said, our preference always is to deal with these things – I don’t want to call it diplomatic – but in a negotiating way.”
He also said he believed that American business could play “a positive role in a future Cuba,” and that any new government would have to be friendlier to business interests. That comes in light of reporting by the Guardian that shows businesses close to the administration have been buying up assets in Cuba in light of chaos wrought by the US’s latest efforts to cripple the island’s economy.
Iranian President to United Nations: "We will never bow our head"
Jakub Krupa
In a speech to the United Nations following on the heels of President Trump’s threats to “annihilate” his country, Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, struck a defiant tone.
“He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying,” Pezeshkian said, referring to Trump. “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”
He continued: “It must be understood by Mr Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations - without accepting the language of force.”
Trump, in his speech the day earlier, said Iran faced a choice between “greatness” and annihilation, warning Iran that he would its people “into hell” if they didn’t make a deal. It was latest of several apocalyptic-sounding threats from Trump toward Iran since the beginning of the conflict.
Earler in his address, during which the US delegation walked out of the room, Masoud also decried the US and Israel’s campaign against his country as “terrorism.”
“The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism,” he said.
He said that while Iran has avoided attacking civilian populations, the US “bombed a school” and “children perished under bombs with weapons used by the US and Israel.”
“They impose the war on us but we have proven that we’re not afraid of fighting, of war, that is defensive in nature, and we will stand in defence of our beloved Iran, our homeland, until our last breath.”
Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him - analysis
Robert Tait
Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.
The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.
Trump administration set to defend its White House press ban in court
Trump administration lawyers will face the three new outlets banned from the White House by the president – Politico, CNN, and MS Now – in court today, as the organizations ask a federal judge to restore their access.
Trump banned the three outlets late last week via a post to Truth Social, sparking a scuffle with the Washington press. The three banned outlets swiftly sued, and other news organizations have halted some coverage of the president in solidarity, including the other rotating members of the president’s standard TV pool (which take turns filming the president’s press-open events and distributing the footage to others).
The three barred news organizations have accused the president of violating their First Amendment rights by retaliating against them over coverage he disliked. The Trump administration, in a new filing, countered by saying that White House access is a “privilege,” not a right, and that the three outlets’ reporting of information the administration deems sensitive constitutes a national security threat.
Trump himself has said he’ll “probably lose” the lawsuit, which has landed in the courtroom of a judge he appointed.
Iran and Ukraine leaders set to address UN after Trump's departure
Trump won’t be back at the United Nations today, but world leaders speaking after him on day two of the General Assembly’s gathering will be reckoning with the international order he’s shaped.
In particular, the leaders of both Iran, the nation Trump started a war with, and Ukraine, whose war with Russia Trump staked his 2024 campaign on ending, will feature in Wednesday’s lineup of speakers.
The President of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is slated to speak first, a day after Trump used his address to the body to threaten to “annihilate” his country and drive its people “into Hell” if Iranian leadership refused to strike a deal to end the war.
Around the same time Trump delivered those remarks, members of Trump’s team, including Middle East envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, held a snap meeting with the Iranian delegation, Trump later said. The President reported that the meeting went “very well,” though Iran has since pushed back on claims that it dropped some preconditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz during those talks.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, president of Ukraine, will also take the podium, a day after he also met with President Trump. His address will follow a UN Security Council meeting on Ukraine. Both will give Zelenskyy a platform to rally international support for the defense of his country from a Russian invasion that has endured for well over 4 years.
In remarks to reporters before his meeting with Trump, Zelenskyy said he wanted to see the war ended before winter.
“I hope we will end this war, and President Trump will help us end this war. We need to do it as quickly as possible, before winter,” he said.
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
The Trump administration is refusing to work with the newly appointed deputy head of the United Nations refugee agency, Reuters reported.
Tressa Rae Finerty, an American who took up the role of deputy high commissioner at UNHCR earlier this month, has taken leave as she seeks a waiver from the US government that would allow her to carry out aspects of her duties, according to seven diplomatic sources.
Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington’s preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues. “We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests,” the spokesperson said.
Trump to meet with China's Xi as Congress mulls bill banning artificial superintelligence
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will meet with the Chinese president Xi Jinping later today, ahead of a three-day visit that will undoubtedly see artificial intelligence (AI) high on the agenda.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, has called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war.
“Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
It comes as two leading progressive US lawmakers, senator Bernie Sanders and representative Greg Casar, were due to unveil legislation later today that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI.
The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill.
“It doesn’t take a genius to say, ‘slow it down,’” Sanders said in an interview with AP. “Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? I don’t think we do.”
Congress has so far done little to rein in the AI industry even as some of its most prominent leaders warn about potentially catastrophic risks.
Xi departed Beijing on Wednesday, state media said, heading to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, where he will be met by Trump on the tarmac.
“President Xi Jinping left Beijing by special plane for a state visit to the United States” accompanied by his wife Peng Liyuan, his right-hand man Cai Qi, and foreign minister Wang Yi, among others, state broadcaster CCTV said.
In other developments:
Speaking at the UN general assembly, Donald Trump re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He also said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war, defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, defended his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions, pointed to regime change in Cuba and said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence.
Shortly after his UN address, Trump signed a Greenland deal, which Greenland’s prime minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen said “underlines the importance of the Nato alliance.” In tricky, carefully worded paragraphs, she said the agreement “recognises the US defining historical and ongoing contributions to the security and defence of Greenland,” but it also “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN general assembly on Tuesday that he was “surprised” the outlet was covering him, saying it ‘shouldn’t be here’ after he banned the network alongside Politico and MS Now from the White House on Friday.
At a joint press conference on Tuesday, vice-president JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces.

articles.title: Iran, US officials confirm 'positive' meeting took place at UNGA
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone at the UN, vowing Iran would never “bend at the knee” to US pressure and accusing Washington of “terrorism” over the killing of former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei
US President Donald Trump said during a press conference at the United Nations General Assembly that US officials had a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials. For its part, Iranian state media confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US special envoy Steve Witkoff met in New York
The war in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government forces continues with no end in sight
Israel continues to attack Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any ceasefire agreements
And so we begin our live coverage of the day...
Libya's al-Menfi condemns exclusion of Palestinians at UNGA
Mohamed al-Menfi, head of Libya's Tripoli-based Presidential Council, told the UN General Assembly that the gathering comes as the world undergoes a “profound transformation” in the “balance of power” and the “ethics” surrounding its use.
Al-Menfi said one of the central challenges facing the international community was building an international order “in which the rule of law is an equal right, not a privilege of the most powerful”.
He also expressed regret over the absence of the Palestinian delegation, whose members were denied visas to attend the assembly, and praised Palestinians for remaining “steadfast” in the face of “oppression”.
“The plight of the Palestinian people continues to worsen after decades of occupation, repression,” he said. “Yet they remain steadfast in their adherence to their right to life and self-determination.”
Miliband: Leaders discuss Gaza aid and two-state solution
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has posted an update from the UN General Assembly, saying the leaders of the UK, France, Canada and Saudi Arabia had “brought together countries to discuss practical steps to improve humanitarian access in Gaza, support recovery and stand up for the two-state solution”.
“The global community will not be silent in standing up for peace and an end to this conflict”, Miliband wrote on X alongside a photograph of the meeting.
At UNGA @AndyBurnham, @EmmanuelMacron, @MarkJCarney and @FaisalbinFarhan brought together countries to discuss practical steps to improve humanitarian access in Gaza, support recovery and stand up for the two-state solution.
Iran's president struck a defiant tone at the UN on Wednesday where he spoke for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never "bend at the knee."
Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of "terrorism" for assassinating former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war.
He held up a photograph of the dead leader, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump had told the UN he was weighing whether to "annihilate" Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington's negotiators.
Pezeshkian made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech.
"(Trump) must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he said.
Pezeshkian insisted that Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz, which it has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war causing global energy prices to spike, to be used for aggression against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
Pezeshkian: Gaza shows resistance cannot be destroyed
Pezeshkian turned to Palestine in his UN General Assembly address, describing it as an issue that “remains an open wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza remains a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to prevent civilian suffering”.
Despite decades of UN resolutions, occupation and violence have continued, he said, arguing that for as long as occupation, aggression and injustice persist, “resistance will continue”.
“If it is weakened in one form, it will re-emerge in others, perhaps stronger still”.
“Gaza, despite relentless killing and widespread devastation, has strengthened the people’s faith in resistance, and resistance cannot be destroyed by bombs and siege; this is human nature”.
“If a human being is driven from his or her land, they will resist. If their homes are subjected to bombings and aggression and attacks, they will resist; what other choice do they have? Succumb to bullying? To be driven from their homes, from their lands, and remain silent in the face of these threats and dangers? And when they defend themselves, they’re labeled as terrorists” he said.
Iran's Pezeshkian says country defended itself with strength
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has begun addressing the UN General Assembly, saying his country defended itself "with utmost strength" after coming under attack by the US and Israel.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said, referring to attacks carried out by countries equipped with advanced weaponry and technology.
Iran's Rezaei says airports doing US sanctions 'won't work'
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said at the UN Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian after the far-right Colombian government last month recognised an illegal Israeli occupation over the strategically important territory.
The rest of the world does not recognise Israel's control over the Golan.
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories. Any other attempts will be thwarted according to Security Council Resolution 497," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
Iranian plane lands in China despite Washington's threats
A commercial plane belonging to the Iranian Mahan Airlines landed in China on Wednesday, despite the United States' threat to impose sanctions on anyone dealing with Iranian airlines.
The "Flight Radar 24" website, which tracks air traffic, reported that an Airbus A340 plane, which took off from Tehran, landed at approximately 16:40 local time (08:40 GMT) in the city of Canton in southern China.
This came in conjunction with the entry into force of a new package of severe US sanctions on the Iranian aviation sector, after Washington pledged to stop all Iranian airline companies from operating and punish any party that deals with them.
Settlement sanctions a start. Ending EU complicity is key
Sanctions by European nations are overdue, but ending complicity in Israel's occupation requires more than trade restrictions and diplomatic statements, writes Tamam Abusalama.
Oil prices fell and stock markets traded steadier Wednesday after recent volatility, as Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives met for "very good" talks at the United Nations.
The US president added that the three-hour meeting was "very productive" and that two countries "have another one scheduled in the very near future".
Brent North crude, the international benchmark, remained under $100 per barrel on hopes of diplomatic progress towards ending the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel noted that the UN "meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure (war) escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant".
Oil prices were dampened also by a report that the world's biggest crude exporter Saudi Arabia had rebooted operations along its East-West Pipeline, a crucial oil export route shut down by drone attacks.
Al-Masirah TV, affiliated with the Houthis, reported that Saudi aircraft launched about 15 strikes on Al-Hodeidah governorate and its districts, hitting communications towers in Al-Maraw’a and Al-Qatee’ and the Bajil Radio building.
According to the channel, Saudi aircraft targeted the Haydan district with missiles, renewing its missile bombardment on the Maran district.
Cargo vessel hit by unknown projectile in Hormuz, two hurt
UKMTO said it received a report of an incident in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday when a cargo vessel was struck by an unknown projectile, leaving it on fire and adrift, with all crew evacuated and two casualties reported.
UKMTO said authorities were investigating, and that there was no reported environmental impact.
Houthi-affiliated media on Wednesday said Saudi airstrikes killed 10 people and left 14 others wounded in Yemen's Taiz and Al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
"Eight civilians were killed and 11 others wounded in Taiz, while two civilians were killed and three others wounded in Al-Jawf," Al-Masirah TV channel said.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement staged a lightning offensive in recent weeks to gain control over the Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, while also aiming drone and missile strikes at Saudi Arabia.
The war in impoverished Yemen began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014. Since a four-year truce collapsed in July, fighting has killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.
Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday, Axios reported.
The 66-project proposal includes estimated spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, the report added, citing a copy of the plan.
The White House and US Department of State did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade, the Axios report added.
It also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects.
Israel continues to attack Gaza on a daily basis. [Getty[
A spokesperson for Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday Iran had maintained its negotiating stance in talks with US officials, demanding the United States end its blockade on Iranian ports and release Iran's frozen assets.
Esmail Baghaei said the indirect talks took place via Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
“This was not anything new,” Baghaei said of Iran’s conditions.
The unscheduled meeting—the first indirect talks between U.S. and Iranian officials since a June ceasefire unraveled—came as intermittent attacks continue in the Strait of Hormuz off Iran's coastline, where commercial shipping remains below prewar levels.
US senator calls Netanyahu 'chronic liar' ahead of UNGA
US Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen has condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a "chronic liar" and a "wanted war criminal" ahead of the Israeli leader's visit to the UN General Assembly.
"Netanyahu lies and lies and lies," Van Hollen said after Netanyahu released a video attacking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Van Hollen pointed to the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant for Netanyahu and accused his government of blocking accountability for American citizens killed in the occupied West Bank by Israeli settlers or security forces.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Van Hollen said Netanyahu's comments about Mamdani "don't change the fact" that he is "a wanted war criminal" who has blocked justice for Americans killed "on his watch".
"If anyone should be shamed & ashamed, it's Netanyahu," the senator added, saying the Israeli leader was "lucky he was even allowed into our country".
Prime Minister Netanyahu's lies about @NYCMayor don't change the fact that Netanyahu is a wanted war criminal who has blocked justice for Americans killed on his watch.
If there's anyone who should be shamed & ashamed, it's him.
An Israeli airstrike killed at least two Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday, local health officials said.
Medics said the two men were killed when an Israeli airstrike hit a vehicle in western Khan Younis, in the south of the enclave. Two other people were wounded, they added.
A spokesperson for the Israeli military confirmed the strike, saying it had struck a militant and that more information would be released later. No Palestinian militant group claimed the two dead men.
Palestinian authorities say more than 73,900 people have been killed by Israel's genocidal assault on Gaza since October 2023.
At least 1,400 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the alleged ceasefire took effect last October.
Which countries are banning Iran flights over US sanctions?
Several countries have begun restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on Wednesday.
The measures are beginning to disrupt international routes operated by Iranian carriers, with restrictions ranging from blanket bans to the suspension of individual airlines or destinations.
The New Arab's West Bank correspondent, Wahaj Bani Moufleh, reported a surge of Israeli settler attacks across the occupied territories.
Israeli settlers attacked a Palestinian home and smash a number of vehicles in al-Mazra'a al-Sharqiya village, northeast of Ramallah, as other settlers began to level Palestinian land in the Zabda area, Ramallah district.
Additionally, an armed settler raided the entrance to Jaba town, south of Jenin, as another group of settlers attacked the al-Hamma community, in the northern Jordan Valley, shooting at the cattle there.
Moreover, armed settlers attempted to raid the home of resident Mohammed Muslim in Khirbet al-Marajim, south of Nablus, as other settlers raided the Salayma neighborhood in Hebron city.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said he held talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on the sidelines of the UNGA.
"Dialogue and diplomacy remain the most effective path to contain tensions and prevent their escalation, and regional security and freedom of navigation require regional cooperation and responsible dialogue among the concerned parties," he wrote on X.
Iran: 50% of South Pars gas production capacity restored
Iran has restored about 50% of damaged production capacity at the South Pars gas field, Deputy Oil Minister Ahmad Zeraatkar was reported as saying on Wednesday by the semi-official Fars news agency, adding that all planned restoration work would be completed before winter.
Zeraatkar said in late August that about 40% of the damaged capacity had been returned to production.
Shipping traffic via Hormuz stays below 10-day average
Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.
The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage.
All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT.
One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data.
The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Israeli war on Iran began last February.
Macron calls Gaza a 'spectacle that shames us all'
French President Emmanuel Macron said that the situation in conflict-devastated Gaza was a "spectacle that shames us all" as he gave his last speech as France's leader to the UN's showpiece diplomatic week.
"What is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza? Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. It is a spectacle that shames us all," he said.
Oil prices fall after Trump hails 'good' talks with Iran
Oil prices fell on Wednesday after President Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had met for "very good" talks at the United Nations.
The international benchmark, Brent crude, and main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, dipped to $98.91 and $89.93 per barrel respectively in early Asian trade -- well below the symbolic $100 mark they have smashed repeatedly since the Middle Eat war broke out in February.
The three-hour meeting was "very good", "very productive" and "they have another one scheduled in the very near future", Trump told reporters as he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Trump's announcement came just hours after he delivered a bellicose address to the UN in which he said he faced a "big decision" on whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".

articles.title: Pezeshkian to UN: Iran will never 'bend the knee' to 'US terror'
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone at the UN, vowing Iran would never “bend at the knee” to US pressure and accusing Washington of “terrorism” over the killing of former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei
US President Donald Trump said during a press conference at the United Nations General Assembly that US officials had a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials. For its part, Iranian state media confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US special envoy Steve Witkoff met in New York
The war in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government forces continues with no end in sight
Israel continues to attack Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any ceasefire agreements
And so we begin our live coverage of the day...
Libya's al-Menfi condemns exclusion of Palestinians at UNGA
Mohamed al-Menfi, head of Libya's Tripoli-based Presidential Council, told the UN General Assembly that the gathering comes as the world undergoes a “profound transformation” in the “balance of power” and the “ethics” surrounding its use.
Al-Menfi said one of the central challenges facing the international community was building an international order “in which the rule of law is an equal right, not a privilege of the most powerful”.
He also expressed regret over the absence of the Palestinian delegation, whose members were denied visas to attend the assembly, and praised Palestinians for remaining “steadfast” in the face of “oppression”.
“The plight of the Palestinian people continues to worsen after decades of occupation, repression,” he said. “Yet they remain steadfast in their adherence to their right to life and self-determination.”
Miliband: Leaders discuss Gaza aid and two-state solution
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has posted an update from the UN General Assembly, saying the leaders of the UK, France, Canada and Saudi Arabia had “brought together countries to discuss practical steps to improve humanitarian access in Gaza, support recovery and stand up for the two-state solution”.
“The global community will not be silent in standing up for peace and an end to this conflict”, Miliband wrote on X alongside a photograph of the meeting.
At UNGA @AndyBurnham, @EmmanuelMacron, @MarkJCarney and @FaisalbinFarhan brought together countries to discuss practical steps to improve humanitarian access in Gaza, support recovery and stand up for the two-state solution.
Iran's president struck a defiant tone at the UN on Wednesday where he spoke for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never "bend at the knee."
Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of "terrorism" for assassinating former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war.
He held up a photograph of the dead leader, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump had told the UN he was weighing whether to "annihilate" Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington's negotiators.
Pezeshkian made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech.
"(Trump) must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he said.
Pezeshkian insisted that Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz, which it has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war causing global energy prices to spike, to be used for aggression against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
Pezeshkian: Gaza shows resistance cannot be destroyed
Pezeshkian turned to Palestine in his UN General Assembly address, describing it as an issue that “remains an open wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza remains a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to prevent civilian suffering”.
Despite decades of UN resolutions, occupation and violence have continued, he said, arguing that for as long as occupation, aggression and injustice persist, “resistance will continue”.
“If it is weakened in one form, it will re-emerge in others, perhaps stronger still”.
“Gaza, despite relentless killing and widespread devastation, has strengthened the people’s faith in resistance, and resistance cannot be destroyed by bombs and siege; this is human nature”.
“If a human being is driven from his or her land, they will resist. If their homes are subjected to bombings and aggression and attacks, they will resist; what other choice do they have? Succumb to bullying? To be driven from their homes, from their lands, and remain silent in the face of these threats and dangers? And when they defend themselves, they’re labeled as terrorists” he said.
Iran's Pezeshkian says country defended itself with strength
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has begun addressing the UN General Assembly, saying his country defended itself "with utmost strength" after coming under attack by the US and Israel.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said, referring to attacks carried out by countries equipped with advanced weaponry and technology.
Iran's Rezaei says airports doing US sanctions 'won't work'
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said at the UN Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian after the far-right Colombian government last month recognised an illegal Israeli occupation over the strategically important territory.
The rest of the world does not recognise Israel's control over the Golan.
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories. Any other attempts will be thwarted according to Security Council Resolution 497," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
Iranian plane lands in China despite Washington's threats
A commercial plane belonging to the Iranian Mahan Airlines landed in China on Wednesday, despite the United States' threat to impose sanctions on anyone dealing with Iranian airlines.
The "Flight Radar 24" website, which tracks air traffic, reported that an Airbus A340 plane, which took off from Tehran, landed at approximately 16:40 local time (08:40 GMT) in the city of Canton in southern China.
This came in conjunction with the entry into force of a new package of severe US sanctions on the Iranian aviation sector, after Washington pledged to stop all Iranian airline companies from operating and punish any party that deals with them.
Settlement sanctions a start. Ending EU complicity is key
Sanctions by European nations are overdue, but ending complicity in Israel's occupation requires more than trade restrictions and diplomatic statements, writes Tamam Abusalama.
Oil prices fell and stock markets traded steadier Wednesday after recent volatility, as Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives met for "very good" talks at the United Nations.
The US president added that the three-hour meeting was "very productive" and that two countries "have another one scheduled in the very near future".
Brent North crude, the international benchmark, remained under $100 per barrel on hopes of diplomatic progress towards ending the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel noted that the UN "meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure (war) escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant".
Oil prices were dampened also by a report that the world's biggest crude exporter Saudi Arabia had rebooted operations along its East-West Pipeline, a crucial oil export route shut down by drone attacks.
Al-Masirah TV, affiliated with the Houthis, reported that Saudi aircraft launched about 15 strikes on Al-Hodeidah governorate and its districts, hitting communications towers in Al-Maraw’a and Al-Qatee’ and the Bajil Radio building.
According to the channel, Saudi aircraft targeted the Haydan district with missiles, renewing its missile bombardment on the Maran district.
Cargo vessel hit by unknown projectile in Hormuz, two hurt
UKMTO said it received a report of an incident in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday when a cargo vessel was struck by an unknown projectile, leaving it on fire and adrift, with all crew evacuated and two casualties reported.
UKMTO said authorities were investigating, and that there was no reported environmental impact.
Houthi-affiliated media on Wednesday said Saudi airstrikes killed 10 people and left 14 others wounded in Yemen's Taiz and Al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
"Eight civilians were killed and 11 others wounded in Taiz, while two civilians were killed and three others wounded in Al-Jawf," Al-Masirah TV channel said.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement staged a lightning offensive in recent weeks to gain control over the Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, while also aiming drone and missile strikes at Saudi Arabia.
The war in impoverished Yemen began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014. Since a four-year truce collapsed in July, fighting has killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.
Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday, Axios reported.
The 66-project proposal includes estimated spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, the report added, citing a copy of the plan.
The White House and US Department of State did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade, the Axios report added.
It also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects.
Israel continues to attack Gaza on a daily basis. [Getty[
A spokesperson for Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday Iran had maintained its negotiating stance in talks with US officials, demanding the United States end its blockade on Iranian ports and release Iran's frozen assets.
Esmail Baghaei said the indirect talks took place via Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
“This was not anything new,” Baghaei said of Iran’s conditions.
The unscheduled meeting—the first indirect talks between U.S. and Iranian officials since a June ceasefire unraveled—came as intermittent attacks continue in the Strait of Hormuz off Iran's coastline, where commercial shipping remains below prewar levels.
US senator calls Netanyahu 'chronic liar' ahead of UNGA
US Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen has condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a "chronic liar" and a "wanted war criminal" ahead of the Israeli leader's visit to the UN General Assembly.
"Netanyahu lies and lies and lies," Van Hollen said after Netanyahu released a video attacking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Van Hollen pointed to the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant for Netanyahu and accused his government of blocking accountability for American citizens killed in the occupied West Bank by Israeli settlers or security forces.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Van Hollen said Netanyahu's comments about Mamdani "don't change the fact" that he is "a wanted war criminal" who has blocked justice for Americans killed "on his watch".
"If anyone should be shamed & ashamed, it's Netanyahu," the senator added, saying the Israeli leader was "lucky he was even allowed into our country".
Prime Minister Netanyahu's lies about @NYCMayor don't change the fact that Netanyahu is a wanted war criminal who has blocked justice for Americans killed on his watch.
If there's anyone who should be shamed & ashamed, it's him.
An Israeli airstrike killed at least two Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday, local health officials said.
Medics said the two men were killed when an Israeli airstrike hit a vehicle in western Khan Younis, in the south of the enclave. Two other people were wounded, they added.
A spokesperson for the Israeli military confirmed the strike, saying it had struck a militant and that more information would be released later. No Palestinian militant group claimed the two dead men.
Palestinian authorities say more than 73,900 people have been killed by Israel's genocidal assault on Gaza since October 2023.
At least 1,400 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the alleged ceasefire took effect last October.
Which countries are banning Iran flights over US sanctions?
Several countries have begun restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on Wednesday.
The measures are beginning to disrupt international routes operated by Iranian carriers, with restrictions ranging from blanket bans to the suspension of individual airlines or destinations.
The New Arab's West Bank correspondent, Wahaj Bani Moufleh, reported a surge of Israeli settler attacks across the occupied territories.
Israeli settlers attacked a Palestinian home and smash a number of vehicles in al-Mazra'a al-Sharqiya village, northeast of Ramallah, as other settlers began to level Palestinian land in the Zabda area, Ramallah district.
Additionally, an armed settler raided the entrance to Jaba town, south of Jenin, as another group of settlers attacked the al-Hamma community, in the northern Jordan Valley, shooting at the cattle there.
Moreover, armed settlers attempted to raid the home of resident Mohammed Muslim in Khirbet al-Marajim, south of Nablus, as other settlers raided the Salayma neighborhood in Hebron city.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said he held talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on the sidelines of the UNGA.
"Dialogue and diplomacy remain the most effective path to contain tensions and prevent their escalation, and regional security and freedom of navigation require regional cooperation and responsible dialogue among the concerned parties," he wrote on X.
Iran: 50% of South Pars gas production capacity restored
Iran has restored about 50% of damaged production capacity at the South Pars gas field, Deputy Oil Minister Ahmad Zeraatkar was reported as saying on Wednesday by the semi-official Fars news agency, adding that all planned restoration work would be completed before winter.
Zeraatkar said in late August that about 40% of the damaged capacity had been returned to production.
Shipping traffic via Hormuz stays below 10-day average
Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.
The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage.
All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT.
One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data.
The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Israeli war on Iran began last February.
Macron calls Gaza a 'spectacle that shames us all'
French President Emmanuel Macron said that the situation in conflict-devastated Gaza was a "spectacle that shames us all" as he gave his last speech as France's leader to the UN's showpiece diplomatic week.
"What is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza? Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. It is a spectacle that shames us all," he said.

Andy Burnham, the U.K. prime minister, left, and Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine's president, with British and Ukrainian troops aboard HMS Queen Elizabeth at HM Naval Base in Portsmouth, UK, on July 27, 2026. (Andy Rain/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

articles.title: Russian military helicopter violates Polish airspace
articles.body:

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
This is a breaking news story and may be updated as further details emerge.
A Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace on Wednesday morning, the operational command of Poland’s armed forces has announced.
The incident is the latest in a series of airspace violations by Russia, which have also involved drones and, most recently, a missile. It follows recent warnings by the Polish government that Moscow has been planning further “provocations” intended to test NATO’s defences and unity.
❗️ Informujemy, że 23 września br. o godz. 11.08, na północ od miejscowości Braniewo, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia przestrzeni powietrznej Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej przez śmigłowiec Mi-8 Sił Zbrojnych Federacji Rosyjskiej.
Śmigłowiec wykonywał lot z Obwodu Królewieckiego.… pic.twitter.com/afULQdSeTc
— Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) September 23, 2026
On Wednesday afternoon, Polish operational command announced that, shortly after 11:00 a.m. that day, an Mi-8 helicopter belonging to the Russian armed forces had briefly entered Polish airspace near the town of Braniewo, after crossing from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
The helicopter did not travel further than 300 metres into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. In response, the Polish military scrambled fighter jets and placed ground forces on standby.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defences,” wrote operational command. At the time of writing, Russia has not commented on the incident.
Today’s violation appears to be the first publicly reported instance of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. Last year, in two separate incidents, a Russian Su-24 bomber and a naval helicopter flew over Poland’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea.
In 2023, two helicopters belonging to the armed forces of Belarus, a close ally of Russia, briefly entered Polish airspace before crossing back over the border.
On one night in September last year, around 20 Russian drones entered Poland over its eastern borders amid Russian attacks on Ukraine. Polish and allied forces shot down some of them, while others hit the ground without causing casulaties.
In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland.
The object that crashed in the Lublin region on Thursday was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a "significant amount" of explosive material.
The missile was "potentially very dangerous,” Poland's defence ministry confirmedhttps://t.co/NoqZwIcaWp
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026
In recent months, Poland and other NATO countries have been warning of Russian plans to carry out further “provocations” intended to test the alliance’s defences and unity, saying that they could include border and airspace violations.
In recent weeks, Poland has regularly intercepted Russian aircraft that have flown close to Polish territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. This month, Russian drones have repeatedly hit targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw.
Just last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
