The future of Artificial intelligence and the stalled US war against Iran, with its ripple effect on the global economy, are expected to dominate the UN gathering of world leaders Wednesday.
Following weeks of worldwide headlines about risks of uncontrollable AI – and calls for a slowdown – industry leaders are set to brief a UN Security Council emergency meeting convened by France.
Sam Altman of OpenAI, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face will brief the 15-strong Council, the United Nation's top body.
Hugging Face, a repository of AI models, was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software, the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology.
Meanwhile, the annual parade of UN General Assembly speeches is set to continue, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arriving late Tuesday, according to Iranian state media, to address the world body for the first time since the United States and Israel launched attacks on his country.
Read moreLive: Pezeshkian set to address UN for the first time since US, Israel launched Iran war
The strikes in late February sparked a war that engulfed the Middle East, and the Trump administration has so far yet to reach a deal with Tehran to end the conflict.
Tehran retaliated by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for energy transit, sparking a surge in global oil prices.
The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast has also heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Pezeshkian's speech will come a day after Trump raised the possibility that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" and "drive them into hell". During his remarks, all but one member of the Iranian delegation walked out.
Ukraine, AI showdown
Trump made the comments in a fire and brimstone speech Tuesday, but he also revealed that there were talks between the two sides for the first time in months.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Trump's roving envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner on the sidelines of the UN's signature diplomatic gathering.
Araghchi said that Tehran's demands included "the immediate lifting of the (US) naval blockade, the prompt payment of all Iranian assets that have been frozen, and an end to the war on all resistance fronts," state news agency IRIB reported.
Outside the UN on Tuesday, there was a vigil with protesters demonstrating against Tehran's use of the death penalty.
Besides conflict in the Middle East, Russia's war against Ukraine will again be raised among global diplomatic circles on Wednesday.
A Security Council meeting on Ukraine is scheduled for 11am (15:00 GMT), while President Volodymyr Zelensky is due to address the UN General Assembly as well.
Zelensky, after meeting with Trump on Tuesday, said that Washington and Kyiv want the war with Russia to end "before winter".
He added that he is ready to halt strikes on Russian energy sites if Moscow agreed to do the same.
In his speech Tuesday, Trump rejected international regulation of AI, calling such proposals a "globalist scheme".
"The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming ... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all," Trump said.
But just hours after Trump spoke, Macron took to the rostrum and defiantly called for the creation of an open-source AI model not dependent on the United States or China.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers," he said. "Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Trump says relations better with Burnham than Starmer after first face-to-face meeting
articles.body:
Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos Islands and the war in Iran.
At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.
Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran.
UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.
On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.
Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.
Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.
Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.
In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.
But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.
“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks.
In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.
“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.
But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.
However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.
UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.
But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”
Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.
In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.
Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.
“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.
Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

articles.title: Nuclear arms unlikely to be deployed in Lithuania soon despite parliament consent — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Nuclear weapons will not appear on Lithuanian territory in the near future, despite the decision by the Seimas (parliament) to lift the ban on their deployment, Ruslan Pankratov, a member of the Officers of Russia expert council, deputy chairman of the Union of Political Emigrants of Europe, and a former deputy of the Riga City Council has said.
On September 22, the Lithuanian Seimas approved lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons within the country. Following a discussion of the issue, the parliament referred a constitutional amendment to the relevant committees for review.
"There is a vast, if not enormous, gap between repealing Article 137 and the actual arrival of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian soil. Decisions to deploy nuclear warheads would require specific consent from the US and NATO, military infrastructure, specialized security and storage procedures, and would entail significant political costs," Pankratov said.
In his opinion, such decisions amount to an "ostentatious demonstration of Lithuania's readiness for the closest possible military-political integration with NATO."
Pankratov also emphasized that the practical value of deploying nuclear warheads in Lithuania for NATO is quite limited.
"The alliance is unlikely to rush the deployment of nuclear weapons right on the Russian and Belarusian borders, as this would sharply increase the risk of actual - rather than merely rhetorical - escalation for its domestic electorate," he explained.

articles.title: Zelensky says Kremlin planning new mass attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was planning a new major attack on his country, in comments published on Tuesday.
Zelensky, posting on Telegram about his meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, said Ukraine was in constant contact with its allies to secure new anti-aircraft defenses.
"There's intelligence right now that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine," Zelensky wrote.
He said that there could not possibly be any discussion of easing sanctions against Russia "when Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone attacks."
Russian forces have long unleashed large-scale overnight attacks by drones and missiles but have altered tactics in recent weeks, launching constant barrages throughout the day.
Russia is deploying new drones capable of evading air defenses
Moscow has also, in recent months, deployed jet-powered drones, which fly at higher altitudes and evade air defenses, disrupting businesses, government and ordinary life on a much bigger scale than previously in the 4-1/2-year-old war.
While in New York, Zelensky discussed efforts to end the war with US President Donald Trump, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.
Russian troops are advancing slowly through eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, but the front line has undergone little change in many months. Ukrainian forces now launch air strikes on Russian targets, many in the oil industry, at sites up to 3,000 km (1,800 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Interviewed in New York by the Wall Street Journal, Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin was neither winning nor losing the war, but did not feel compelled to hold direct negotiations on ending the conflict.
"The situation on the battlefield is not successful for Putin. He is not winning, it is true. And he is not losing, it is also true, because for him human losses are not to lose ... but his society is losing people," Zelensky said.
"He doesn't feel that he has to stop."

articles.title: ‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
articles.body:
‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
The European Union maintains a large sanctions list drawn up in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. It includes more than 3,000 people and companies. EU countries used to review the list every six months. On September 22, they agreed to extend it for a full three years, but with an important caveat: two billionaires with close ties to Russia, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, were removed from the list. Both men had long sought to have the sanctions lifted, both through European courts and other means. The final decision on their cases was political rather than judicial: Luxembourg intervened on behalf of Fridman, who has filed a lawsuit against the country for a huge sum, while France intervened for Usmanov and, in exchange, received a pardon for one of its citizens who had been convicted in Azerbaijan.
The lifting of European restrictions on Fridman and Usmanov has outraged figures in the Russian opposition in exile, Ukrainian officials, and some European politicians. Meduza has collected their reactions, presented here with minor cuts.
Russian opposition
Vladimir Kara-Murza
opposition politician
Shame on you [in the European Union].
Yulia Navalnaya
leader of the Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation
It turns out that for Europe, it doesn’t matter whether you support the war or not, or whether you’re friends with Putin or opposed to him. In the end, it seems, what matters far more is how much money is in your bank accounts.
If you’re rich, have a couple of yachts and the right connections, apparently your sanctions can be lifted without much trouble. But if you fled Russia with little more than a few belongings because of political persecution or the draft, because you don’t support the war, it’s a different story: you might be denied a visa, refused a bank account, faced with a mountain of obstacles, and effectively pushed back into the arms of Putin’s system. And accused of supporting the war on top of it.
Thanks to the European Commission for yet another reminder that in big politics, money still speaks louder than principles, and the fates of ordinary people often end up somewhere near the bottom of the list of priorities.
Leonid Volkov
head of political projects at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
On Fridman, this is simply a mistake. He hasn’t done anything, hasn’t changed anything, hasn’t even spoken up. Lifting his sanctions “just because” is foolish. Four years ago I proposed, and I still believe, that clear and transparent mechanisms should have been created for exiting sanctions for entrepreneurs like Fridman, in exchange for concrete steps to weaken Putin’s regime: everything from condemning the war to providing substantial help to Ukraine. That was entirely achievable, but it was never done.
On Usmanov, this isn’t just a mistake, it’s a moral catastrophe, and a double one at that. First, Usmanov is no “rank-and-file oligarch.” He is one of the key people in the system. And it’s not just that his personal kept man is former president and current drunken bully Medvedev, but also which assets Usmanov bought up on behalf of and at the direction of the Kremlin for censorship and lawlessness: from MegaFon to Kommersant. Remember: “I don’t use the internet, I develop it”? Well, Usmanov is one of the people who developed it into its current state.
Second, Usmanov achieved the lifting of sanctions through hostage-taking. Azerbaijani dictator Aliyev helped out as a friend, detained French citizens, and France came running to sort things out. Great! The path out of sanctions has been shown: expect new hostages!
In 2022, Leonid Volkov signed a letter to the European Commission asking that sanctions against Mikhail Fridman and other senior Alfa Group executives be lifted. The letter proposed that the EU adopt “a clear and simple set of criteria” for removing people from the sanctions list. “These criteria could be tied to a public condemnation of the war, compensation for damages, and severing ties with Putin and his regime,” the letter said.
The letter became public in 2023. Volkov called it his “major political mistake” and stepped down as head of the international Anti-Corruption Foundation, ACF International, though he remained one of its key figures.
Meduza wrote in detail about this story here.
Maria Pevchikh
former head of the investigations department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
What a colossal, planetary-scale disgrace this lifting of sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov is. As I said a couple of years ago, when I proposed trading yachts for political prisoners (which for some reason caused quite a scandal), if that isn’t done, the sanctions will simply be lifted for nothing. There will be no yachts and no political prisoners released. That is exactly what is happening now.
A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy. Some people, to get a measly work visa in Europe, have to bend over backwards proving they’re sufficiently anti-war, that none of their relatives, down to a seventh cousin, work for Putin’s regime, and produce stacks of convictions handed down in absentia in Russia. But these two assholes, pardon my language, haven’t said a single word against the war, and yet, please, come on in, cruise around on your yacht, live in your villas, no problem at all.
Vyacheslav Gimadi
head of the legal department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
Putin’s oligarchs Usmanov (against whom I won at the European Court of Human Rights over Navalny’s investigation into Medvedev’s corruption) and the no less notorious Fridman are being removed from EU sanctions. How could this happen? These decisions are made unanimously, meaning any of the 27 countries can block them regardless of the “interests of the majority.” That’s what the Hungarians, Austrians, and Slovaks did, and now apparently France too, from what I’ve read. This vulnerability and pliability, I believe, diminish the institution itself, since it encourages terrorists to pressure individual countries, or maybe even offer them [financial] incentives, though I have no proof of that, and to blackmail them. Other people on the list will surely want to follow the same successful path.
Ivan Zhdanov
former director of the Anti-Corruption Foundation
If the European Union adopts this decision (or has already adopted it), it will collapse the entire system of personal sanctions. Today I sent an urgent letter through whatever channels I had, describing Usmanov’s personal role in the persecution of Navalny and of me (my first criminal case was over Usmanov) and his funding of the warmonger Medvedev. A terrible injustice and an abandonment of its own values [on the part of the European Union].
Alexey Navalny had long been in conflict with Alisher Usmanov. Their dispute began in 2017, when the Anti-Corruption Foundation released an investigation titled On vam ne Dimon “He Is Not Dimon to You,” about Dmitry Medvedev’s alleged corruption. The film said that Usmanov had given a charitable foundation linked to Medvedev a mansion in the Rublyovka area. Navalny called this a bribe, and Usmanov sued him and won. The court ordered the film removed from all platforms, but Navalny and his associates never complied.
In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Anti-Corruption Foundation published a “list of corrupt officials and warmongers” naming 6,000 people. The foundation proposed adding them to Western sanctions lists for strengthening Putin’s regime and supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Usmanov, like Fridman, is on this list.
That history may explain why current and former Anti-Corruption Foundation representatives have been so vocal in criticizing the decision to lift sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov.
Ukrainian authorities
Volodymyr Zelensky
president of Ukraine
At a time when Russia is carrying out brutal attacks on our people – and even now, during the UN General Assembly, air raid alerts are ongoing in many regions because of drones and ballistic missiles – signals about lifting sanctions on individual Russian oligarchs are self-defeating and counterproductive. Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor’s entourage. I’m grateful to [European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen] for her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions lists. These are the kinds of steps that bring a just peace and guaranteed security closer.
Andrii Sybiha
foreign minister of Ukraine
The decision to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list is shameful and entirely unjustified. Moscow is celebrating, having gotten exactly what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the European Union, and a split among Europeans. I call on all EU member states to declare now that they will impose their own national sanctions against these two individuals.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk
Ukrainian presidential commissioner for sanctions policy
We consider the EU’s decision not to extend sanctions against Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman very strange. […] Lifting restrictions on individual Russian businessmen should not become a new practice. That is why we will keep proposing new sanctions measures, in particular regarding Russian oligarchs connected to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
European politicians
Pina Picierno
vice president of the European Parliament
The decision to delist Usmanov and Fridman is disgraceful, cowardly and completely unacceptable. But let’s be crystal clear about where political responsibility lies: with the Member States in the Council, not the Commission.
Under the EU treaties (such rules that must change!), the High Representative proposes sanctions, working with the Commission on their economic aspects. But restrictive measures can only be adopted unanimously by the Council.
This unanimity rule makes the EU fragile and weak. We need a politically strong, sovereign Europe: one that is more than the sum of its Member States.
Andris Kulbergs
head of Latvia’s government
Latvia agreed to a compromise but is not changing its principled stance.
We opposed the removal of Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the European Union’s sanctions list until the very end. […] However, the government had to make a responsible decision. The choice was between changing the status of two individuals and risking the loss of the entire sanctions regime. That is why Latvia’s representative will abstain in the vote. […]
Latvia is not backing down. The Foreign Ministry has been instructed to prepare the legal grounds for imposing national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman.
Mindaugas Sinkevičius
prime minister of Lithuania
Oligarchs are part of Russia’s war machine. The regime’s “wallets” must not be allowed to feel at ease in Europe while Ukrainians are being killed. I have instructed the relevant authorities to initiate the process for imposing national restrictive measures on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Margus Tsahkna
foreign minister of Estonia
The EU has just extended sanctions against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s aggression for another three years. This is a significant achievement, as it reduces the risk of future sanctions renewals becoming hostage to political bargaining.
However, to secure this agreement, sanctions against two prominent Russian businessmen, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, both known supporters of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, were lifted.
Estonia did not support this decision and abstained from the vote. We will now impose national sanctions on both individuals. Russia has not changed course. Neither should we.
Maciej Wąsik
member of the European Parliament from Poland
A compromising of the EU. Russian billionaires Usmanov and Fridman have been removed from the sanctions list. Only Latvia protested. Where was the Polish government? Where was the Polish protest?
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Baltic states try secret dip into EU defense purse – media
articles.body:
Baltic states try secret dip into EU defense purse – media
The Baltic states have secretly asked the European Commission for hundreds of millions of euros to boost their defense against drones, citing an alleged Russian threat, Lithuania’s Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told to Reuters on Wednesday.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it has aggressive designs against Europe, saying that they are only made by Western politicians to scare the population at home and justify growing military spending. It maintains that a conflict is only possible if NATO members attack Russia.
Finnish newspaper Iltalehti said on Tuesday, citing foreign policy and security sources, that the defense ministers of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had sent a letter to EU chief Ursula von der Leyen the previous day, asking Brussels to urgently provide them with €500 million (around $570 million). There has been no public announcement about the request being made, it added.
The minister claimed that the funds are needed due to the possibility of Russia trying to test NATO’s resolve by carrying out drone strikes against the bloc’s eastern flank, the report read.
Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius expect a positive response from von der Leyen in a matter of weeks, with the money arriving by the end of the year, according to the sources.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Russia could fire drones or missiles into NATO countries backing Ukraine in “the next few months.” Despite Tusk providing no proof to his claim, French President Emmanuel Macron described it as “sound and well-documented.”
On Tuesday, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius told the BBC that his country feels “constantly threatened” by Russia because of drones entering its airspace.
Since spring, there have been a number of incidents of Ukrainian UAVs crossing into Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia or crashing in their territory as Kiev has intensified its long-range attacks on energy infrastructure in Leningrad Region in northwestern Russia.
The Baltic states claimed that the incursions happened because of the UAVs being diverted off course by Russian electronic warfare equipment. Moscow has warned Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius that it could act in accordance with its right to self-defense if it turns out that the three countries are knowingly providing their airspace to the Ukrainian military.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics claimed in an interview with the Kiev Independent the same day that his country is facing an “alarming” period due to possible Russian interference in the wake of an election on October 3.
On Wednesday, high-ranking Estonian Foreign Ministry official Jonatan Vseviov said that warnings of an alleged Russian attack on the Baltic states were “blown out of proportion.” According to Vseviov, Moscow “ultimately seeks… to change the entire European security architecture,” but it’s currently fully focused on the Ukraine conflict.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that “some European leaders are openly declaring that they are preparing for war with Russia” in an attempt to “cover up mistakes in their economic and social policies.”
“Instead of stopping and listening to their citizens, who have made it clear during the elections that they don’t want any war with Russia, these leaders continue to escalate the situation,” Putin stressed.

articles.title: The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
articles.body:
The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
The inaugural summit of the new Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation format, initiated by Ukraine with EU support, took place on September 18-20. Leaders and representatives from eight countries in the Carpathian region were invited to discuss security, energy, logistics, and cross-border cooperation. The initiative – intended to unite nations, some of which do not officially supply weapons to Ukraine but wish to foster “good-neighborly relations” – has turned into a zero-sum game. Yielding no significant economic benefits and failing to address real economic challenges, it only serves to isolate the region from pan-continental logistics corridors.
Is the Carpathian Initiative a Ukrainian or European project?
The foundation for the Carpathian Initiative was laid by Ukraine back in 2001-2003, when it acted as the primary initiator and depositary of the Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians. Initially, the format was strictly environmental and conservation-oriented. Countries of the Visegrad Group, and primarily Poland, breathed geopolitical life and economic scale into the concept. For years, Warsaw actively advocated for the creation of a full-fledged EU Macro-Regional Strategy for the Carpathian Region (EUSCARP), aiming to transform the shared mountain range into a major logistics and infrastructure hub.
Over time, the EU fully took over this regional initiative, turning it into a systemic tool for the “soft integration” of Ukraine. After developing a strategic vision for the region in 2009 and adopting the Carpathian Roadmap in 2019, Brussels institutionalized the project in line with its own bureaucratic standards. What began as a modest environmental initiative has, through the efforts of European neighbors, transformed into a large-scale EU geopolitical project aimed at drawing Ukraine into the European orbit via infrastructure grants.
The September summit marked the latest stage of this project. Ukraine (backed by EU funding) attempted to reclaim its role as the primary “driving force” of the whole initiative by shifting the focus from environmental issues to matters essential for bolstering Ukraine’s influence on NATO’s eastern flank.
Ukraine’s autonomy is illusory, however. For the European Commission, the Carpathian region serves as a convenient geographic ‘sandbox’; the supranational bureaucracy seeks to bind the EU’s eastern fringes together through mutual dependency. Brussels’ ultimate goal is to dilute the agency and curb the independence of countries like Hungary and Slovakia, whose ‘Eastern’ initiatives – such as linking Central and Eastern Europe with Greater Eurasia – are gaining momentum. Ultimately, this measure would allow regional financial and other flows to be fully contained within the EU.
What’s wrong with the project, and why is it a zero-sum game?
Beneath the facade of discussions on “cross-border cooperation” set against the picturesque backdrop of the Ukrainian Carpathians lie pragmatic objectives that turn the Carpathian Eight into a classic zero-sum game. This is confirmed by the project’s geography: countries with the greatest interest in the initiative find themselves subordinate to those countries for whom the project is not a key priority. Ukraine’s actual geographic weight in the project is minimal; despite Kiev’s ambition to act as the main engine of regional integration, the Carpathians account for a mere 3.6% of Ukraine’s total territory. Ukraine possesses only 10% of the total area of the mountain range, yet it attempts to dictate the agenda to Romania and Slovakia, where the Carpathians form the backbone of national geography, covering 47% and 72% of the territory, respectively. Such evident disparity between Ukraine’s actual geographical “contribution” and its political ambitions sows the seeds of conflict within the project.
Moreover, the Carpathian macroregion is considered depressed and heterogeneous. Unlike the economically developed, navigable, and homogeneous Danube region – which served as a model for this project conceived by the Visegrad Group – the Carpathians are a patchwork of isolated mountainous areas. For centuries, this 190,000 sq km area has remained a remote periphery. Due to the highly underdeveloped infrastructure – the lack of modern roads, tunnels, and logistics hubs – the border regions of these eight countries have been trapped in a state of deprivation. In the past 25 years, no amount of targeted European funding has been able to rectify this situation. This should have compelled Brussels to step out of its comfort zone and realistically assess the physical boundaries of the region. This also explains why the Visegrad Group supports eastern initiatives in Greater Eurasia. However, instead of this, along with the economically unfeasible Three Seas Initiative and the “frontline zones” project, the Carpathians are being turned into another logistical dead end resembling an artificial buffer zone.
This perspective reveals the true purpose of the revived format: to serve as a covert logistical corridor for NATO. The projected budget of €9.4 billion ($10.7 billion) for 90 infrastructure projects is specifically aimed at modernizing narrow-gauge railways, bridges, and tunnels in the Carpathian Mountains. Under the guise of Euro-integration, Brussels is aggressively attempting to create a secure alternative route through the complex mountainous terrain for rapid deployment of heavy equipment, weapons, and NATO reserves, bypassing vulnerable border logistics nodes. Consequently, supranational strategists get to fully benefit from this venture while Central European countries bear all the attendant military and strategic risks.
Intrigues, scandals, and investigations
For the countries physically located in the Carpathians and those interested in developing the region, the hidden agenda of the initiative is apparent. Citing a sudden illness, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico canceled his visit to Bukovel and expressed his outright opposition to turning the region into a frontline zone and dragging Bratislava into the conflict under the guise of NATO obligations. As a result, Slovakia was represented at the summit only by the state secretary for foreign and European affairs. Local experts openly stated that Bratislava guessed the proposed zero-sum game: under the guise of cross-border corridors, Brussels and Kiev are attempting to establish a rear hub for supplying NATO’s eastern flank. For Slovakia, participating in such “road modernization” carries direct military risks, not security benefits. This forces the country to navigate a precarious line – seeking economic grants while sabotaging the military-political agenda of the proposed C8.
Following Slovakia, the Czech Republic demonstrated passive resistance to the project by adopting a stance of cautious pragmatism. Unlike Warsaw, Prague notably refrained from sending top officials to Bukovel, opting instead to send the vice-president of the senate. Czech economic analysts expressed doubt about the €40 billion investment portfolio announced by Kiev. The most important indicator of the failure of the “unified front” was that the Czech Republic effectively refused to sign the summit’s final declaration. As regional analysts point out, the country has “cooled” towards Ukraine’s ambitions. Moreover, unlike Ukraine, the Czech Republic has a realistic grasp of its geography; possessing only 8.5% of Carpathian territory, Prague saw no tangible economic benefit in a project burdened with militarization issues rather than cross-border development. Consequently, it chose to remain on the sidelines, unwilling to endorse someone else’s frontline agenda.
Predictably, only Poland and Romania expressed full and unconditional support for the project, emerging as the principal political beneficiaries of the initiative. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Romanian President Nicusor Dan signed the final declaration, explicitly linking it to military-strategic objectives. For Warsaw, the Carpathian Eight provided a convenient platform for lobbying an anti-ballistic missile defense coalition on NATO’s eastern flank, while for Bucharest, it offered a means to logistically connect the Ukrainian border with NATO’s largest European base, which is being constructed on Romanian territory. As a result, the document was signed only by those players intending to gain direct benefits from the region’s militarization, firmly establishing the C8 as a frontline coalition.
Hungary’s reaction is particularly noteworthy. On X, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar compared Kiev’s actions to village sports: “Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrey Sibiga, expressed surprise over Hungary’s attitude, but the situation is very clear and leaves no room for doubt.
Budapest was expected to sign the memorandum between its oil and gas company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz to establish joint strategic fuel reserves along the border. However, Magyar firmly blocked this initiative, fully aware of the risks involved in turning Hungary’s bordering territories with oil depots into targets for someone else’s military needs. Apparently, even Euro-Atlantic solidarity has its physical boundaries.
Moreover, Budapest’s negative stance is reinforced by the situation in Transcarpathia. From 2014, the Hungarian population in the region has decreased from 150,000 people to around 70,000-80,000 due to stringent Ukrainianization policies in schools. The remaining population is facing selective forced conscription, with military recruitment offices compiling lists of Hungarian students and workers to send to the front lines, resulting in several widely reported casualties, including the death of 45-year-old Jozsef Sebestyen. Notably, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry is closely monitoring these developments: mobilized residents of Transcarpathia occasionally end up as prisoners of war, and Russian diplomatic agencies, in coordination with intelligence services, work on their direct transfer to Hungary, bypassing Ukraine. Aware that Brussels and Kiev are attempting to exploit Hungarian resources and territory, Magyar chose to flip the script. Budapest refused to fund this military version of ‘Carpathian soccer’ which is too costly for it, and vetoed Ukraine’s integration efforts.
In summary, we must note that despite the ambitions of European supranational entities to create artificial buffer zones (essentially ‘sandboxes’) in Central and Eastern Europe, their era is coming to an end. Attempts to impose a zero-sum game on other countries only exacerbate the internal rift which is becoming inevitable, considering the region’s actual geography and the projects gaining momentum across Greater Eurasia.

articles.title: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.body:
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title: India's proposal under consideration for safe Black Sea shipping, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Picture credit: PTI)
India has emerged as one of the countries whose proposals are being considered for restoring safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Egypt, India and Turkey have outlined options for a maritime truce between Russia and Ukraine.Speaking to leaders at the United Nations on Wednesday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to support a maritime truce based on the proposals and that Russia now needed to respond.“We are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere,” Zelenskyy said.The remarks came at Ukraine's Crimean Platform summit on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, ahead of a UN Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.
India has been pushing for dialogue
The reference to India's role comes amid New Delhi's efforts to remain engaged with both Moscow and Kyiv and encourage an end to the conflict.External affairs minister S Jaishankar said earlier this month that India had been in continuous touch with both Ukraine and Russia and was exploring ideas that could contribute to mitigating and eventually ending the war.“What we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they will contribute to the mitigation, ideally, the cessation of the conflict,” Jaishankar said during his visit to Warsaw.
Jaishankar has also said India's position is that the conflict should end through dialogue and diplomacy.During his visit to Kyiv earlier this month, he met Zelenskyy and Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, with discussions including possible approaches to ending the conflict.“If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there,” Jaishankar said in Kyiv.
Black Sea shipping remains key concern
According to Reuters, Zelenskyy said Egypt, India and Turkey had proposed options to restore safe navigation for merchant vessels in the Black Sea, where cargo movements have been severely disrupted by attacks on ships and port infrastructure by both sides.Ukraine has been seeking ceasefires covering attacks on energy infrastructure as well as shipping in the Black Sea. Kyiv has also expressed concern that Russia could target power and heating facilities with missiles and drones during the winter.The disruption has also affected countries dependent on grain supplies from the Black Sea region. Reuters reported that wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East and Africa have faced difficulties securing supplies, while global wheat prices have risen.Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to ensure safe shipping and food security if Russia was prepared to take steps towards de-escalation.
Russia yet to back proposals
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said after meeting Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov on Wednesday that both Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy.
The Kremlin has not publicly backed the proposals.Ahead of the Rubio-Lavrov meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there were currently no grounds for broader peace talks, while maintaining that Russia remained open to negotiations.“For now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks,” Peskov said.Zelenskyy also said he was ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a trilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump.The latest developments come as India continues its diplomatic engagement with both sides.Jaishankar met US secretary of state Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday and discussed the Ukraine situation, as well as India's concerns over the US Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: We have intelligence that Russia is preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: We have intelligence that Russia is preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said during a conversation with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham that intelligence reports indicate Russia is preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media
Quote: "Our intelligence is now reporting that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine."
Details: Zelenskyy also said he had discussed "everything related to security", the protection of Ukrainians, preparations for winter and available diplomatic opportunities in detail with Burnham.
He added that there was "constant communication" with partners about finding additional means to strengthen Ukraine's air defence.
Quote: "When Ukrainians are living every day under the threat of missile and drone strikes, lifting sanctions is out of the question."
Previously: It was announced that the UK was providing £100 million (€116 million) for an air defence package for Ukraine ahead of winter, including Patriot missiles. The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, a US-NATO initiative under which European NATO allies purchase American weapons for Ukraine.
Background: Zelenskyy said that US President Donald Trump was positive about granting Ukraine licences to produce missiles for Patriot systems.

articles.title: Battlefield sees 247 Russian attacks, heaviest fighting on two fronts – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Battlefield sees 247 Russian attacks, heaviest fighting on two fronts – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 247 combat clashes occurred on the battlefield on 22 September.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 23 September
Details: The Russians launched a missile strike and carried out 87 airstrikes, dropping 309 guided aerial bombs. They deployed 9,377 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,693 assaults on settlements and Ukrainian troop positions, 34 of which involved multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Rocket Forces and Artillery units struck one Russian drone ground control station on 22 September.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, four Russian assaults were recorded over the past day. The Russians launched three airstrikes using six guided aerial bombs and conducted 149 attacks on Ukrainian troop positions and settlements, eight of which involved MLRS.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian forces repelled 14 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance near Starytsia, Hrafske and Lyman and towards the villages of Malyi Burluk, Putnykove and Radkivka.
On the Kupiansk front, Russian troops made one attempt to improve their positions by conducting an assault towards the village of Borova.
On the Lyman front, Ukrainian forces repelled Russian attempts to break through their defences. The Russians conducted three attacks near Novoselivka and Stavky.
On the Sloviansk front, Russian soldiers conducted two assaults near Kalenyky and Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians conducted one attack towards the village of Fedorivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 25 Russian attacks were recorded, according to updated information. The Russians conducted assaults near Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Rozkishne, Novopavlivka, Kucheriv Yar and Vilne.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 23 attacks, seeking to advance near Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Novohryshyne, Vodianske, Molodetske, Muravka, Myrne, Serhiivka, Novopidhorodnie and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, Russian forces conducted two assaults near Berezove and Solodke.
On the Huliaipole front, Russian troops attacked the positions of Ukrainian defenders four times, attempting to advance near Huliaipole, Charivne and Vozdvyzhivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made two attempts to improve their positions near Mali Shcherbaky and Mala Tokmachka.
