articles.title: Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Iran’s president Pezeshkian to address UN general assembly before Zelenskyy takes the stage - live
articles.body:
Iran’s president said his country’s people had been the “victims of terrorism” by the United States. Delivering a rare wartime speech at the UN General Assembly, Pezeshkian displayed images of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” Pezeshkian said at the General Assembly. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us.”
On the strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said: “We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways.”He also warns that any “expansion of warfare will not result in security.”
Argentine president Javier Milei attacked the UN in a speech to the world body, calling it a “useless organization” filled with “arrogant parasites.” The firebrand Milei, one of US president Donald Trump’s closest Latin American allies, has repeatedly used the UN platform to criticise global governance and its “woke” agenda.
Milei accused the United Nations of having failed in its duty to guarantee collective security and human rights, saying it had instead allowed “chaos, violence and international terrorism” to flourish. The UN, he said, “has become a useless organization, serving only to feed a caste of fatally arrogant parasites disguised as well-intentioned bureaucrats.”
The United States has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit of world leaders being held in Miami in December, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with, so we’ve invited president Putin to the G20.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said after meeting with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov that both Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy. “We would be open to playing a constructive role in making that happen,” he said, quoted by Reuters.
Paraguay’s president Santiago Pena called for Venezuela’s reintegration into the South American trade bloc Mercosur, speaking to world leaders at the UN General Assembly earlier today. Venezuela has been indefinitely suspended as a member of Mercosur, which comprises some of South America’s biggest economies, including Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Syria’s interim president harshly criticized Israel’s occupation of southern Syria and said the Golan Heights is an inseparable part of his country. In a speech to the UN General Assembly, Ahmad al-Sharaa said that Israel has carried out more than 500 air and artillery strikes on the country since he took power nearly two years ago. Israel has also carried out 1,200 land incursions and detained nearly 300 people, he said.
The Kremlin has responded to Andy Burnham’s speech at the UN general assembly, accusing the UK prime minister of “stoking anti-Russian sentiment”. Burnham told the UN yesterday that his government would set up a new national centre to tackle information attacks by foreign powers and singled out Russia over what he described as the spread of disinformation.
President of the Central African Republic, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, is now on the podium, speaking about the country’s ongoing sectarian conflict and political instability.
“A fragile country needs security for development,” he says, calling for international support. “Peace cannot be decreed, it must be built day after day through dialogue, justice and shared development.”
“Holding out your hand to yesterday’s opponent is not a sign of weakness”, he says.
He also warns about the worsening impacts due to the global climate crisis and calls for a greater role for women in public life to help end instability in the country.
Zelenskyy ends by describing Russia’s continued war as “madness”, urging global action to secure peace.
“Please, everyone here, don’t be the last to join those who defend life. Be the first to say ‘we guarantee security’. Thank you to everyone who helps and everyone who stands with us – with our people, with our children.”
Zelenskyy urges leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, telling the UN General Assembly that “Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”
“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he says.
'Ukraine did not choose this war': Zelenskyy addresses UN general assembly
Zelenskyy is using his appearance at the UN General Assembly to remind delegates of the scale and impact of the war on Ukraine, claiming that even a partial victory would not be enough for Vladimir Putin.
Putin will claim Donetsk isn’t enough for him, and will come for other Ukrainian cities, Zelenskyy says.
“Russia has used over 2,100 missiles against us. More than 950 of them were ballistic missiles.”
“They launch jet-powered Shahed [missiles] every hour… We are fighting them 24/7”.
He says this is “to make life harder for the economy and to disrupt our lives. They disrupt children at school. Would your country survive something like this?”
A reminder that Zelenskyy’s speech comes after he met with Donald Trump on the sidelines of the gathering in New York yesterday, after the US president insisted he was working with both sides to end the war, despite little evidence of Vladimir Putin being open to any settlement.
“It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” Trump said in his UN speech.
But Washington has since held separate talks with Moscow - and today said it had invited Putin to the G20 summit in Miami later this year.
Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, reasserted Israel’s claim to the occupied Golan Heights, in response to Syria’s interm president Ahmed al-Sharaa’s address to member nations earlier.
“But no speech will change reality, al-Jolani: the Golan Heights will always be part of Israel,” Danon wrote on X, using the nom de guerre al-Sharaa went by when he was HTS leader.
Al-Sharaa harshly criticized Israel’s occupation of southern Syria and said the Golan Heights is an inseparable part of his country.
In his speech, he said that Israel has carried out more than 500 air and artillery strikes on Syria since he took power nearly two years ago. Israel has also carried out 1,200 land incursions and detained nearly 300 people, he said.
He also repeatedly invoked UN security council resolution 497, adopted in 1981, which declared Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights “null and void and without international legal effect”.
Most of the Golan Heights plateau has been occupied by Israel since 1967. It was fully annexed in 1981, a move not recognised by most of the international community.
Cypriot president calls out Turkish 'hypocrisy' and urges Erdoğan to implement UN charter
Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, told member nations:
The international order is not simply changing. It is being tested in an unprecedented way.
But it is in such times of uncertainty that the fundamental values of multilateralism must be protected:
International law. The charter of the United Nations. Respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. The peaceful resolution of disputes. Respect for human rights. The equality of states.
In these rapidly changing times, he said, “the credibility of the UN must be preserved. And credibility requires consistency in the application of international law.”
Christodoulides said that 52 years since the illegal Turkish invasion of Cyprus:
More than a third of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus remains under Turkish occupation
Tens of thousands of displaced people and their descendants have been prevented from returning to their homes
Varosha has remained sealed off, with Turkey still defying its clear and specific obligations set out in the relevant UN security council resolutions
And “we have been experiencing violations of fundamental human rights, the destruction of religious and cultural heritage, and the organized transfer of settlers that constitutes demographic alteration”
“Respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity are not rhetorical figures,” he said. “Nor should they be applied selectively, depending on who the perpetrator is.”
UN Resolutions cannot be applied in one case and ignored in another.
And the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a state cannot depend on its size, its strength, or the passage of time.
This is not just an issue that concerns Cyprus.
It concerns the credibility of the international system itself.
Christodoulides said he listened carefully to Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s speech yesterday in which he spoke of international law, and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states, the illegal occupation, the refugees (in relation to Israel and Palestine).
“However, in relation to Cyprus, Turkey is doing the exact opposite. Maximum hypocrisy,” Christodoulides said.
Mr Erdoğan, if you wish to invoke the charter, you must first implement it.
I remain fully committed to achieving a comprehensive solution.
I am ready to resume negotiations from where they were interrupted in 2017, building on the substantial work that has already been accomplished, within the agreed United Nations framework.
He called on Erdoğan “to allow meaningful negotiations within the framework agreed upon by the UN” to find a solution “that will allow Greek Cypriots, Turkish Cypriots, Maronites, Armenians and Latins to live together in peace, security and prosperity.”
For my part, let me repeat, I am absolutely committed.
Because partition will not be accepted. This cannot and will not be the future of my homeland and my people. Never.Our determination to reunite our island is unwavering.
Iran’s president said his country’s people had been the “victims of terrorism” by the United States. Delivering a rare wartime speech at the UN General Assembly, Pezeshkian displayed images of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” Pezeshkian said at the General Assembly. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us.”
On the strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said: “We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways.”He also warns that any “expansion of warfare will not result in security.”
Argentine president Javier Milei attacked the UN in a speech to the world body, calling it a “useless organization” filled with “arrogant parasites.” The firebrand Milei, one of US president Donald Trump’s closest Latin American allies, has repeatedly used the UN platform to criticise global governance and its “woke” agenda.
Milei accused the United Nations of having failed in its duty to guarantee collective security and human rights, saying it had instead allowed “chaos, violence and international terrorism” to flourish. The UN, he said, “has become a useless organization, serving only to feed a caste of fatally arrogant parasites disguised as well-intentioned bureaucrats.”
The United States has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit of world leaders being held in Miami in December, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with, so we’ve invited president Putin to the G20.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said after meeting with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov that both Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy. “We would be open to playing a constructive role in making that happen,” he said, quoted by Reuters.
Paraguay’s president Santiago Pena called for Venezuela’s reintegration into the South American trade bloc Mercosur, speaking to world leaders at the UN General Assembly earlier today. Venezuela has been indefinitely suspended as a member of Mercosur, which comprises some of South America’s biggest economies, including Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Syria’s interim president harshly criticized Israel’s occupation of southern Syria and said the Golan Heights is an inseparable part of his country. In a speech to the UN General Assembly, Ahmad al-Sharaa said that Israel has carried out more than 500 air and artillery strikes on the country since he took power nearly two years ago. Israel has also carried out 1,200 land incursions and detained nearly 300 people, he said.
The Kremlin has responded to Andy Burnham’s speech at the UN general assembly, accusing the UK prime minister of “stoking anti-Russian sentiment”. Burnham told the UN yesterday that his government would set up a new national centre to tackle information attacks by foreign powers and singled out Russia over what he described as the spread of disinformation.
The United States has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit of world leaders being held in Miami in December, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said.
“In order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with, so we’ve invited president Putin to the G20.
“We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio said.

articles.title: Year ago, only 12 Ukrainian brigades could order weapons online. Now, 500 units participate in revolutionary program that has delivered 1.3 million drones to front
articles.body:
A year ago, 12 Ukrainian brigades could order their own weapons off a state marketplace. Now, more than 500 units can. DOT-Chain Defense, which lets frontline units order necessary supplies using state funds or bonuses with just a few clicks, has scaled across most of Ukraine's Defense Forces, the Defense Ministry said.
The platform is the delivery backbone of Ukraine's soldier-led procurement revolution. It lies in a shift in the philosophy of defense procurement. Ukraine is abandoning the Soviet principle of "fight with whatever is handed down from above" and transitioning to a market-based model that centers on the choice of the individual soldier.
Over its first year, it has put more than 1.3 million drones and other systems into units' hands, worth about $1.9 billion, and the orders show what this war runs on: 84 percent are drones, with electronic-warfare gear and ground robots making up most of the rest. It is also the engine behind the points-for-kills system that lets units bank credit for battlefield results and spend it on their own equipment.
Access jumps from 12 to 500 units
The growth has been steep. DOT-Chain Defense is now used by combat units across the armed forces, the National Guard, the border and special transport services, the police, the Security Service, and Defense Intelligence, says Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik.
Assault regiments and the "Drone Line" project have joined, ordering unmanned systems to their own specifications.
Drones dominate the orders
By the ministry's count, electronic-warfare systems make up 8.6 percent of everything ordered, ground robotic complexes 7.2 percent, and ammunition a sliver at 0.2 percent.
The gear, worth about $1.9 billion, came both through direct marketplace purchases and through the "Army of Drones. Bonus" program, the points system tied to the same platform.
The US copies the model
The approach has drawn imitators. The US has launched its own Amazon-style marketplace for military drones, explicitly modeled on Ukraine's Brave1 Market and DOT-Chain Defense. For Ukraine, the payoff is data: a running record of which weapons work on which part of the front, which the state uses to scale up what performs.

articles.title: Czech Republic expels Russians who were exposed filming for propaganda project Rybar, gives them three days to leave the country
articles.body:
Czech police have detained and questioned Russians Vitaliy Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom local journalists from the publication Seznam Zprávy had lured to a meeting in Prague that they secretly recorded. Chashchukhin and Dolmatov, who were working on behalf of the sanctioned Russian propaganda project Rybar, have now both been ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons, Seznam Zprávy reported on Sept. 22.
Czech police confirmed that procedural steps had been taken involving Chashchukhin but declined to disclose the outcome.
“We performed procedural acts with the mentioned person. Unfortunately, it is not possible to inform third parties about their result,” Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Police Presidium, told Seznam Zprávy.
According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, cameraman Igor Dolmatov received the same order to leave the country. The expulsion orders came after both of the Russians said during questioning that they worked for the Russian outlet Izvestia, a media organization that is also under European Union sanctions.
Filming organizer Boris Dvorkin, who was not physically present in Prague, told journalists that Chashchukhin was questioned for about nine hours.
“Vitaliy was interrogated by the Czech police for approximately nine hours. Subsequently, he was issued a document ordering him to leave the Czech Republic, after which he returned to Germany, where he legally resides. He obeyed this order,” Dvorkin said.
According to his own words during the hidden camera conversation he had with Czech journalists after his arrival in Prague, Chashchukhin has held permanent residency in Germany for about a decade and has performed work there for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline and argues that an end to arms supplies to Ukraine and a restoration of relations with Russia would remedy the situation. According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, Czech security agencies are continuing to review Chashchukhin’s activities and have already informed their German counterparts.
Meanwhile, André Lenz, a spokesperson for Germany’s General Customs Directorate, told journalists that it is impossible to determine in advance whether working as a journalist for a sanctioned Russian media outlet constitutes a crime.
“Specific facts indicating a possible violation of sanctions are carefully reviewed in all individual cases. The competent public prosecutor's office decides on the initiation of investigative proceedings,” Lenz explained.
Seznam Zprávy’s operation to lure in the propagandists to Prague
Seznam Zprávy published an investigation on Sept. 22 describing how its journalists set a trap for participants in Rybar’s European influence operation. Representatives of the sanctioned Russian project had approached Czech media literacy and disinformation expert Bohumil Kartous and asked him to give an interview for a documentary series about the political and economic situation in Europe. Kartous agreed, and the Czech journalists then arranged a hidden-camera recording.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov traveled from Berlin to Prague for the meeting. During the conversation, Chashchukhin acknowledged on hidden camera that: “It’s the Rybar project. You might know it. It’s Rybar.” Then, when Seznam Zprávy journalists approached, identified themselves, and began asking questions, both of the Russians ran off in different directions.
Journalists established that the filming was organized by Moscow-based documentary filmmaker Boris Dvorkin, who had not previously been publicly linked to Rybar. One of Dvorkin’s past projects was funded by the History of the Fatherland Foundation — an organization created by the decree of Vladimir Putin and chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
After the first investigation, Dvorkin claimed that Chashchukhin had only helped him with one interview in his spare time and had not been paid. However, journalists found that Rybar representatives had organized filming in other European countries and had tried to recruit politicians, experts, and public figures to take part as subjects.
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk is under European Union sanctions, and official documents state that he is a member of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers. In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about the project’s employees as part of an effort to combat Kremlin-backed influence operations.

articles.title: No pause in Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
articles.body:
No pause in Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
Moscow will not pause its special military operation while peace negotiations are underway, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday, asserting that a temporary ceasefire only benefits Kiev.
Ukraine and 51 of its allies released a statement on Wednesday demanding that Russia accept an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire” so that peace talks between Moscow and Kiev can take place. The statement, whose signatories included the EU and its member states, the UK, Canada, and Australia, was published before the security council met to discuss the conflict.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov said during the meeting. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
Kiev is “clearly and blatantly using terrorist methods,” Lavrov added, referring to Ukraine’s long-range strikes on civilian targets in Russia.
Ukraine and its allies issued their ceasefire demand less than four days after Ukrainian forces launched their largest-ever drone raid on the Russian capital. The attack killed two civilians in its suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the “unprecedented” raid involved more than 1,600 UAVs from all directions.
Throughout the conflict, Ukraine has repeatedly followed such attacks with appeals for ceasefire, which Russia has rebuffed. Moscow maintains that it will only cease military action when both sides seek a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict.
Russia has dramatically stepped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian military and dual-use infrastructure in recent months, in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day “influence campaign” of long-range strikes on civilian targets.
Zelensky’s stated aim was to foment discontent among the Russian public, but the campaign ultimately ended with the destruction of Ukraine’s Black Sea port infrastructure and an earlier-than-usual start to Russia’s winter campaign against its power plants and substations.
In a statement released after the latest drone raid on Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said that the Russian army would further “intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kiev” in response.

articles.title: US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
articles.body:
US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Iranian airlines are being cut off from international routes and airport services as Washington steps up pressure on the country’s aviation sector. Several regional connections have already been suspended or restricted, although some foreign flights continue, RT’s Saman Kojouri has reported from outside the Tehran headquarters of Mahan Air, one of Iran’s major carriers.
The US Treasury targeted 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month as part of a broader campaign against the country’s aviation sector. Foreign companies providing services to the carriers risk US secondary sanctions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the restrictions would effectively shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation from September 23.
”If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.
The impact is already spreading across the region, according to RT’s Kojouri. Azerbaijan has suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers, while Iraq has reportedly stopped accepting Iranian aircraft. Flights between Tehran and Muscat have also been suspended, while Georgia has said it will comply with sanctions affecting Iranian carriers.
Mahan Air is among the airlines facing the squeeze. Washington first sanctioned the carrier in 2011, accusing it of providing support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF). The Treasury has since targeted companies abroad accused of providing commercial and logistical support to the airline.
The aviation crackdown comes as Washington ramps up pressure on Tehran while simultaneously pursuing diplomatic contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. President Donald Trump threatened on Tuesday to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if negotiations fail, saying he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement and further military escalation.
Most of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall during Trump’s speech, leaving only one representative seated. The US president defended the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war and accused Tehran of pursuing nuclear weapons and supporting terrorism.
Despite the hostile rhetoric, indirect contacts continued later in the day. US envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had shuttled between the American and Iranian delegations during “lengthy talks,” while Tehran said it had used the channel to clearly convey its conditions to Washington, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

articles.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”.
Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president.
Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000.
President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO
— Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026
The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”.
On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage.
“The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.”
Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland.
Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president.
However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy.
On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location.
Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican.
💬Kiedy poznamy ostateczną decyzję w sprawie stałej bazy amerykańskiej w Polsce?
💬Jestem przekonany, że pan prezydent @realDonaldTrump będzie chciał zrobić wszystko, aby tak decyzja zachęcająca Polaków do głosowania na Republikanów mogła zapaść przed wyborami – Stanisław… pic.twitter.com/uPWkmdGQod
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”.
In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis.
The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level.
When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”.
💬Ilu w tej chwili w Polsce jest żołnierzy amerykańskich? Ilu będzie docelowo rotacyjnych żołnierzy i w stałej bazie?
Odpowiada Stanisław Wziątek @MON_GOV_PL w #RozmowaRMF o 7:00 w @Radio_RMF24@RMF24pl @Radio_RMF24 pic.twitter.com/1Zl66upkp8
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. In 2023, under President Joe Biden, it established its first permanent military garrison in Poland at Camp Kościuszko in the city of Poznań. The following year, a US missile defence base opened in Redzikowo on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.
This week, the mayor of Poznań, Jacek Jaśkowiak, told newspaper Fakt that his city was one of two locations being considered for the planned new US base. Recent Polish media reports have also identified the provinces of Lower Silesia and West Pomerania as potential locations.
While the Trump administration has chastised many NATO member states for failing to meet the alliance’s defence spending targets, it has hailed Poland, whose defence budget is one of NATO’s highest in relation to GDP, as a “model ally”.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Main image credit: Mikołaj Bujak/KPRP
Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Zelenskyy met with British Prime Minister Burnham and warned of Russia preparing a new massive attack
articles.body:
Zelenskyy met with British Prime Minister Burnham and warned of Russia preparing a new massive attack
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham discussed air defense, winter, energy, and sanctions. Intelligence reported that Russia was preparing an attack.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham, during which the parties discussed security, strengthening Ukrainian air defenses, preparations for winter, and sanctions pressure on Russia. Following the talks, Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian intelligence had information about Russia preparing a new massive attack, UNN reports.
Details
We discussed in detail with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham everything related to security, protecting our people, preparations for winter, and the diplomatic opportunities available. I thank the United Kingdom for its continued support for our energy sector. There is a new contribution, and we especially appreciate it as winter approaches
The President noted that Ukraine continues negotiations with its partners to obtain additional air defense systems.
Zelenskyy warned of a new massive attack
There is currently information from intelligence that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine
According to him, Ukraine and the United Kingdom also share a common position on the need to maintain sanctions pressure on Russia.
When Ukrainians live under the threat of missile and drone strikes every day, there can be no talk whatsoever of lifting sanctions. The Prime Minister and I have a shared position on this issue: as long as the war continues, sanctions must be maintained and strengthened

articles.title: Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
articles.body:
Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
Ukrinform reports this, citing the official Facebook page of the President of Ukraine.
“I discussed in detail with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham everything related to security, the protection of our people, preparations for winter, and available diplomatic opportunities. I thank the United Kingdom for its steadfast support for our energy sector. There is a new contribution, and we particularly value it as winter approaches,” the post says.
At the same time, the President added, Ukraine is in constant communication with its partners about finding additional air defense capabilities.
According to him, intelligence currently indicates that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine.
“When Ukrainians are living every day under the threat of missile and drone strikes, lifting sanctions is out of the question. The Prime Minister and I see this eye to eye: as long as the war continues, sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened,” Volodymyr Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticized the EU’s decision to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Belgium has received 3 more F-35s, bringing the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine closer
articles.body:
Belgium has received 3 more F-35s, bringing the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine closer
Kyiv • UNN
The number of Belgian F-35As has risen to 7. The country plans to transfer 53 F-16s to Ukraine, with the first of them potentially arriving in 2026.
Another 3 American fifth-generation F-35A fighter jets have arrived in Belgium, with which the country is gradually replacing its F-16s. The decommissioned F-16s are planned to be transferred to Ukraine, Defense Express reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The new aircraft landed at Florennes Air Base, bringing the number of F-35As based directly in Belgium to 7. A total of 15 such fighter jets have already been manufactured for the country, although 8 remain in the United States for pilot training.
Belgium ordered 34 F-35As back in 2018. The new fleet is planned to achieve full combat readiness in 2030, while the aircraft are expected to be ready to conduct rapid-response operations as early as 2027.
Belgium plans to transfer 53 F-16s to Ukraine
As F-35s are delivered, Belgium will gradually decommission its F-16 fighter jets and transfer them to Ukraine. According to the publication, the first 7 aircraft may arrive as early as 2026.
Overall, Belgium plans to keep the F-16s in service until 2028 and transfer 53 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
The Ukrainian Air Force is already operating F-16s received from other European partners. They are used, in particular, to strike ground targets and intercept Russian missiles and drones.

articles.title: Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
articles.body:
Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” Tuesday as he made his final address to the annual gathering of world leaders convening to face a formidable menu of challenges, from climate change and war to inequality and the rise of artificial intelligence.
In a no-nonsense farewell speech, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged global leaders Tuesday to respond to the defining challenge today: Will the world continue on its path to fragmentation, or cooperate to tackle the existential threats from climate crisis, runaway artificial intelligence and intensifying inequalities?
Read more'No peace without justice,' Macron tells UN General Assembly
The UN leader has long implored leaders not to give up on cooperation and shared decision-making in the face of accelerating global challenges and increasing great-powers competition. Tuesday’s message at the UN General Assembly took on additional urgency because he leaves office at the end of this year.
“The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing raging wars, rising temperatures and artificial intelligence, among other matters. Instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections”.
His speech opened the main portion of the world's biggest diplomatic meeting of the year. Leaders from the UN's 193 member countries address each other and the international community and air their hopes, plans and grievances.
Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognise “that their power isn’t so super”. Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said.
Yet about an hour after Guterres spoke, US President Donald Trump offered a different and equally frank view of power.
Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
“While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said, touting his country's economic, technological and military footprint.
He reiterated his view that the UN has “great potential” but rebuked it for what he called “imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”. He went on to criticise such bodies as the International Criminal Court, to which the US is not a party.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will be consumed with wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living?
The future of the United Nations itself will also be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. Member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the UN next. Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged. Guterres closed his speech by acknowledging the forthcoming departure and vowing to “never, ever give up” on the values for which the UN stands.
“Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible,” he said, before leaving the rostrum amid a sustained, standing ovation. He put his hand on his heart.
There is still no question that the UN remains the key gathering place for its member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly, along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners Tuesday: Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the US refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
Read moreUS again denies Palestinian leader visa for UN General Assembly
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said ahead of the gathering that it is “extremely critical” for world leaders to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet – especially at a time of such polarisation.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation”.
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in rocky shape.
“While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change," said former UN deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member.
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax”, and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
Read moreTrump calls concerns over rogue AI a 'hoax' promoted by a ‘sick conspiracy’
The UN Security Council added a meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
(FRANCE24 with AP)

articles.title: Türkiye follows Ukraine, adapts anti-tank missile against drones
articles.body:
- Roketsan's KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, following a pattern seen in Ukraine of anti-tank missiles adapted against drones.
- The Turkish Army has used KARAOK against ground targets since 2022, and Roketsan has not disclosed further details on the aerial test.
Roketsan, the Türkiye-based missile manufacturer, said its KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, firing the shoulder-launched weapon from a turret mounted on a light tactical vehicle. The company announced the milestone in a Sept. 23 post on X, along with footage showing the missile launching from a turreted mount on a pickup truck and intercepting a target drone built to mimic a Shahed-type one-way attack drone.
KARAOK is a man-portable, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile designed to be operated by a single soldier from a shoulder-fired tube. It weighs less than 16 kg (35 pounds) including its launch tube, measures 125 mm in diameter, and uses an imaging infrared seeker to track targets in day or night conditions, with an effective range beyond 2,500 meters. Mounting the missile on a vehicle-based turret lets it be aimed and fired without a soldier holding the launcher, a configuration more common among dedicated air-defense systems than infantry anti-tank weapons. Türkiye’s army has used KARAOK against ground targets since it entered service in 2022.
The test follows a pattern that has become common in Ukraine’s war with Russia, where anti-tank guided missiles built for armor have repeatedly been adapted to hit aerial targets, including the Shahed-type drones Russia has used extensively against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment demonstrated its Stugna-P anti-tank system shooting down a Russian drone on Sept. 13, and Ukrainian forces have separately built an improvised air-defense system called STASH that pairs U.S.-made AGM-114 Hellfire anti-tank missiles with a RADA radar to intercept jet-powered Shahed-type drones traveling too fast for interceptor drones to catch.
That overlap exists because many anti-tank guided missiles already carry the sensors needed to track a moving target and the terminal guidance to steer into it, qualities that work against a drone or slow cruise missile almost as well as against a tank. The U.S. Javelin was designed with some capability against slow, low-flying aircraft from the outset, and Hellfire missiles fired from Apache helicopters have long been used against aerial drones in addition to their primary anti-armor role.
KARAOK has also drawn interest beyond Türkiye. Malaysia signed a contract to become the system’s first foreign buyer, with Roketsan planning to deliver an initial batch of launchers and missiles to the Malaysian Armed Forces in early 2026 to replace the Russian-made Metis-M anti-tank system already in service there. Roketsan has not said whether the turreted, anti-drone configuration shown in this test will become a standard offering or remains experimental.

articles.title: Britain forms squadron to strike threats in orbit
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force is today forming No. III Space Effects Squadron, the first British unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in space, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The squadron is being announced by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, at the first UK Space Power Conference today, and will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the country depends on.
Sir Harv will say: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.”
The new unit completes a trio of squadrons, since No. I Space Operations Squadron gives the Royal Air Force the ability to watch what is happening in orbit and No. II Space Warning Squadron provides warning of threats, while according to the department No. III will act against those threats using advanced technology including electronic warfare. It will support both offensive and defensive space operations and is expected to expand as new capabilities enter service.
The department describes the formation as contributing to developing British capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons, and delivering the Control of Space Requirement set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month. That requirement covers maintaining freedom to operate in space while denying adversaries the same freedom.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, the kind that generates long-lived debris fields, and the department says it continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms and principles of responsible behaviour in orbit. The government describes itself as committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space while protecting critical infrastructure.
Alongside the announcement, the department restated an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and in space control activities.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily life, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, a trilateral programme with the United States and Australia whose British site is due to begin construction in April 2027 and which will provide continuous radar coverage of geostationary orbit.

articles.title: Britain prepares for war in space as threats grow
articles.body:
Britain is developing capabilities for what it explicitly describes as “orbital warfare”, including systems able to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity in space as the Armed Forces prepare for conflict extending beyond the Earth’s atmosphere.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, Chief of the Air Staff and professional head of the Royal Air Force, set out the direction of travel at the UK Space Power Conference in London, warning that adversaries are not waiting for Britain to complete its preparations.
The conference is delivered by UK Space Command and led in partnership with the Freeman Air & Space Institute. Its programme brings together senior figures from Defence, government, the UK Space Agency and allied military organisations.
Smyth said: “Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives, and our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them.”
He added: “We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace.”
The most direct indication of how far that effort is moving came when Smyth described the development of capabilities specifically intended for operations against hostile activity in orbit.
He said: “To help our nation fulfil the control of space requirement, UK Defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.”
Smyth defined this as “actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives”, alongside electronic warfare, systems intended to counter anti-satellite weapons and other supporting operations.
He said: “These capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure, and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.”
The language marks a shift from treating space primarily as a supporting domain for communications, navigation and surveillance towards preparing to contest it directly if necessary.
Smyth said the objective was to secure freedom of action for Britain and NATO while denying an adversary the same advantage.
He said: “Through a whole-of-government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests. We will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.”
That effort is being backed by several large investment lines. Smyth said £2.3 billion is being committed to satellite communications between now and 2030, alongside £880 million for space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and space control, and £440 million for novel space technology.
Skynet remains central to the military communications architecture. Smyth described the satellite system as the backbone of Britain’s sovereign global communications capability and said an additional £50 million had been allocated to extend the life of the existing Skynet 5 satellites.
Skynet 6A is due to join them next year, while allied and commercial satellite communications are also expected to provide additional capacity and resilience.
Britain is also expanding its ability to detect and understand activity in orbit. Smyth pointed to RAF Fylingdales, the planned Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability being developed with Australia and the United States, and a growing network of optical and commercial sensors feeding the National Space Operations Centre.
He said the Borealis command, control and data-processing system had reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule under a five-year, £65 million programme, giving commanders a better picture of activity in space.
The UK is also examining newer sensor technologies, including neuromorphic systems intended to search large areas of space for unexpected activity around satellites while using considerably less power and communications bandwidth.
Those surveillance systems are intended to support the wider military effort rather than operate in isolation. Smyth described space as the “connective tissue” of the integrated force, linking communications, surveillance and targeting systems across land, sea and air.
Space-based intelligence is also expected to feed the Digital Targeting Web, a £1.8 billion programme intended to connect sensors, commanders and weapons and reduce the time between detecting a target and acting against it.
Alongside the new technology, Defence is expanding the military organisation responsible for operating it. No. 1 Space Operations Squadron already supports activity through the National Space Operations Centre, while No. 2 Space Warning Squadron carries out operations associated with RAF Fylingdales.
A new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will provide personnel specifically for offensive and defensive space operations, with Smyth saying it will “disrupt, degrade, and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.”
Plans are also being developed for further numbered squadrons covering areas including tactics and training, the deep-space radar programme and space defence as part of a wider integrated air, space and missile defence structure.
Smyth was careful to frame the build-up as deterrence rather than an intention to initiate conflict.
He said: “No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.”
But he also made clear that Defence is preparing for the possibility that deterrence fails.
He concluded that Britain must be able to “monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and, if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.”

articles.title: 3 killed, over 40 injured as Russia, Ukraine trade accusations about overnight airstrikes
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
- Ukraine claims it shot down 122 drones launched by Moscow overnight
 
At least three people were killed and over 40 others were injured in Russia and Ukraine as both countries continued to trade accusations concerning overnight airstrikes on Wednesday.
 
In Ukraine, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said on Telegram that a warehouse, a fuel station, and an office building in the Holosiivskyi district and another fuel station in the Darnytskyi district were damaged in an overnight attack on the country’s capital, during which drone debris also fell at a location in the Solomianskyi district.
 
“As of 10 am (0700GMT), one person has died and seven others have been injured following a hostile attack on the capital,” it said.
 
*The KMVA later said that the number of those killed in the Ukrainian capital had risen to two, while 23 others were injured.
 
Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that one person was killed after Russian strikes targeted port and civilian infrastructure in the southern region, including an Antigua and Barbuda-flagged commercial cargo vessel and an unspecified number of warehouses.
 
“Due to numerous Russian attacks, rescuers from the Mykolaiv region have joined in the efforts to extinguish the fires,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said, commenting on strikes in the Odesa region.
 
The DSNS also reported that 12 others were injured due to strikes in the country’s Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions.
 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 122 Russian drones overnight.
 
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed hitting a storage facility and an industrial enterprise in Kyiv and its surrounding region that are allegedly involved in the production of drones and drone components.
 
It also claimed striking three logistics centers in Odesa used to supply Ukraine’s military, a drone warehouse in the Odesa region, and a vessel “while it was delivering military cargo to the port of Odesa.”
 
Earlier, the ministry further claimed that it shot down 514 drones launched by Ukraine overnight over 18 regions, as well as the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
 
Alexander Shuvaev, acting governor of Russia’s border region of Belgorod, said in a statement that eight people were wounded in five districts due to Ukrainian strikes over the past day, with two of them in serious condition.
 
In the border region of Bryansk, acting governor Yegor Kovalchuk said two people were injured due to Ukrainian drone strikes in the villages of Kryukov and Churovichi.
 
Ukrainian authorities have not yet commented on strikes in Russia.
 
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
 
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
articles.body:
Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
Vladimir Zelensky has attempted to blame New Delhi over the West’s failure to end the conflict in Ukraine, right after the Indian foreign minister discussed peace efforts and bilateral cooperation with his Ukrainian counterpart in New York.
”Russia is basing its economy on India, sometimes Turkey and China,” Zelensky said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader is in New York seeking more weapons and cash amid a $27 billion hole in Ukraine’s budget and a frontline collapse. The conflict is now in its fifth year, laying bare the West’s foreign policy failures, and Zelensky seemed to be making a case to US President Donald Trump to use his new sanctions authority to punish Russia’s trading partners.
But in India, the largest buyer of Russian oil besides China, the pitch has come across more as a call to punish New Delhi specifically.
Trump, who is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping soon in New York, would be loath to sanction China, especially after Beijing retaliated against earlier US tariffs with restrictions on exports of rare-earth metals and magnets that are crucial to US industries.
“Russia is basing its economy on India” and “ sometimes Turkey and China”. 
How can he make this ridiculous assertion?
China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy.
Turkey is very critical as a country for Russia. Russia and Turkey are connected by major… https://t.co/Jr7IsZzcOS
Russian oil accounted for about 45% of New Delhi’s crude imports in August, at around 2.1 million barrels per day. The numbers were slightly lower in September, tracking at about 1.9 million barrels per day, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler.
India has said it remains committed to securing energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people and will take the necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests amid repeated US tariff threats. New Delhi has also warned Washington of the sanctions impacting bilateral ties and global energy markets.
”This conflict … will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or alumina or minerals or metals or fertilizer,” Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar had said earlier this month in Kiev. He had discussed peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, and developments in the Black Sea, affecting markets with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha in New York just before Zelensky gave his interview.
Moscow’s oil revenue has increased amid the disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, but its non-energy trade with the Global South has also expanded.
Russia remains an important source of minerals and metals throughout the world amid supply chain disruptions. The US, too, has carved out exemptions for Russian uranium in the sanctions law it just passed.
Zelensky’s interview triggered some anger in Indian foreign policy circles. “How can he make this ridiculous assertion?” former Indian foreign secretary Kanwal Sybal posted on X. “China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy. Zelensky is targeting us openly.”

articles.title: Lukashenko will gladly let Putin use Belarus to attack Ukraine – Belarusian opposition leader
articles.body:
Lukashenko will gladly let Putin use Belarus to attack Ukraine – Belarusian opposition leader
Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya has warned of a real threat of increased Russian provocations against Ukraine from Belarusian territory.
Source: Tsikhanouskaya on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, as quoted by Ukrinform
Quote: "Of course, this is a real possibility. If Russia at some point again wants to attack Ukraine in any way from the northern border, then [self-proclaimed Belarusian President Alexander] Lukashenko will be very happy to provide territory, logistics, and Belarusian infrastructure to help [Russian leader Vladimir] Putin achieve his goals and intentions."
Details: Tsikhanouskaya said that hopes that Lukashenko can be distanced from Putin are futile.
"It is impossible because they have this special symbiotic friendship; they use each other, and they need each other," she explained.
She also pointed out that Belarusian infrastructure – "logistics and antennas for directing drones – is already being used, and at any moment, if the Kremlin needs it, Belarusian capabilities will be used".
According to Tsikhanouskaya, repeaters are being installed not only along the border with Ukraine but also along the border with European Union countries.
Quote: "So, the escalation or provocation may not only be against Ukraine but also against European countries. And, of course, we need to closely monitor what is happening in Belarus."
Details: Asked whether Lukashenko was acting out of fear of Putin, she answered in the affirmative, while stressing that this in no way justifies his policies.
Quote: "He has allowed Russia to penetrate our Belarusian system – the media, education, economy, and defence industry – meaning that he is allowing Russia to quietly occupy Belarus. Russification is being carried out intensively in our country – all of this with Lukashenko's consent."
Details: Tsikhanouskaya believes that Lukashenko is not interested in Ukraine's victory because Russia is his main ally and supports him economically and politically.
"He would, of course, like Russia to win," she stressed.
Lukashenko, in her view, "understands that Ukraine's victory would be a catastrophe for him personally, because a weakened Putin would mean less support for the regime in Belarus".
She also noted that Lukashenko benefits from the war, "making money from the blood of Ukrainians". She noted that 500-600 Belarusian companies produce optics and microchips, purchase various components for Russia's military machine while bypassing sanctions and supply Russia with petroleum products. In addition, the Belarusian regime is also building warehouses for Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries.
Background: At the beginning of September, Tsikhanouskaya said that Russia could use Belarusian territory and military infrastructure for provocations against NATO countries and further escalation of tensions.
