articles.title: Leader’s advisor: Iran fully prepared for defense; US aggression will bring heavy casualties
articles.body:
Leader’s advisor: Iran fully prepared for defense; US aggression will bring heavy casualties
TEHRAN – A senior military advisor to Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, says Iran’s armed forces are fully prepared to defend the country in every field, warning the United States would face heavy casualties in the event of any aggression.
“In the missile, air-defense, and territorial-defense sectors, we have reached a level where, God forbid, if they (American forces) intend to land anywhere in Iran, they will certainly be destroyed,” Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, said during a televised broadcast on Tuesday.
“We have at least 10 million trained Basij personnel, who can defend all parts of the country through a distributed, mosaic-style approach and asymmetric warfare,” he said.
“People are the main pillar of the Islamic Republic’s power and national security.”
Safavi, a former chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also pointed to Iran’s significant advances in missile, drone and air-defense capabilities, as well as its monitoring of foreign military activity in the region.
“In the maritime domain, whether in the skies over the Persian Gulf or even in the Indian Ocean, we detect with our radar systems the US naval vessels currently in the region…and determine where they are located,” he said.
Safavi said Iran could carry out both defensive and retaliatory operations, adding that the outcome of a conflict would also depend on the resilience and determination of the societies involved.
“What matters is whether their social resilience in the United States is greater than Iran’s. Iran’s is certainly greater. War is a battle of wills,” Safavi said.
“Iran knows its objectives and wants to defend itself, its national interests, and its dignity.”
Safavi’s remarks come amid heightened tensions over US military activity in the region. Iran has repeatedly emphasized deterrence and territorial defense, including the role of missile and drone capabilities and the mobilization of forces across the country.
The advisor also addressed the Strait of Hormuz, saying its reopening would depend, among other things, on the lifting of the United States’ illegal naval blockade.
“The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened through US military pressure. It is Iran and Oman that can establish the mechanism for this. We are in contact with the Omanis, although public reporting indicates that the United States is preventing this,” he said.
“The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is conditional on [the US’s] accepting Iran’s terms.”
The strait connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is a major route for international energy shipments. Its security and freedom of navigation have long been central issues in relations between Iran and the United States.
Safavi said Iran’s broader objective was to establish a Persian Gulf security framework with regional states, without US involvement.
“Our objective is to permanently remove the threat to the Iranian people and, together with the countries of the region, establish lasting security and sustainable development in the Persian Gulf without the presence of the United States,” he said.

articles.title: Taiwan to maintain 'close contact' with US on arms sales ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.body:
Taiwan will continue to keep in close touch with the US to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan, a defense ministry official said on Wednesday, ahead of a meeting between the US and Chinese leaders in Washington.
China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly demanded US arms sales end.
While US President Donald Trump approved an $11 billion package for Taiwan in December, the largest ever, he said in May after visiting Beijing that a second package, worth some $14 billion, was being kept in abeyance.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to press Trump to halt sales when the two of them meet in Washington this week.
Speaking to reporters in southern Taiwan's Tainan during a media trip, Taiwan defense ministry deputy spokesperson Chiao Fu-chun said maintaining security and stability in the Indo-Pacific region was a "common interest of democratic nations."
"The US government and Congress have repeatedly expressed their support for Taiwan's ability to defend itself," he added.
"Therefore, we will continue to maintain close contact with the US Department of War and continue to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan."
Taiwan's domestic weapons development
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te has embraced Trump's call for US allies to spend more on their defense.
While the US is Taiwan's most important arms supplier, Taipei has its own weapons development program, covering everything from submarines and fighter jets to long-range missiles.
Taiwan's army on Wednesday showed off its new eight-wheeled armored combat vehicle fitted with a 105mm gun, practicing live-fire exercises to demonstrate the domestically made weapon's fighting abilities.
The military also put on display, but did not fire, some of its US-made weapons, such as Lockheed Martin-made HIMARS rockets.
Taiwan routinely holds live-fire drills and takes reporters to military bases to watch exercises.
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, and its military operates around the island on an almost daily basis.
Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.

articles.title: Zelenskyy summed up what he managed to discuss with Trump and what the next steps will be to end the war with the Russian Federation
articles.body:
Zelenskyy summed up what he managed to discuss with Trump and what the next steps will be to end the war with the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine proposed an energy truce and called for China to be involved in pressuring Russia. Zelenskyy is also asking for Patriot missiles and a trilateral meeting.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the results of the talks with U.S. President Donald Trump and the next steps that could help end the war with the russian federation. These include an energy ceasefire, involving China in diplomatic efforts, strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, and a possible trilateral meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States, and the russian federation, reports UNN.
Details
President Trump, our teams, and I discussed how to end the war. This is a priority. We are ready. I am not sure whether russia is ready today, but in any case, we discussed an energy ceasefire
The President emphasized that Ukraine is ready for such a ceasefire provided that russian strikes on energy infrastructure, power grids, heating systems, and water-supply systems cease. According to him, the American side should convey this proposal to the russian federation.
Zelenskyy asked Trump to involve China
A separate topic was Trump’s upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelenskyy urged the U.S. president to use Beijing’s influence over russia.
I told the President very frankly that we believe that if he also involves President Xi, he has influence over Putin. If we want to end this war not only in words, then we all must work on it around the clock—for the sake of the people
The presidents also discussed Ukraine’s preparations for winter. Kyiv asked Washington to provide a winter package of missiles for Patriot systems and licenses to produce such missiles. Zelenskyy also emphasized the need for security guarantees for Ukraine.
In the Ukrainian president’s view, one of the key next steps could be a trilateral meeting of the leaders.
In my opinion, the most important step President Trump can take is to organize a trilateral meeting at which the leaders will be able to raise all sensitive issues and try to end the war

articles.title: Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Briefly Violates Polish Airspace, Poland Scrambles Fighters
articles.body:
A Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace on Wednesday, flying up to 300 meters (984 feet) into Polish territory near the town of Braniewo, Poland’s Operational Command said.
The helicopter entered Polish airspace from Russia’s Kaliningrad Oblast at 11:08 a.m. local time and remained there for 42 seconds, according to the statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Polish military radar systems detected the aircraft, prompting the scrambling of fighter jets. Ground-based air defense forces and other military assets were also placed on standby.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense,” the Operational Command said.
Polish air defense crews remain on round-the-clock watch, the command added.
Earlier incidents
The incident is the latest in a series of Russian military aircraft and drone incursions into Polish airspace since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On Feb. 11, 2025, a Russian Su-24MR military aircraft entered Polish airspace over the Gulf of Gdańsk, penetrating about 6.5 kilometers (4 miles) and remaining there for roughly 72 seconds. Russia later acknowledged the incident and attributed it to a navigation-system malfunction.
On April 25, 2025, a Russian military helicopter also entered Polish airspace over the Baltic Sea’s territorial waters. Poland said the incident appeared to be an attempt to test its air-defense readiness.
NATO Keeps Article 5 Trigger ‘Deliberately Ambiguous’
The most serious incident came on Sept. 9-10, 2025, when 19 Russian drones violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland scrambled fighter jets and subsequently requested NATO consultations under Article 4.
Most recently, Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine and increased military activity near its borders, although not every such incident has involved a violation of Polish airspace.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive near Lyman just got help from behind Russian lines: partisans say they cut rail supply to three Russian regiments, no explosion needed
articles.body:
Ukrainian partisans say they have sabotaged the railway signaling that keeps Russian troops supplied on the Lyman front. The ATESH movement reports that its agents disabled four relay cabinets on a line through Voronezh Oblast that carries military cargo to Russian forces there, delaying ammunition to three regiments.
The strike was timed to help Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the counteroffensive the Third Army Corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk. In its first phase, the operation cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and de-occupied another 10.
Cutting the rail line that feeds the Russian units facing that offensive is, by ATESH's account, part of the same fight, targeting the supply line rather than the front.
Four cabinets go dark
The sabotage hit a rail corridor running through the Voronezh, Novovoronezh, Liski, and Ostrogozhsk areas of Voronezh Oblast, a route ATESH says Russia uses to move military cargo toward the Lyman axis.
Relay cabinets house the switching gear that runs a line's automatic signals. Knocking them out can freeze traffic on a stretch of track without a single explosion, and ATESH says its agents disabled four of them. As with the movement's other claims, the account could not be independently verified.
Ammunition backs up
By ATESH's telling, the signaling failure delayed shipments of ammunition and engineering materiel to the 1st and 15th Guards regiments and the 254th Motor Rifle Regiment. Russian commanders, it said, had to rush in repair crews and divert resources to guard the infrastructure. A delayed shipment, far behind the front, can be felt at it, where an assaulted position waits for the ammunition that does not arrive.
ATESH hunts the supply lines
ATESH is a network of pro-Ukrainian agents operating inside Russia and Russian-occupied territory, and it has increasingly gone after the rail and power infrastructure that sustains Moscow's war. This month, the group also said it knocked out the power supply of a plant in Voronezh that makes components for Russian missiles.

articles.title: Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
articles.body:
Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
After a long pause, Russia’s authorities have renewed their campaign of nationalizing assets held by foreign companies — and they’ve gone big. On Thursday, Vladimir Putin issued a decree putting assets worth €6 billion under external management — specifically, the Russian divisions of retail chains Auchan and Leroy Merlin, food manufacturer Nestle and FM Logistics. Putin appointed an obscure company to manage them, with a former police general as its figurehead.
- Officially, the measure is not nationalization. Putin has imposed external management on the companies, not legally transferred their assets. This scheme was devised in 2023 and formed the basis by which Russia’s authorities seized hundreds of assets from Western owners — from energy firms to brewers and dairy companies. Foreign shareholders retain technical ownership but are stripped of all management rights (the right to repatriate profits was removed in 2022).
- Once a Russian asset is placed under external management, Western shareholders are often forced to sell to a Kremlin-backed owner, as in the case of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg. To complete the deals, Putin then suspends his own decree. But this is not always the case. Dozens of subsidiaries of Western companies have remained under external management for years.
- By default, Rosimushchestvo (the Federal Agency for State Property Management) takes charge of any assets that are put under local management by a presidential decree. But that route can be overruled. Often, assets are immediately acquired by a third party with the Kremlin's blessing. That is what is happening here. The Russian operations of Auchan, Nestle and FM Logistics went to a special purpose vehicle called LEV Management, a ready-made legal entity purchased by unknown individuals just before Putin issued his decree. The CEO is an obvious figurehead: Police Major General Andrei Krayushkin, who worked as deputy head of the Interior Ministry’s migration department in the late 2010s. Nobody has yet uncovered who is behind him.
- The Kremlin often justifies asset seizure on political grounds. For example, in 2023 many linked the decision to place Denmark’s Carlsberg under external management to Copenhagen’s willingness to supply F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine. Moscow views EU countries — and those in the “coalition of the willing” in particular — as its main opponents. With the exception of Switzerland’s Nestle, most of the affected companies are French. But why France has been singled out is unclear. Right now the Kremlin is in a bigger conflict with Germany, yet Metro Group, a German rival to Auchan, works without problem in Russia.
- Beyond politics, there are economic issues at play. First, amid fresh reports of a budget shortfall in Ukraine, plans to confiscate €200 billion of Russian reserves frozen in Europe since 2022 are back under discussion. This is a highly sensitive issue in Moscow, and all Russia has to threaten in return is the confiscation of foreign assets and funds already frozen in Russia. In this context, placing French companies with assets worth at least 600 million rubles (€6 billion) under external management looks like an attempt to gain a bargaining chip in the event of a future war of asset freezes.
- The Russian government’s own dire need for funds should not be overlooked. Over the first eight months of 2026, the budget deficit has already reached 2.5% of GDP. Placing a company under external management is not the same as nationalization. Russia does not have the right to sell Auchan and FM Logistics, nor plunder funds from their accounts to finance, for example, military expenses. But if Western countries move to confiscate Russian assets, this is the most likely next step.
Why the world should care
For whatever reason, the Russian government is reopening its battle with Western companies, in the biggest cases of de facto nationalization since 2024.

articles.title: Russian Mi-8 helicopter violates Polish airspace
articles.body:
Russian Mi-8 helicopter violates Polish airspace
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported on 23 September that a Russian Mi-8 helicopter had violated Polish airspace.
Source: a statement by the command, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Polish military said the violation occurred at 11:08 north of the town of Braniewo. "The helicopter was flying from Kaliningrad Oblast. It entered Polish airspace to a maximum depth of approximately 300 m and remained there for 42 seconds," the statement said.
The helicopter's flight was tracked by radar systems operated by the Polish Armed Forces. Fighter jets were scrambled, while ground forces and assets were placed on standby.
"The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence," the command added.
Polish air defence crews maintain round-the-clock surveillance and remain on constant standby to ensure the security of Polish airspace.
Background:
- On 15 September, an unidentified drone approached a US ballistic missile defence base in Redzikowo in Poland's Pomeranian Voivodeship.
- On 17 September, a Russian strike drone fell near the Polish border in Volyn Oblast.

articles.title: 51 Countries Issue Joint UN Statement Urging Russia to Accept Immediate Ceasefire as Sybiha Condemns Latest Strikes
articles.body:
Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations as large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine continue in the fifth year of war.
The statement was delivered during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York by Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, alongside Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, according to Democrata.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the decision in a statement on Telegram.
“We stand with Ukraine and support it in confronting Russian aggression,” the statement by the 51 UN member states read. “As early as March 2025, Ukraine agreed to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire. We call on Russia to finally do the same,” it continued.
Call for civilian returns
Russia was also urged to ensure the immediate, safe and unconditional return of Ukrainian civilians who have been illegally detained, forcibly transferred or deported.
Children have been particularly singled out.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale war in February 2022, Russian forces have killed at least 707 Ukrainian children and injured 2,548 others, while more than 2,318 minors remain officially classified as missing, according to official statistics released by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.
More Range, More Payload: Ukraine’s Race to Build Better Drone Batteries
The number of casualties and unlawful adoptions is believed to be much higher than the released information shows. However, verifying the true extent remains impossible due to lack of access to Russian-occupied territories.
Independent experts appointed under the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Moscow Mechanism presented their assessment to the OSCE Permanent Council in July, concluding that Russia has systematically militarized and indoctrinated Ukrainian children in violation of international humanitarian law using intimidation, coercion and other forms of violence.
Ukrainian authorities and international war crimes prosecutors continue gathering evidence on Russia’s crimes, with Kyiv repeatedly stating that the unconditional return of all displaced children must be a core part of any possible settlement.
Sybiha condemns latest strikes
The diplomatic support came as Ukraine faced renewed Russian attacks overnight and Wednesday morning.
At least two people were killed and more than 40 injured, while Russian strikes also targeted major Ukrainian data centers and a college building in Kyiv where students were present.
“While the 81st session of the UN General Assembly is focused on peace efforts and diplomacy to end the war, Ukraine is once again under a massive Russian attack,” Sybiha said, calling for stronger sanctions and more missile interceptors.
“These attacks must not become the new normal,” he added.
His remarks came as the EU extended sanctions on Russia for three years on Tuesday, after Latvia dropped its opposition to the new version that would delist two Russian oligarchs.
Black Sea crisis continues
The 51 states accused Russia of trying to impede Ukrainian grain exports, warning again that continued disruption in the Black Sea threatens global food security.
They endorsed efforts to safeguard freedom of navigation and protect commercial maritime traffic and infrastructure tied to shipping routes.
The concern follows months of intense reciprocal strikes between the two countries at war.
Civilian vessels, export terminals and other shipping infrastructure have been targeted, constraining shipments of grain, oil, fertilizers and other crucial commodities, creating a large disruption to the Black Sea trade.
Speaking during the sixth International Crimea Platform Summit earlier on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to support a safe-passage regime for vessels in the Black Sea, provided Russia took genuine and reciprocal steps toward de-escalation.
On Tuesday, during a meeting with US President Donald Trump, Zelensky offered Russia a truce on energy strikes.

articles.title: SSU detains Russian strike spotter on Sloviansk front
articles.body:
SSU detains Russian strike spotter on Sloviansk front
According to Ukrinform, the SSU reported this.
The investigation established that the spotter was a resident of a frontline settlement who had been recruited by Russian forces and was evading mobilization.
The Russian intelligence service took notice of him because of anti-Ukrainian comments he posted in chats on Telegram channels, while rarely leaving his home.
After being recruited, the suspect began discreetly questioning his wife about locations where Ukrainian troops were concentrated, which she might have seen while staying in Sloviansk and nearby areas.
He stored the information he gathered on his smartphone as approximate markers on Google Maps for subsequent reporting to his Russian handlers.
It was established that the agent was in contact with the Russian GRU through a liaison officer from the Joint Strategic Command of the Moscow Military District.
They used a popular messaging app with anonymous accounts to communicate.
SSU officers exposed the agent at an early stage of his work for the GRU, documented his espionage activities and detained him at his place of residence.
The suspect’s mobile phone and tablet containing evidence of his cooperation with the enemy were seized.
SSU investigators notified him that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Security Service of Ukraine recently exposed an electrician who had been directing Russian strikes against facilities in Dnipro.
Photo: SSU

articles.title: Sybiha calls for stronger sanctions pressure on Russia, more air defense systems amid attacks on Ukrainian data centers
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Russia is currently focusing its efforts on strikes against Ukrainian data centers, critical civilian infrastructure, and called for stronger sanctions pressure and more air defense systems.
“Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid warnings about missile and drone threats are crucial – they save lives,” he said in a post on X on Wednesday.
Sybiha stressed that “this is critical civilian infrastructure that provides people with access to life-saving information. It is not a military target. It is necessary for the normal functioning of everyday life.”
“As Russia fails to achieve its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians. Increasing sanctions pressure and the number of air defense systems is the only way to stop this terror. These attacks must not become the new normal,” Sybiha said.
The minister said that while the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is focused on peace efforts and diplomatic measures to end the war, Ukraine is again facing powerful Russian attacks. Two people were killed and more than 40 injured in the Russian strikes, which continued throughout the night and morning, he said. A university building in Kyiv was also hit while students were on campus.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts
Ukrainian forces struck a drone warehouse belonging to Russia’s Rubicon unmanned systems unit in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region, along with several UAV command posts and logistics facilities, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 23, the strikes were carried out on September 22 and overnight into September 23 against Russian military facilities across the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Ukrainian forces targeted Russian UAV command posts near Novoselivka Persha and Dachne in the Donetsk region. A separate strike hit a drone warehouse operated by the Rubicon unit near Volnovakha, according to the General Staff.
The operation also targeted Russian military logistics. A fuel and lubricants depot was struck near Kundriuche in the Luhansk region, while logistics warehouses were hit near Hirnyk and Velyka Shyshivka in the Donetsk region.
Near Krasnohorivka, Ukrainian forces also struck a concentration of personnel belonging to a Russian UAV unit, the General Staff said. The extent of the damage at the sites was not immediately disclosed.
Rubicon, formally known as Russia’s Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies, was established in August 2024 under the Russian Defense Ministry to centralize the development, testing, training, and battlefield deployment of unmanned systems. The unit operates FPV and fixed-wing drones and also maintains dedicated electronic warfare and counter-drone capabilities.
According to a June 2026 analysis by the Foreign Policy Research Institute, Rubicon expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to around 5,000 by spring 2026. Its combat detachments have been used to target Ukrainian drone crews and logistics networks behind the front line while testing new equipment and tactics for wider use by Russian forces.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian attack drone storage and launch site in the Oryol region, damaging five launchers and at least three storage facilities, according to Ukraine’s General Staff. The facility was reportedly used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones against Ukraine.

articles.title: Explosions, smoke reported near oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan
articles.body:
Drones reportedly struck an area near an oil refinery in the city of Ufa, the capital of Russia's Republic of Bashkortostan, on Sept. 23, Russian independent outlet Astra reported, citing local residents.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 514 drones overnight over 18 regions, including Bashkortostan, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
Local residents reported hearing explosions in Ufa, while local Telegram channels said air defenses were operating over the city, according to Astra.
Astra's OSINT analyst suggested that smoke rose in the area of the Ufa oil refinery, although the analyst said it could also have originated from a nearby thermal power plant.
A "drone threat" alert was also issued in Bashkortostan, while temporary restrictions were imposed on arrivals and departures at Ufa airport, according to Rosaviatsiya.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the accuracy of the report. Russian authorities had not commented on a drone attack on the region as of publication, and the Ukrainian military hadn't confirmed the strike.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone strategy, contributing to nationwide fuel shortages and sharply reducing refinery output over the summer.
Half of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries have cut or completely halted output in September following Ukrainian drone attacks.
As Ukraine continues to target Russian energy facilities, U.S. President Donald Trump has called for Kyiv to halt its strikes on oil refineries, claiming the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage as his war against Iran disrupts fuel supplies worldwide.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said on Sept. 13. "Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel."

articles.title: Witkoff, Kushner meet mediators as Iran sets demands for reopening Hormuz
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with mediators to discuss a possible deal to end the Iran conflict.
Trump told reporters at the United Nations that US officials had had a "very good" three-hour meeting on Tuesday with the Iranian delegation.
He said that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
"We are completely isolating Iran financially and simply applying pressure, because we hope they will do the right thing quickly-before it’s too late," Trump said. "You know, there will come a point when it’s too late, and we will no longer have the option of allowing them to survive as a nation."
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in a meeting during which Iran's conditions to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz were conveyed to the US, according to Iran's state media.
Iran sets Hormuz reopening conditions amid renewed US talks
Conditions for reopening the strait include immediate lifting of the naval blockade, immediate release of frozen Iranian assets and end of war across all 'resistance' fronts, state media added.
Trump's remarks came just hours after he repeated a threat at the UN General Assembly to annihilate Iran if it failed to strike a deal.
Speaking after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations in New York, Trump said: "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us; even today they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing.
"But we can't let them - and they understand that - we can't let them have a nuclear weapon."
Trump meets with Middle East partners
US President Donald Trump also met with Middle Eastern leaders on the sidelines of the UN to discuss bringing an end to the war in Gaza and addressing tensions with Iran.
During the meeting, Trump commended the US and its partners' efforts in the region and praised the participating nations for their regional cooperation, crediting them with successfully delivering humanitarian aid to Gaza and securing the release of hostages held there.
Trump said the nations represented at the meeting "invested billions of dollars in helping Gaza - in helping the people."
"The people around this table made that possible," he added.
Referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Trump stated that he's a "tough cookie, don't mess around with him, he's tough, he's a fantastic guy."
Trump also warned Iran in his speech to "do the right thing fast before it's too late."

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
Kyiv • UNN
During the night of September 23, Russia launched 161 drones at Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense shot down or suppressed 122 targets.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones during the night of September 23; 122 of them were shot down or suppressed, including three "Banderols." UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force.
What Russia used to strike and where from
According to the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force, during the night of September 23 (starting at 18:00 on September 22), the enemy attacked with 161 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones, launched from the following areas: Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Millerovo—in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and Hvardiiske—the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were destroyed by air defense
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had shot down/suppressed 119 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, drones of other types, and three "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones,
Hits by the enemy’s means of air attack were recorded at 18 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at eight locations.
The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: When Kremlin energy talking points come with an Oxford address
articles.body:
We have come to know the Kremlin's energy playbook well: "Europe will freeze without Russian gas," "sanctions hurt Europe more than Russia," "a managed, indefinite return to Russian supply is simply pragmatic." The respected European project EUvsDisinfo has repeatedly exposed these false narratives, carried by Russian state media, proxy outlets, and paid commentators. But Kremlin-friendly energy narratives do not travel only through obvious propaganda channels. They also enter policy debate through expert commentary, think tanks, media quotes, and institutional platforms, where they are far harder to see.
None of the apocalyptic forecasts came true. Europe cut Russian gas imports from 45% in 2021 to 13% by 2025 without blackouts or economic collapse. Yet the narratives predicting ruin kept circulating, sometimes from unexpected addresses. One of them, in my view, is worth a closer look: the work of Katja Yafimava, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
Across nearly two decades, her analysis has landed with remarkable consistency exactly where Gazprom would want it, the same firm whose money once helped fund her program. The record is public, and it is worth reading in full.
The narrative you don't notice
The most effective version of Kremlin-friendly energy messaging does not shout. It hedges, reframes, and omits. It raises "legitimate concerns" about sanctions costs, stresses the "legal complexities" of an LNG ban, and warns of "supply disruption risks" from moving too fast, without weighing Ukrainian lives or the cheaper, homegrown clean-energy alternative. Real concerns about European energy security did exist. What is worth noting is how reliably certain voices amplified concerns and how rarely they weighed counter-evidence.
This is not abstract. Surging oil and gas prices since the Iran war have handed Russia windfall revenues averaging, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, €604 million a day, money that funds the missiles falling on Ukrainian cities. Every argument for delay has a price, and Ukrainians pay part of it.
The Oxford label, and the money behind it
Katja Yafimava is a Senior Research Fellow at the OIES, which she joined in 2006. The institute is not part of the University of Oxford, though it carries the Oxford name, and its researchers appear regularly as authoritative, independent voices in UK and European media.
That independence has been questioned. Democracy for Sale, an investigative outlet, has documented the proximity between Russian oil and gas industry money and OIES, which previously received funding from Gazprom and its subsidiaries. The OIES Gas Program, where Yafimava works, was sponsored before the 2022 sanctions by Gazprom Marketing & Trading and by Nord Stream consortium partners, including Shell, OMV, Wintershall Dea, Uniper, and Engie. Gazprom Marketing & Trading and other firms with Russian business, such as Fluxys and TotalEnergies, appear as former benefactors in OIES annual reports up to the 2024 edition.
None of that, on its own, tells you what any individual researcher believes. What makes it worth raising is the alignment between that funding context and a published record that, across nearly two decades, has been remarkably convenient for Gazprom's positions.
Remarkable consistency
Consider the pattern. In 2017, Yafimava characterized EU and Polish legal objections to Gazprom's full access to the OPAL pipeline as an illogical obstruction driven by politics, language that would sit comfortably in Gazprom's own filings. In 2019, she framed the EU's Gas Directive amendment as an instrument "aimed primarily at Nord Stream 2." Russian state media have quoted her approvingly in pieces casting Brussels or Washington as acting in bad faith.
In 2021, she told Bloomberg the United States could not stop Nord Stream 2, a message Kremlin-controlled media amplified as proof of inevitability. In late 2021, as evidence mounted that Gazprom was deliberately withholding supply to squeeze Europe before the invasion, she described the company's conduct as "sensible, pragmatic behavior," at the very moment the IEA and EU lawmakers were pointing to deliberate "artificial tightness."
Each judgment is defensible in isolation. It is the direction of the whole series that is striking: over years and across cases, the analysis lands where Gazprom would want it to land.
The pattern holds as the war grinds on
Through 2022 and 2023, Yafimava warned that cutting Russian gas too fast risked "unavoidable" blackouts in Central and Eastern Europe. The blackouts never came. In 2025, she argued that REPowerEU created dangerous legal traps for importers and advised against a Russian gas phase-out, while a competing Forum Energii report concluded that full EU independence from Russian fuel by 2027 is feasible, and that Russia needs EU markets more than the EU needs Russian supply. In early 2026, she wrote that no complete phase-out "will happen either by 2027 or by 2028."
A forecast is not a crime. But the forecasts, like the analyses, keep pointing one way.
She has also stepped beyond technical commentary. In January 2025, she posted that peace in Ukraine "could only be achieved via a common European security architecture that would have to include Russia," a framing that mirrors a longstanding Kremlin strategic goal. And since March 2025, she has served as Vice-Chair of the UNECE Group of Experts on Gas, an agenda-setting role in a UN body that includes Russia. EUvsDisinfo has documented how the Kremlin uses UN platforms to lend its narratives multilateral legitimacy. A quieter UN gas group is a less visible version of the same channel, and quiet is what makes it effective.
The real question is why independent analysis, over nearly twenty years, has aligned so reliably with the interests of the company that once helped fund her program. That is a matter of record, and it deserves an answer.
Here is what the arguments for delay leave out: the alternative to Russian energy is not economic ruin. It is cheaper renewable power. The International Renewable Energy Agency found that in 2024, 91% of new renewable projects were cheaper than any fossil-fuel alternative; solar came in 41% below fossil power, and onshore wind 53% below. Renewables saved $467 billion in fossil-fuel costs in 2024 alone, and battery storage has fallen more than 93% in price since 2010.
This is the point that "supply disruption" warnings tend to bury, and it is why the warnings matter. Every year of delay, justified by the risks of moving too fast, is a year of continued payments to Moscow when a cheaper, domestic, un-weaponizable alternative already exists. Renewables reached 47% of the EU electricity mix in 2025; EU gas demand fell more than 17% between 2022 and early 2025; and the gas import ban agreed in December 2025 phases out Russian pipeline gas and LNG by the end of 2027, precisely the direction the delay arguments have worked against. The transition is not the risk. The delay is.
What should change
Editors, producers, and conference organizers could apply to energy analysts the conflict-of-interest standards already routine for pharmaceutical research: prior employment or program funding from Gazprom, Sberbank, or Russia-linked entities disclosed clearly every time such an analyst is presented as independent. UNECE could ask whether agenda-setting roles over European energy policy are well placed with analysts whose published record aligns so consistently with Kremlin positions. And Europe could close the transparency gaps that let think tanks with Russian-adjacent funding operate without disclosure requirements.
Every euro Russia earns from energy funds the war against Ukraine. The least we can do is know who is arguing for the payments to continue, and on whose past dime they built their expertise.

articles.title: At least 16 senior Russian officials have been killed after going to war in Ukraine, The Insider finds
articles.body:
At least 16 former and serving senior officials in Russia’s regional and municipal executive branches have been killed after going to war against Ukraine, The Insider has calculated based on data from open sources. The tally includes officials ranging from deputy heads of municipal districts or urban districts to deputy governors. Ten of the 16 had been convicted or were facing criminal cases before going to war, mostly on bribery and abuse-of-office charges.
The latest known case is that of former Belgorod mayor and Belgorod Region deputy governor Konstantin Polezhayev. The Kremlin-aligned media outlet Kommersant reported his death on Sept. 22, citing two people close to the former official. One said Polezhayev had served in an assault unit and was killed in a missile strike in the Kharkiv Region.
Polezhayev served as mayor of Belgorod from 2015 to 2019 before becoming a deputy governor. He was detained in 2023 on charges of bribery, with state investigators alleging that a construction company gave him two luxury SUVs, a Porsche Panamera, and a Range Rover worth a combined 18 million rubles ($214,000) in exchange for favorable treatment connected to government contracts. In August 2024, a court sentenced Polezhayev to five years in prison, after which he signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
In April 2025, the independent Belgorod-based outlet Pepel reported that Polezhayev was allegedly only formally listed with a BARS reserve unit and was in fact still living at home. It is not clear when he was actually first sent to the front.
The other casualties
Of the 16 cases of officials’ deaths identified by The Insider, three involved figures who had held positions at the deputy governor level. Sergei Efremov, who was then serving as deputy governor of Primorsky Krai, was killed in early 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region. He had overseen domestic policy in the region while also commanding the Tiger volunteer unit. Former Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug deputy governor Alexei Zolotukhin, who had been responsible for security in the regional government, volunteered for the war after leaving office and was killed in 2026. The third was Polezhayev.
The Insider found three more cases involving senior city officials. Former first deputy head of Yugorsk Dmitry Krylov signed a contract with the military and commanded an assault platoon before being killed in battles for Avdiivka in February 2024. Former Chelyabinsk Deputy Mayor Sergei Reprintsev went to war after being arrested in a 10 million-ruble ($119,000) bribery case and was killed in May 2025. Former Magnitogorsk Deputy Mayor Dmitry Gavrilov, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for bribery, also signed a contract with Russia’s MoD and was subsequently killed in Ukraine. His death became public only in September 2026.
Another 10 cases involved the heads and deputy heads of districts and urban districts. Igor Ustyuzhanin, the former head of Manturovo, was killed after going to war after receiving an 8.5-year prison sentence for corruption. The former head of the Ketovsky District in the Kurgan Region, Alexander Noskov, also joined the Russian army from prison, where he was serving a six-year sentence for abuse of office; he was killed in Ukraine in February 2024. The former head of the Tsimlyansky District in the Rostov Region, Vladimir Svetlichny, had been convicted of abuse and exceeding his authority; he was also killed after being deployed to the front.
Former first deputy head and acting head of the Kortkerossky District in the Komi Republic Alexander Arteyev, who had received an 11-year prison sentence for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of office, was killed in June 2024. The former head of the Perm Region’s Gornozavodsky District, Alexander Afanasyev, who was sentenced to three years for abuse of authority, signed a contract in December 2024 and was later killed. The former head of the Tselinny District in the Kurgan region, Alexander Sytov, was declared dead in summer 2026. Before the war, he had been sentenced to seven years in prison for bribery, fraud, and embezzlement, including the theft of 100,000 rubles ($1,200) collected for mobilized soldiers.
Fyodor Ivashchuk, head of the Ulchsky District in the Khabarovsk Region, resigned in March 2025, voluntarily signed a contract with the Russian army, and joined the BARS-8 Khabarovsk unit. He was killed that August while carrying out a combat mission. Aidar Zagirov, deputy head of the Uchalinsky District in Bashkortostan, was also serving under contract and was killed during a combat mission. The former deputy head of Novorossiysk’s intracity district, Oleg Skornyakov, signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense in spring 2025, went missing several months later, and was officially confirmed dead in March 2026.
Former deputy head of the Tugulymsky Urban District in the Sverdlovsk Region Sergei Utkin, who had been sentenced to eight years in prison for taking an especially large bribe, signed a contract with the Russian army while incarcerated and was also killed at the front.
Ten of the 16 were involved in criminal cases
Ten of the 16 officials The Insider identified had faced criminal prosecution before going to war. Nine — Polezhayev, Gavrilov, Ustyuzhanin, Noskov, Svetlichny, Arteyev, Afanasyev, Sytov and Utkin — had been convicted. Reprintsev was under investigation on charges of bribery when he signed his contract.
The Insider reported in 2024 that the war had allowed some former officials to leave prison or put criminal cases on hold, former Vladivostok Mayor Oleg Gumenyuk and former Khakassia Deputy Governor Sergei Novikov prominent among them. Some later returned to Russia after serving their allotted time in the military.
The tally does not, however, include former Krasnodar Region Deputy Governor Sergei Vlasov. Reports of his death surfaced in spring 2026, but Kommersant found that Vlasov was officially listed as missing and that his body had not been found.
The Insider also excluded judges, security officials, election commission members, heads of individual administrative departments, members of parliaments at all levels, and officials killed by shelling or mines while performing their civilian duties. The count includes only serving or former executive officials at the level of deputy district head or higher who entered military service or joined volunteer formations.
A broader count now includes at least 51 dead
If the count is expanded beyond senior executive officials, the number is significantly higher. In February 2025, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty counted at least 32 Russian government officials who had been killed in Ukraine. That category included election commission officials, members of parliament at various levels, and a federal judge in addition to government officials.
In June 2026, the independent outlet Meduza found open-source reports of at least 16 additional deaths that were published after RFE/RL had completed its project, bringing the minimum estimate to 48. Since the Meduza study was published, at least three more deaths have become publicly known: those of Alexander Sytov in July, Dmitry Gavrilov in September, and Konstantin Polezhayev on Sept. 22. Using the broader definition of “government representatives,” the minimum toll now stands at at least 51, according to The Insider’s calculations.

articles.title: Trump’s U.N. Address Offers a Doctrine of Peace Through Force
articles.body:
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump spun a familiar web of rhetoric regarding U.S. foreign policy—one that highlights force as a method of achieving peace.
In a speech that moved from Iran to Venezuela, Cuba, and beyond, Trump presented something approaching a foreign-policy doctrine: American military might is not the alternative to diplomacy but the leverage that makes it possible.
David Satterfield, Director of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, tells TIME that the speech Tuesday demonstrates a position held by the Trump Administration that “force is the only currency of value.”
“The strong do as they will and the weak suffer as they must,” he says, further characterizing the approach.
In Trump’s telling, strength is not merely a deterrent. It is something to be used—through military action and economic isolation—to force negotiations or impose an outcome.
How Trump defines ‘peace through strength’
Trump has repeatedly distilled his foreign policy strategy into three words: “peace through strength.” The examples he gave of this policy in action illustrate how he may see the U.S. functioning as a global enforcer going forward.
His definition of the phrase has previously been suggested by its use in Department of Defense ads and in his online endorsements of fellow Republicans. He recently credited this approach for the joint U.S.-Israel strikes that initiated the current conflict with Iran, posting to Truth Social in March: “PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH TO PUT IT MILDLY!!!”
Trump’s approach also encompasses economic coercion. In the case of Iran, he said the U.S. had initially offered economic cooperation, turned to military action when Tehran refused, and was now seeking its “complete economic isolation” to push it back toward negotiations.
Trump grouped Cuba among those affected by U.S. economic pressure campaigns on Tuesday. He described a government under mounting strain and predicted political change, declaring that Cuba was a “failed” nation but that “freedom will be coming.” Cuban delegates departed in protest.
Yet Trump presented such coercion as compatible with his role as a global peacemaker. He claimed credit for resolving eight wars since returning to office, although that claim has been widely disputed.
In tandem, these elements suggest that Trump sees taking action as a superior means of enacting change. He proposes the approaches as being almost diametrically opposed: While others only speak of making a difference, he acts.
“While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” Trump said in front of the General Assembly. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.”
Satterfield says that this speech is mostly “old wine rebottled” for Trump. But it clarified how the President is applying his longstanding ideas today: using military action and economic coercion not merely to deter adversaries, but to force negotiations and shape political outcomes.
Trump defends military force against Iran and drug cartels
While Trump sees Iran as an example of his “peace through strength” ethos, the conflict is ongoing, and it remains to be seen how it fits into the pattern that he is hoping to establish.
Addressing the topic seemed all but unavoidable heading into the General Assembly. In doing so, Trump said that he had a choice ahead of him: Move forward with a peace deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
The comments came amid stalled negotiations in the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Members of Iran’s delegation walked out during Trump’s remarks, an immediate demonstration of the gulf between his coercive message and the adversary that he may hope to persuade by it.
In his speech, he also issued threats against cartel leaders, defending his campaign of drone strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean. These strikes have been criticized by international organizations, legal experts, and human rights groups, which state that the military actions violate international law and constitute extrajudicial killings.
“The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere—not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
But while these messages are largely meant to promote the very strength that Trump relies upon in his endeavors, the potency of his remarks may be dwindling amid contested claims of success.
Venezuela is Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ model. But Iran is testing its limits
Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, tells TIME that Trump’s speech seems “consistent with the narrative of American dominance” that he has long used to justify military action.
Trump suggested Tuesday that he considers Venezuela a leading example. In January, the U.S. military launched Operation Absolute Resolve—a nighttime raid in Caracas that captured Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Both were transported to New York City to face federal drug-trafficking indictments.
The move paved the way for a transition of power in Venezuela, with former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez ascending to the role of acting President. It also led to an August agreement giving a U.S.-linked venture a controlling stake and long-term development rights in fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil. Trump said the deal “more than doubles” American oil reserves.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people,” Trump said in his speech. “Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously.”
Trump also suggested that U.S. actions had established peace and a route to prosperity for Venezuelans. However, with an acting President who is yet to be elected making deals that may take years to reach fruition, and are likely to draw legal challenges in the meantime, the full picture remains to be seen.
But there is one thing the Venezuela operation might have helped accomplish, which is to establish a potential pattern of a U.S. foreign policy that is defined by unilateral intervention. Following a large show of force, Trump has been quick to claim victory, even while the impact of U.S. involvement is still playing out for the people whom it directly affects.
Another example is the conflict between Israel and Hamas. In his remarks, Trump gave himself credit for ending the war in Gaza, even though key aspects of the peace deal Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’s disarmament, a long-term governance plan, and the delivery of needed humanitarian aid in Gaza—are largely stalled.
Perceived success in Venezuela “arguably triggered the overreach that we saw in the decision to begin military operations against Iran without a Plan B if initial objectives were not achieved,” Ulrichsen says.
But the limitations of such rhetoric are most “visible” in the Iran conflict, according to Ulrichsen, who says the U.S. has not been able to “translate rhetoric into gains on the ground.”
Trump has repeatedly predicted that the war would end after the November midterm elections, saying last week that it would end “immediately after” them. He endorsed this belief on Tuesday, as well. Trump initially told reporters that U.S. envoys had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with “mediators of Iran."
“They had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out. But certainly, it's to their advantage to make a deal, and we can do that,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior nonresident fellow at the Center for International Policy, emphasized the point that concrete outcomes in the Middle East may prove critical for Trump.
“President Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ approach has yet to produce the agreement he wants with Iran,” Mortazavi says. “Trump’s argument leaves a central question unanswered: How does further destruction secure an agreement on Washington’s terms when the pressure so far has not?”
“For now, Trump can point to the damage U.S. forces have inflicted, but the war’s central political disputes remain unresolved,” she adds.
The outcomes of these most recent efforts—and whether they moved the needle on peace efforts—remain undetermined. Subsequently, Trump turned to the same takeaway that he shared in his speech, which is that Iran is facing either “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“It does seem as if such rhetoric is producing diminishing results as his tone gradually loses its shock value,” Ulrichsen observes.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: We are ready not to strike Russian energy facilities if they do not strike ours
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: We are ready not to strike Russian energy facilities if they do not strike ours
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US will convey Ukraine's proposal for an energy truce to Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy's press conference after his meeting with US President Donald Trump on 22 September
Quote: "We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire. We are ready for an energy ceasefire if they do not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating, and water supply.
This is our proposal. We are thankful to the American side. They will share it with the Russians. I don't know the Russian position."
Details: Zelenskyy added that he is grateful to the US side for conveying this proposal to Russia.
He also expressed hope that the US will find a way to bring Russia and Ukraine to negotiations.
He said he had discussed the winter with his US counterpart Donald Trump, including a package of missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
According to Zelenskyy, nobody said no when asked about supplying Ukraine with the missiles, but there was no specific answer.
Zelenskyy also said that Trump had not asked Ukraine to unilaterally stop strikes on Russia. Instead, they had discussed an energy truce.
Zelenskyy believes Putin will tell everyone that he is ready to end the war before the elections. However, he said that after the elections, there will be attacks, with Putin then claiming that they had been carried out because of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy added that there had been an attack the previous night and that Ukrainian intelligence already knew that the Russians were saying it had supposedly been carried out because Ukraine had attacked during the elections.
Background: Before the conversation, US President Donald Trump said he would discuss with Zelenskyy the possibility of granting Ukraine licences to produce missiles for Patriot systems.

articles.title: Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
Poland deployed military aircraft, air defense systems, and electronic reconnaissance assets on September 23 in response to renewed Russian strikes on Ukraine, while airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command said military aviation had begun operating in Polish airspace as Russia carried out attacks against Ukraine using airborne weapons.
“In connection with the strikes by the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, carried out using airborne assault means, military aviation operations have commenced in Polish airspace,” the command said.
Polish authorities also activated the necessary air defense and equipment to protect the country’s airspace during the Russian attack.
The heightened military activity also affected civilian aviation. The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency reported that airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations to ensure military aircraft had sufficient freedom to operate.
Later, both airports resumed normal operations after the Polish military operation concluded.
The September 23 deployment follows a similar response less than a week earlier. On September 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russian drone strikes had taken place in Ukraine’s Volyn region near the Polish border.
Poland scrambled military aircraft in response, while operations at the same airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended.
The latest Polish response came as Russia launched another drone attack on Ukraine, including Kyiv. The September 23 strike on the Ukrainian capital killed at least one person and injured seven others, with strikes and falling debris reported across several districts, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Klitschko said one of the victims, who had been hospitalized in serious condition, later died from their injuries. Four other people remained hospitalized following the attack.

articles.title: Foreign volunteers retrain as drone operators as Ukraine’s battlefield changes
articles.body:
Four foreign volunteers serving in the Babai rifle battalion are training to operate FPV drones in Ternopil Oblast in western Ukraine, where they have formed a dedicated drone team, Suspilne reported on 22 September.
Ukraine's military increasingly looks to unmanned systems for roles traditionally carried out by soldiers. In May, an adviser to the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps said the corps planned to replace roughly 30% of its infantry with ground robotic systems by the end of 2026 "to save the lives of our soldiers." The plan concerns ground robots rather than FPV aircraft, but reflects the broader move toward using unmanned systems on the battlefield.
From mortars to FPV drones
The team was assembled by Harry, a British volunteer who has fought in Ukraine since arriving in March 2022. He served as a machine gunner in Kharkiv and during the Kharkiv counter-offensive, as well as in Bakhmut and Zaporizhzhia.
Before coming to Ukraine, Harry served with People's Defense forces against ISIS in Syria. He said Ukraine's battlefield is fundamentally different, with drones and artillery making combat more dangerous.
For Fuzzy, a former British Army infantryman and counterterrorism specialist, the transition came after more than two years as a mortar operator. He arrived in April 2022 and initially trained Ukrainian defenders before moving into combat roles.
Fuzzy said he had initially been reluctant to switch from mortars to FPVs but found the drones not as difficult to operate as he had expected after training for more than two months.
Not everyone on the team flies. Rupert, who served in the British and Israeli armies, called Ukraine the clearest case of right against wrong since 1939 and said anyone who does nothing will regret it. His role on the team is technical: setting up antennas and checking drones before flights. "The younger guys can fly," he said.
Mac, an American with no previous military service, joined the war in a different role. He arrived in February 2025 and served with the Azov brigade as a logistics specialist in Donbas. Ukraine first appeared on his radar with the 2014 Maidan protests, he said, and when Russia's full-scale invasion began—"seeing the massacre in Bucha, the maternity hospital blown up in Mariupol"—he called it a higher calling and began preparing to come.
Adapting to the battlefield
The volunteers came to Ukraine with different backgrounds and have taken different roles during the war. Harry assembled the FPV team from fighters he had served with in different Ukrainian units. Fuzzy said the changing nature of the war made the transition necessary.
"The war has changed so much that what I was teaching could no longer be applied everywhere," Fuzzy added. "At this stage of the war, we have to keep pace with the times—everything is improving now."
Harry said his long-term goal is to live permanently in Ukraine and open a business. "I see Ukraine as my home," he said. "I want to defend not just the Ukrainian people but also the place where I want to live the rest of my life."

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis to target US interests if supports Saudi strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis to target US interests if it supports Saudi-led strikes
A Houthi military adviser said that the group would attack US interests in the region if Washington intervenes in Yemen's war in support of Saudi Arabia or tries to unblock the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the narrow shipping lane, gateway to the Red Sea, this month, while Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested American and international military assistance against them.
"If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab al-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else... we will fight over it," military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday.
The Houthi blockade has shaken Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, which was already hit by Tehran's strangehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz as part of its war with the United States.
The pro-Iran Houthis dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen's Red Sea coast in fighting that left hundreds dead. Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh for the first time in years.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis, according to US reports. Yemen's government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.
'Iron fist'
"If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with airstrikes or air support... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything," Thawr told AFP, adding that they will "close Bab al-Mandeb completely to American ships".
While the Yemen war predates the US-Iran war by years, renewed fighting in Yemen pits allies of Washington and Tehran against each other while the two foes are stalemated in the Gulf.
Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they are "one alliance and one body".
"Iran is a friendly, allied, and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty," he said.
The United Nations on Tuesday said the number of people displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.
"As long as Saudi Arabia insists on and continues killing our country and striking our people, we will strike with an iron fist," Thawr said. "We possess sufficient capability to discipline Saudi Arabia, punish it, and force it out of the game in the fields of oil and the economy."

articles.title: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
articles.body:
Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”.
In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way.
Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point.
Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services.
Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks.
Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.”
He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!”
Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza.
Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.”
Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said.
Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said.
“Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Hit Major Ukrainian Manufacturers
articles.body:
Russian missile strikes on Tuesday hit the facility of Interpipe located in Dnipro, a leading manufacturer of steel pipes and railway products, and destroyed a warehouse in the Odesa region belonging to Snizhna Panda, a major tissue and toilet paper manufacturer.
A Russian missile strike overnight on Tuesday-Wednesday hit an Interpipe facility in Dnipro, resulting in four deaths and leaving seven others wounded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This marks yet another Russian strike since early August as part of a massive assault on Ukraine’s metallurgical and civilian retail sector. The ongoing attacks have forced the suspension of operations at plants that previously accounted for 90% of Ukraine’s steel output.
“Specialists are currently assessing the impact of the terrorist attack and the timeline for recovery, while also carrying out essential emergency repair work,” Interpipe said in a statement.
Interpipe reported a net profit of Hr.107.5 million ($2.6 million), up from Hr.59.8 million ($1.4 million) a year prior, despite revenue falling to Hr.7 billion ($168.1 million), according to financial statements published on the company’s website.
Snizhna Panda
On Tuesday, Russian forces also destroyed a warehouse belonging to the prominent paper products manufacturer Snizhna Panda.
“The most important thing is that people are alive and unharmed,” the company said on Facebook.
This marks the second attack on their facilities. On July 1, a Russian missile strike hit their warehouse containing paper and household chemicals that supplied various regions of Ukraine.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
“As a result of an enemy missile strike and a large-scale fire, part of our production and warehouse facilities were completely destroyed,” the company noted according to Forbes.ua.
According to the head of the Odesa Oblast Armed Forces, Oleh Kiper, two people were killed and 13 others were injured as a result of the attack, 11 of whom were hospitalized.
The company reported a revenue of Hr.846.2 million ($20.2 million) in 2025, with a 6.6% increase from the previous year. Net profit also grew slightly, reaching Hr.32 million ($764,800) compared to Hr.31 million in 2024, according to an Opendatabot report.
