articles.title: UK arms broker jailed for 16 years over Libya and Sudan deals
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK arms broker jailed for 16 years over missiles and fighter jet deals with Libya and Sudan
A British arms broker who arranged illegal deals to supply ex-Soviet surface-to-air missile systems to South Sudan and fighter jets to Libya during its civil war was on Wednesday jailed in a London court for 16 years.
David Greenhalgh, 68, was convicted in June of 10 counts of involvement in the unlicensed supply of arms, also including AK-47 rifles, battle tanks and hundreds of thousands of rounds of ammunition, between 2009 and 2016.
Greek national Christos Farmakis, 48, was convicted of nine offences, though he was tried in his absence and his current whereabouts is unknown.
Judge Sally-Ann Hales sentenced both men to 16 years' imprisonment, saying they repeatedly sought to breach arms export bans to sell weaponry for significant profits.
Prosecutors said only one charge involved the actual supply of weaponry, with the pair selling a former Ukrainian S-125 Pechora missile system to South Sudan, where Greenhalgh and Farmakis had "very close connections to senior figures."
South Sudan was still formally part of Sudan until it achieved independence in 2011, prosecutor Edmund Burge told jurors at Southwark Crown Court, meaning the semi-autonomous region was subject to a British arms embargo.
Greenhalgh and Farmakis also arranged to supply weapons to Iran, Iraq and Syria in breach of arms embargoes, before Farmakis was arrested in 2016.
Farmakis was caught after using his email address for his job at the government-funded Greater London Enterprise to privately arrange arms deals.
Burge said Farmakis' email account forwarded an email to his boss, which led to the authorities discovering documents relating to plans to sell fighter jets and other arms to Libya in the wake of the 2011 Arab Spring.

articles.title: Latvian trade mission begins in the United States, with meetings planned with global technology leaders
articles.body:
A Latvian business trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) has begun in the United States. Running alongside Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs’s working visit until 27 September, the mission covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. Its four sector programmes bring together representatives of start-ups, the film industry, defence and dual-use technology companies, and biomedical and pharmaceutical businesses.
“The United States is Latvia’s strategic partner and trusted ally, and this September marks 35 years since the restoration of diplomatic relations. Successful cooperation with US partners, including those in California, demonstrates the international competitiveness of Latvian companies. The delegation includes representatives of the defence and dual-use sectors, biomedicine, start-ups and the film industry. I hope this visit will help Latvian businesses establish valuable contacts in the United States and, in turn, support Latvia’s economic growth,” said President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
The first business meetings are taking place in New York and Los Angeles on Wednesday, 23 September. Over the following days, Latvian entrepreneurs will meet major US companies, investors, universities and technology transfer centres to pursue export deals, joint technology projects and investment partnerships.
“Trade between Latvia and the United States reached €1.63 billion in 2025, up 13% year on year. This is more than a strong statistical result: it is a foundation for much greater ambition. We need Latvian companies to enter US supply chains, become partners in joint product development, and attract US capital to new projects in Latvia. The United States is a strategically important economic and security partner for Latvia, and the President’s visit lends additional weight to these economic discussions. The goal is clear: new projects, orders and investment,” said Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Economics.
Three cities and four sector programmes
In New York, representatives of Latvia’s start-up ecosystem will meet US investors and representatives of ServiceNow, a global developer of enterprise AI and digital workflow platforms. Latvian start-ups will present their solutions at the “Pitch to a President” event, receiving feedback from US investors on their prospects in the market.
In Los Angeles, the film industry programme will begin with a meeting at Paramount. Separate programmes for Latvian defence and dual-use technology, biomedical and pharmaceutical companies are also scheduled in the city over the following days.
“Three cities, four sector programmes and dozens of carefully prepared meetings within just a few days make this one of LIAA’s largest and most complex trade missions. Its pace and scale match the ambitions of Latvian companies in the United States. Last year, Latvia’s services exports to the US rose by 10% to €510 million, with information and communications technology services accounting for more than 40% of the total. Latvian companies have the expertise and technology to sit at the same table as global leaders as equal partners. We will judge the mission’s results by the deals, joint technology projects and investments that follow these discussions,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Latvian delegation includes 44 companies and organisations
The trade mission includes 44 Latvian companies and organisations.
The defence and dual-use technology programme includes Aumeux, SAF North America, Origin Robotics, Raw-tech, SIA Ardlat, Perkons Energy, LMT, LMT Defence, VIC TEC and LAT Security, as well as the Latgale Special Economic Zone, the Latvian Exporters’ Association “The Red Jackets”, the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the University of Latvia and Riga Technical University.
The biomedical and pharmaceutical programme includes the National Research and Innovation Institute (NIRI), Double Helix Technologies, Rīga Stradiņš University, Riga East University Hospital, Daugavpils University and the University of Latvia.
The film industry programme includes Nafta Films, RED DOT MEDIA, Mistrus Media, Trickster Pictures, Baltic Pine Films, CINEVILLA FILMS, Ierakstu Māja and the Latvian Film Service Producers Association.
BDO Latvia and representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are also part of the trade mission delegation. The start-up programme includes BirdyChat, Monetizr, Engycell, Submerge, Spotwise, Supliful, Tournated, Capture Study, HoneyB AI, Cellbox and Crowdable.
Los Angeles: From film studios to autonomous defence systems
On 24 September, film industry participants are scheduled to visit the Warner Bros. and HBO studios and meet representatives of Disney and Netflix. Discussions will focus on Latvia’s capabilities in film production, post-production and animation, as well as opportunities for international co-productions.
Defence and dual-use technology companies will take part in a roundtable with representatives of Southern California’s defence industry and visit Anduril, a US defence technology company developing autonomous systems and AI-based solutions. Discussions will focus on using Latvian technology in joint solutions, developing new products and bringing Latvian companies into US supply chains.
Biomedical and pharmaceutical representatives will meet economic development and life sciences organisations in Los Angeles County. They will also visit the Technology Development Group at the University of California, Los Angeles, and the Office of Technology Transfer and Corporate Partnerships at the California Institute of Technology. Discussions with researchers and technology transfer specialists will cover the commercialisation of research, joint product development and cooperation between Latvian companies and US universities.
The day will conclude with a business event hosted by the US Ambassador to Latvia at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library, bringing together the Latvian delegation and representatives of the US business community.
San Diego: Semiconductors, unmanned systems and genomics
On 25 September, the defence and dual-use technology programme will continue in San Diego, a major US centre for defence, aviation and unmanned systems technology.
Latvian companies are scheduled to meet Shield AI, a developer of autonomous aircraft and AI pilot technology, and Kratos, a national security technology company active in unmanned systems, space, hypersonics and missile propulsion. Meetings are also planned with Qualcomm, a global communications, connectivity and semiconductor company; public safety technology company Axon; and Starling Systems.
Representatives of SAF Tehnika and Riga Technical University will meet senior executives at Analog Devices. The global semiconductor company has more than 100,000 customers and reported revenue of $11 billion in its 2025 fiscal year.
“SAF Tehnika regularly takes part in LIAA trade missions to the United States because they allow us to meet senior executives at partner and customer companies and strengthen our reputation with them. For example, during this September’s mission to California, we and Riga Technical University will meet the senior management of a major US semiconductor manufacturer. Opportunities like those offered by LIAA produce results only when a company has done its homework and can say precisely whom it wants to meet and what it hopes to achieve. If you don’t know where you’re going, any road will do,” said Jānis Bergs, Member of the Board and Vice President of Sales and Marketing at SAF Tehnika.
In San Diego, biomedical and pharmaceutical companies will meet Thermo Fisher Scientific, one of the world’s largest suppliers of laboratory, life sciences and pharmaceutical technologies, with annual revenue exceeding $45 billion. Meetings are also planned with Illumina, a leading developer of genomics and DNA sequencing technologies, and DNA sequencing technology company Element Biosciences.
The Latvian delegation will also visit the Technology Transfer Office at San Diego State University and the Office of Innovation and Commercialization at the University of California, San Diego, to discuss research cooperation, technology transfer and bringing new biomedical products to market.
LIAA organises participation in overseas trade missions under the EU co-financed Innovative Entrepreneurship Development Programme for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs), supported by the European Regional Development Fund and national funding. Companies may participate either on a paid basis or with support to cover eligible costs.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: There is a high risk of attack on European countries; they must respond
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: There is a high risk of attack on European countries; they must respond
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes there is a high risk of Russia attacking European countries.
Source: Zelenskyy's answers to journalists after his meeting with Trump
Details: Zelenskyy said that, in his view, it was important for Putin to demonstrate certain results of the war to Russian society.
Quote: "It's not about us, not about Americans, not about Ukrainians. He doesn't respect anybody. His [Putin's] main issue is the Russian people, his internal society, and pressure. He fears only his nation. That's why when you have one million people on the battlefield, on the territory of another country, who are dying – 32,000, 33,000 per month – how can you explain what it is for, if you don't have any victories?"
Details: Zelenskyy believes that this is why Putin wants to break the unity between European countries or between Europe and the US in order to reduce support for Ukraine and increase pressure.
Quote: "How to divide the unity in Europe? If we build what we didn't have before the war, but we built it together. How to do it? To attack somebody else? To strike and say, 'Look, I will go further if you don't stop this'.
To do this or really to divide societies in Europe when societies will be afraid. What he's doing now, with drones attacking Moldova, Romania, crossing borders of Poland, Germany airports, Nordic countries. So he will continue doing this.
That's why the risk of an offensive by drones, missiles, or land operations is very high against other countries bordering Russia or Belarus."
"What would they have to do? Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond to Russians, they will go further."
Background: Zelenskyy said at a press conference after talks with US President Donald Trump that he is ready to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin and that the White House could help organise a trilateral meeting.

articles.title: Inside Trump's bid to shut Iran out of global aviation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Inside Trump's bid to shut Iran out of global aviation
The US has issued an ultimatum to countries and companies continuing to provide services to Iranian airlines.
In the latest salvo under the Trump administration's "Operation Economic Outcast", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced that organisations that continue to have ties to the country's airlines after Wednesday risk being frozen out of the global financial system.
Here's what we know about Washington's bid to shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation.
What has the US done?
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that, from 23 September, the US will impose secondary sanctions on airports and aviation service companies that continue to work with Iranian airlines.
Companies that continue to deal with Iranian carriers after this date risk being locked out of the dollar-based financial system.
That includes airport operators, cargo service providers, ground handlers and fuel suppliers.
"On 23 September all Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC.
"How do we do that? That if they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he said.
This follows a decision by the Treasury on 8 September to slap sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines and another nine aviation service companies.
"Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran's remaining airlines: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system," Bessent said at the time.
How have countries responded?
Several countries have announced restrictions in the days since the sanctions were announced.
Mahan Air announced it had suspended flights to Istanbul and Ankara at the request of Turkish authorities on 21 September. A few days earlier, the carrier halted its Tehran-Muscat route.
Georgia has also introduced a blanket ban on Iranian carriers using the country's aviation sector.
Meanwhile, AFP reported that Iraq is expected to comply with the US measures, citing several sources, including a senior Iraqi government official.
However, Baghdad had not formally announced the restrictions as of Tuesday, while online flight data seen by The New Arab continued to show Iranian-operated flights available to Baghdad and Najaf.
The uncertainty has already caused disruption for Iraqi travel agencies, particularly in Najaf, where many businesses depend heavily on flights carrying pilgrims between Iraq and Iran.
Some agencies have stopped taking flight bookings or begun switching customers to land routes, while others have warned that the restrictions could cause major losses. Travelling overland can also significantly increase journey times, particularly for elderly passengers and Iraqis travelling to Iran for medical treatment. A journey to the holy city of Qom, for example, can take more than 12 hours from the border.
Mahan Air routes to key countries, including the United Arab Emirates, China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Thailand, also do not appear to have been affected so far.
Beijing sharply criticised the measures as "illegal".
"China consistently opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that lack a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters.
How will this impact Iran's aviation industry?
Iran's aviation industry has already been severely degraded after years of US sanctions that have made it extremely difficult to modernise and maintain its ageing civilian aircraft fleet.
Airlines have struggled to obtain crucial spare parts and components needed for repairs and maintenance, raising longstanding concerns about the safety and reliability of the country's ageing aircraft.
The impact of the latest measures will depend largely on how many countries and aviation companies comply with Washington's threat of secondary sanctions.
The most immediate effects will be felt by carriers operating international routes. The bulk of Iran's overseas routes are handled by three airlines - state-owned flag carrier Iran Air, Mahan Air and Qeshm Air - while smaller carriers operate short-haul routes to Iraq and Gulf countries.
If airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies comply with the US measures, Iranian carriers could find it increasingly difficult to operate abroad even in countries that have not formally banned them.
Why is the US doing this?
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's so-called "economic D-Day", which aims to further isolate Iran from the global economy.
Aviation was among five sectors the administration said Tehran was using to circumvent existing US sanctions, move money and provide military support to its allies in the region.
"Iran continues to use its supposed 'commercial' airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and the IRGC, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and hard cash to its proxies," the Treasury wrote.
The return to economic pressure comes amid continued deadlock after almost seven months of war.
Concerns about munitions stockpiles, souring public opinion and limited military options have left the White House hesitant to return to open conflict but unwilling to negotiate a peace deal.
The deadlock comes at a particularly sensitive time for Trump, less than two months before the crucial US midterm elections, with polls showing declining public support for both the war and his presidency.

articles.title: ADF down 119 drones, three Banderols in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
ADF down 119 drones, three Banderols in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, September 22, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 161 Shahed-type UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as Banderol/Dan-T drones launched from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and Millerovo in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Wednesday, September 23, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 119 drones and three Banderol/Dan-T drones.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at eight locations.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs still present in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, in the morning of September 23, a Russian drone struck a gas station in Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district.

articles.title: Ethiopia civil war fears escalate after rebel forces ‘seize airport’
articles.body:
Ethiopia civil war fears escalate after rebel forces ‘seize airport’
Forces in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region have reportedly taken control of the airport in its capital, Mekelle, prompting state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to suspend services to three local destinations. The takeover marks a sharp escalation nearly four years after a peace deal ended a brutal two-year civil war in the East African country.
The carrier announced in a social media post on Wednesday that services to Mekelle, Shire, and Axum have been halted “due to the current situation in Tigray region,” without elaborating. “We sincerely apologize to our valued customers for any inconvenience caused by this suspension. We will inform you when flight operations resume,” the state-owned airline stated.
Two local sources told Reuters that Tigrayan forces have taken control of Mekelle airport from federal police in an overnight operation.
In a statement on Wednesday, Tigray’s regional government said its forces have entered a defensive war against federal troops. It accused the federal government of launching a ground offensive after air and artillery strikes across parts of Tigray on Tuesday.
The federal government has yet to publicly comment on the alleged takeover and the airstrikes.
The development came days after seven armed groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the political party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. In a statement on Sunday, the coalition, known as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, accused the ruling Prosperity Party of imposing “dictatorial” rule and pushing the East African country toward disintegration.
On Monday, Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, accused the alliance of collaborating with financial backing from neighboring Eritrea. The authorities in Eritrea have repeatedly denied backing the groups.
Ethiopia has struggled to secure lasting stability in Tigray since a 2022 peace agreement ended the two-year war between federal forces and the TPLF. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people. Recent clashes and reported drone strikes have threatened the fragile peace. World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned last month that Ethiopia was on the brink of renewed war.
The latest disruption to Ethiopian Airlines schedule follows an earlier suspension of flights to Tigray in January amid reports of renewed military activity. At the time, passengers received cancellation messages citing unplanned circumstances, while a security official linked the interruption to fighting between federal and regional forces.

articles.title: Microamp establishes cooperation with the faculty of electronics at the Military University of Technology
articles.body:
Microamp, a global leader in resilient 5G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations, and the Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology (MUT), a premier academic and research institution based in Warsaw, Poland, have signed a cooperation agreement. The inaugural meeting for this joint initiative took place on 4 September 2026. One of the initial outcomes of this collaboration is the delivery of the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit to the Faculty, which will serve advanced research and educational purposes.
Key representatives from Microamp attended the meeting, including Dr Marcin Góralczyk (Chief Technology Officer) and Adam Olesiński (Head of RAN Solutions). The Faculty of Electronics at MUT was represented by Col. Prof. Jan Kelner (Dean of the Faculty of Electronics), Lt. Col. Dr Jarosław Wojtuń (Deputy Director of the Institute of Communications Systems) and Dr Paweł Skokowski (Head of the Mobile Communications Systems Department) alongside staff members.
The delivered Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit is a comprehensive solution enabling the rapid deployment of a fully functional LDI/LPD mobile architecture. The Microamp mmWave wireless platform consists of radio access network elements, mmWave RAN software, a core network and user equipment. Operating in Standalone mode, the system is fully compliant with the 3GPP standard. The network supports n257, n258 and n261 bands across the 24.25-29.5 GHz frequency range, ensuring throughput exceeding 4 Gbps and latency below 5 ms.
The Microamp mmWave network will be extensively utilised in scientific and research activities conducted by the Faculty of Electronics staff, particularly in developing specialised publications and reports for international NATO working groups. Furthermore, the provided solution forms a foundation for joint research initiatives and projects. This Microamp mmWave system will also facilitate commercial scientific research, proactively addressing the current demands of the industrial market and the defence sector. Access to the complete 5G mmWave environment creates an opportunity to practically verify advanced communication scenarios essential for civil and military applications.
Within the academic framework, the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit will support specialised training sessions and laboratory classes dedicated to the latest connectivity standards. The supplied mmWave wireless platform will allow students to acquire practical skills in configuring, deploying and testing 5G mmWave architectures. Access to this Microamp solution will enable the completion of diploma and design projects, including experimental research on wave propagation, network architecture optimisation and the integration of specialised end devices.
Establishing cooperation with the MUT Faculty of Electronics marks a vital step for Microamp in developing expertise within modern telecommunications. The provided mmWave system will enrich the laboratory facilities of the Faculty and integrate academic education with the practical application of modern 5G connectivity.
About Military University of Technology
The Military University of Technology (MUT) in Warsaw is a public academic institution established in 1951. As a military-civilian university, MUT educates cadets and civilian students while conducting advanced research and development in engineering, technical, exact and social sciences. MUT serves as a strategic research and development facility for the Polish Armed Forces and a leading innovation centre for national security and defence.
The Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology is one of the leading academic and research centres in Poland, specialising in advanced technologies across electronics, telecommunications, radar systems, electronic warfare and communication systems. The Faculty conducts scientific research, implementation projects and educational programmes for both the defence sector and civilian industry.
About Microamp
Microamp is a global leader in resilient 5G and 6G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations. The company designs, builds and delivers ultra-high-capacity, near-zero-latency end-to-end networks powered by its own purpose-built radios. By merging deep-tech know-how with a broad portfolio of technology partners, Microamp empowers industries, system integrators, MNOs, DSPs, governments, and research institutions worldwide. Its networks support applications requiring deterministic performance and high-uplink throughput, in both commercial and defence sectors, where resilience, security and jamming resistance are crucial. Engineered for the most demanding environments, the Microamp system supports critical infrastructure, ports, logistics hubs, public transportation, media production, mass events and specialised military missions.

articles.title: Finland and Ukraine sign drone production deal
articles.body:
Finland and Ukraine have signed a defence cooperation agreement that sets the framework for producing drones and other weapons systems in Finland, as Kyiv seeks more production capacity and Helsinki expands cooperation between the two countries’ defence industries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the agreement in New York on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly. Stubb had travelled to New York for the UN’s high-level week, which runs from 20 to 24 September.
The agreement covers joint production of defence equipment, transfers of technology and expertise, and industrial projects between Finnish and Ukrainian companies.
Most drones produced in Finland under future projects are expected to go to Ukraine. Stubb said during an August visit to Kyiv that about 90 per cent of drones manufactured in Finland under the planned cooperation would go to Ukraine, while the remainder would stay in Finland or go to other customers.
The agreement itself does not transfer funding. Instead, it provides a framework for companies to negotiate production projects and other contracts.
“Ukraine needs all our support in its fight,” Stubb wrote on X after the signing. He said Finland would also use lessons from Ukraine to develop its own defence capabilities.
Stubb told Finnish media in New York that the speed of implementation would depend on cooperation between Finnish and Ukrainian companies. He said some Ukrainian drone models could be produced in Finland.
The two countries had worked on the agreement for several months. Finland and other Nordic and Baltic countries had already committed in August to expanding joint defence production with Ukraine, including drones, air defence equipment, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
Finland has also started building company-level links with Ukraine. Stubb travelled to Kyiv in August with representatives from Insta, Boomeranger, Patria, Nokia, ICEYE, Sensofusion and NestAI. Insta, Boomeranger and Patria signed letters of intent with Ukrainian partners during the visit, according to the Finnish president’s office.
The projects under discussion extend beyond aerial drones. Cooperation also covers unmanned ground vehicles and maritime systems.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the two countries’ defence ministries had negotiated the framework for months. He said it would create opportunities for Finnish defence companies and support Ukraine’s defence capacity.
HT

articles.title: Europe frets about Trump. But soon he could be the least of our problems | Mujtaba Rahman
articles.body:
I addressed a group of more than 100 European ambassadors recently on the big challenges facing the continent this year and next. My main point to these senior diplomats was that, perhaps counterintuitively, Europe’s biggest external challenges over the next 12 months will come from Russia and China, rather than the US.
Europe’s relationship with Trump’s America remains difficult. The US president has weakened confidence in Nato, raised new transatlantic trade tensions and introduced uncertainty into everything from US support for Ukraine to his territorial designs on Greenland. Yet paradoxically, and notwithstanding Trump’s latest tariff threats over the EU’s outreach to Canada, the transatlantic relationship is becoming the more stable part of Europe’s external environment. Not stable, but more stable.
Compared with Russia and China, Europe’s disputes with Washington remain somewhat bounded – and largely negotiable. Ukraine’s rapidly expanding drone capabilities, its military innovation and battlefield experience have made Kyiv a more valuable partner for Washington. US defence companies are also benefiting from Europe’s military support for Ukraine and rearmament against Russia. The US, Denmark and Greenland now say they have struck a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland. The devil will be in the detail, but they have much stronger incentives to reach an accommodation than to allow the issue to become a lasting source of confrontation.
Trade tensions more broadly will persist, particularly over European regulation of American tech companies. The same is true of Nato, which has lost credibility because of Trump’s frequent admonishments. Nonetheless, these disputes are among countries with deeply interconnected security and economic interests. The risks posed to Europe by Russia and China are more structural – and increasingly point towards escalation.
Russia is becoming more dangerous because it is becoming weaker. The Kremlin is running out of cheap and politically painless ways to finance its war in Ukraine. Its original budget assumptions for 2026 have been overtaken by events. Military spending continues to rise, driven not only by the need for equipment but by the growing cost of recruiting soldiers for the frontline and paying compensation to casualties.
How Vladimir Putin funds his war is now the battlefield behind the battlefield. Further tax increases would damage an economy that, outside the military sector, is approaching recession. Borrowing has become more expensive, while public spending – on everything from schools and hospitals to infrastructure – is being squeezed to preserve the war effort.
Rather than push Putin towards compromise, Russia’s economic challenges are likely, initially at least, to produce the opposite effect. If he expects his economic position to worsen next year, the Kremlin has a powerful incentive to improve its military position now. That means escalation in Ukraine and against Nato. This explains the recent impromptu visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe.
In Ukraine, Russia is likely to accelerate its mobilisation efforts and engage in heavier attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, intensifying its efforts to undermine Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale this winter. The coming months will also see an escalation of Russia’s hybrid warfare activity against Nato countries.
China presents a different but equally serious challenge. For years, Europe has debated whether China is competing fairly. That argument is essentially over. A broad consensus now exists that China’s subsidies, industrial overcapacity, undervalued exchange rate and export-led economic model require a political response. The question is no longer whether Europe should defend itself against unfair Chinese competition, but how far it is prepared to go.
Beijing, meanwhile, has reached a very different conclusion. It increasingly sees Europe’s trade-defence measures, industrial policy and economic security agenda as an attempt to constrain China’s growth.
The European commissioner for trade and economic security, Maroš Šefčovič, and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, met in late June and committed to resolving a number of outstanding issues by October. That may delay confrontation. It is unlikely to avert it.
China is not going to abandon its use of industrial subsidies, the exchange rate or its export-led growth model. These are central features of China’s economic-strategy, and not subject to negotiation. Equally, the EU is not going to retreat from its economic security agenda. The union is developing investment controls, procurement restrictions and new industrial and trade-defence instruments. Although formally country-agnostic, many are clearly directed towards China.
Every European measure to reduce dependence on China is therefore likely to prompt a Chinese response, while every Chinese retaliation will strengthen the political case in Brussels to go further. That makes compromise harder, and escalation between the two sides more likely over the medium term.
The most likely outcome is managed confrontation, rather than a full-scale trade war. The EU will expand targeted restrictions limiting China’s access in additional sectors. China will respond with selective tariffs, procurement barriers, regulatory pressure on European companies and tighter controls on critical minerals. Both sides will try to increase pressure without losing control.
Europe has leverage, too. China remains extraordinarily dependent on access to the EU single market, one of the world’s last large and wealthy export destinations. Europe can withstand coercion – if its governments remain united.
That is why France’s presidential election next year could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a credible path to victory. She is scoring 35% to 38% in first-round polling at present, and is a more formidable candidate than her younger lieutenant, Jordan Bardella, who many assumed would be the Rassemblement National’s candidate in next year’s race. Her prospects will depend heavily on whether France’s fragmented centre can unite behind a single candidate. If it cannot, Le Pen could face the hard-left renegade Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the second round – and would probably win.
A Le Pen presidency would be profoundly disruptive for Europe. She would probably oppose further support for Ukraine, obstruct sanctions against Russia, undermine the bloc’s approach to China and initiate battles with Brussels over Schengen, fiscal rules, electricity pricing and the single market. Her threat to withhold France’s contribution to the EU budget could plunge the union into an unprecedented financial and constitutional crisis.
Europe’s external challenges, while substantial, are manageable. But the decisive variable is Europe itself: whether it can maintain the political coherence required to deal with the US, Russia and China. A Le Pen victory would call that coherence into question, precisely when Europe needs it most.
- 
  Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

articles.title: Smuggled Western arms from Ukraine end up in Africa, Middle East — Russian envoy
articles.body:
GENEVA, September 23. /TASS/. Western weapons and military equipment smuggled out of Ukraine have been found in Africa and the Middle East, Yulia Zhdanova, head of the Russian delegation to the Vienna talks on military security and arms control, stated.
"Specific cases involving the discovery of contraband items (Western weapons and military equipment - TASS) have already been identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Niger, Somalia, Sudan, and the Central African Republic. Official statements by the authorities of Mali and Burkina Faso in late 2025 and early this year mentioned the appearance, during armed clashes in the Sahara-Sahel region, of Western small arms and anti-tank missile systems previously transferred to the Ukrainian armed forces," she noted during a regular session of the OSCE Forum for Security Cooperation.
The diplomat explained that weapons and military equipment are being transported by sea from Ukraine to countries in the Middle East and Africa via port infrastructure in the Odessa region, including the commercial port of Izmail and the Orlovka-Isakcha ferry crossing.

articles.title: Who Will Be the Next Leader of the U.N.? Meet the Contenders
articles.body:
With António Guterres’s nearly decade-long tenure as the Secretary-General of the United Nations drawing to a close amid rising conflict around the globe, the race to succeed him as the leader of the world’s most powerful diplomatic body is already underway.
Guterres this week delivered his final address to the U.N. General Assembly, in which he called for a greater focus on climate change, a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, “de-escalation and dialogue” in the Middle East, and regulations for artificial intelligence.
At the end of his speech, Guterres bid goodbye to a crowd filled with many diplomats and world leaders who he has worked with over his two five-year terms.
"So, on January 1st, when I am no longer Secretary-General, be sure of this. Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible," he said. "I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter and I will never, ever give up. Thank you."
Guterres’s successor is set to step in as Secretary-General at a consequential moment for global diplomacy. Research indicates that last year saw the highest number of active global conflicts since World War II and the greatest number of fatalities since the Rwandan genocide. Tensions in other parts of the world are threatening to boil over. Climate change is exacting a growing toll. AI's development is prompting increasing alarm. And the U.N. itself is confronting a growing funding crisis.
Seven candidates are so far in the running to shepherd the U.N. through those challenges. Here’s what to know about the race.
How will the next Secretary-General be chosen?
The process to choose the next Secretary-General began in November, when a joint letter from the presidents of the U.N. General Assembly and Security Council invited the nominations of candidates from member states.
The initiation letter noted “with regret that no woman has ever held the position” and encouraged member states to “strongly consider nominating women as candidates.”
Member states nominate candidates by submitting an application to the U.N. including a personal statement with that candidate’s vision for what they’d do in the role, a resume, and campaign finance disclosures.
The General Assembly then holds “interactive dialogues” in which candidates express their hopes for the position and the U.N. in an opening statement, which is followed by questioning from the assembly. These televised hearings continue as candidates are submitted to the U.N.
Who becomes Secretary-General ultimately comes down to a decision from the U.N.’s 15-person Security Council, which recommends one individual to the General Assembly. The General Assembly then appoints that person to the position.
As part of its selection process, the Security Council holds “straw polls,” in which members of the council select one of three options for each candidate: “encourage,” “discourage,” or “no opinion expressed.” This anonymized process is used to gauge whether candidates would be able to secure the nine votes needed for a formal recommendation by the Security Council.
Who’s in the running?
So far nine candidates have been nominated for the position of Secretary-General. Two of those candidates have withdrawn, leaving seven individuals vying to replace Guterres.
Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has been Guyana’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2020 and previously served as foreign minister for her country and held senior roles at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. Nominated by Guyana, her vision statement emphasizes refocusing on the U.N.’s core principles and “a more agile and effective United Nations.”
Rebeca Grynspan is the former vice president of Costa Rica, which nominated her for the position, and current secretary-general of trade and development for the U.N. She named three principles that define the mission she would undertake as Secretary-General: making the U.N. “more useful,” “more agile,” and “more accountable.”
Ivonne A-Baki, nominated by Tonga, is a long-time Ecuadorean diplomat who has twice served as the country’s ambassador to the U.S. She has also served as ambassador to countries including Qatar and France. Her platform highlights her involvement in the 1998 Ecuador-Peru peace settlement. “Where others speak of reform, I speak of renewal,” A-Baki’s vision statement reads. “An institution can be indispensable and in need of renewal at the same time, and ours is both. It is failing to live up to its own Charter, not for want of purpose but for want of focus and discipline.”
María Fernanda Espinosa is the former Foreign Minister and Defense Minister of Ecuador and served as President of the 73rd U.N. General Assembly in 2018. She was nominated by Antigua and Barbuda. Her vision consists of five pillars: “peace and security, development, digital and energy transformation, closing the delivery gap, and rebuilding credibility.” Garcés in her statement contended that “what is now in question is not the relevance of the United Nations, but its credibility.”
Rafael Mariano Grossi is an Argentine diplomat who has served as the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) since 2019. “The world does not need more declarations. It needs a United Nations capable of responding to the real demands of our time, with impartiality and a results-oriented approach grounded in facts,” Grossi, who was nominated by his country, wrote in his vision statement.
Olara Otunnu was Uganda’s permanent representative to the U.N. for five years and briefly served as the country’s foreign minister. He was also the U.N. under-secretary-general and the special representative for children and armed conflict. “Reform is no longer an optional choice. It is an imperative,” he said.
Macky Sall was the president of Senegal for twelve years and has served as the chair of the Africa Union, a continental organization spanning 55 member states. He expressed a goal to “restore trust in multilateralism” if chosen as Secretary-General and said that “peace, security and development are intrinsically linked.”
Where does the race stand?
“We're at a moment right now where the race is entering a pretty pivotal phase,” says Daniel Forti, head of U.N. affairs at the International Crisis Group, a non-profit think tank dedicated to preventing deadly crises around the world.
With just over three months remaining in Guterre’s term, it won’t be long before a successor is chosen. The Security Council, though, “is not especially enthusiastic about any of the current contenders,” Forti tells TIME. He cites the last three straw polls, which have favored Greenspan and Birkett, but without “a real consolidation of overwhelming support.”
This lack of consensus, Forti believes, could suggest that other candidates may enter the race late in the game. Although there have been no formal announcements of new candidates, Forti has heard chatter surrounding certain individuals: Nickolay Mladenov, the former Bulgarian foreign minister and former U.N. Middle East envoy who currently serves as the Board of Peace’s High Representative for Gaza; U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed; and former Mexican Foreign Minister Alicia Bárcena.
“At this late stage, new candidates don't have the luxury of time to really socialize their candidacies, build out their visions, and elaborate very detailed policy platforms and bring them to U.N. member states, and try and win over the P5,” Forti says, referring to the five permanent members of the Security Council. The support of these members—China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.
—is the most critical because they have the power to veto candidates before being recommended to the General Assembly.
Regardless of the outcome, Forti asserts that whoever is chosen to replace Guterres will inherit a fraught state of international affairs, and certainly be tested.
“You have a really fragmented global landscape,” he says. “The challenges for whoever takes over the office are going to be immense.”

articles.title: Fifty countries and EU call on Russia to cease fire, US does not support statement
articles.body:
Fifty countries and EU call on Russia to cease fire, US does not support statement
A total of 50 countries and the European Union have issued a joint statement at the UN in support of Ukraine, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
Source: European Pravda citing the text of the statement provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine
Details: The statement was released ahead of a UN Security Council meeting on 23 September. The signatories expressed solidarity with Ukraine and deep concern over the escalation of Russian attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure across the country.
They also voiced concern about attacks in the Black Sea and supported efforts to reach an agreement there to ensure freedom of navigation.
In the statement, the countries reiterated that Ukraine had agreed as early as March 2025 to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire.
Quote: "We call on Russia to finally do the same, as a necessary step towards meaningful diplomacy and negotiations leading to peace."
More details: The signatories also called on Russia to ensure the immediate return to Ukraine of all arbitrarily detained, forcibly transferred or deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, as well as the full return of all prisoners of war and all interned persons as important confidence-building measures.
Quote: "Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must stop its aggression, accept a ceasefire, and engage meaningfully in negotiations towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law."
More details: The statement was signed by 50 countries and the European Union (Ukraine, Albania, Andorra, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Honduras, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Montenegro, the Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom).
The United States, which is playing a mediating role in talks between Ukraine and Russia, was not among the signatories.
Background:
- The 81st session of the UN General Assembly is taking place in New York. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to address it on 23 September.
- The day before, US President Donald Trump urged Russian leader Vladimir Putin to end Russia's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
articles.body:
EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
The General Court of the European Union annulled the Council of the EU’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions to keep former Federation Council member Oleg Tkach on the sanctions list. An entry for the ruling is posted on the court’s website.
The EU initially imposed sanctions on Tkach in March 2022 because, as a Federation Council member, he had voted to ratify the treaty “on friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance between the Russian Federation and the Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.”
The court ruled that Tkach’s vote had provided sufficient grounds to impose sanctions on him but was not enough to keep him on the list in subsequent years.
The court concluded that Tkach had “withdrawn from Russian political life”: He did not seek reelection in September 2022 and had also acquired “citizenship in two other countries,” which disqualified him from holding political office in Russia.
The court also rejected the Council’s argument that the former senator had not publicly condemned the invasion of Ukraine. The ruling said his failure to do so could not automatically be taken as a sign of support, particularly given the harsh repression of anti-war views.
The Council also cited Tkach’s ties to the publishing company Olma Media Group, which he founded in 1991, as grounds for extending the sanctions. The group included the publisher Prosveshcheniye, which helped promote anti-Ukrainian narratives through school textbooks.
The Council maintained that although Tkach had formally stepped away from managing the company long ago, he continued to exert influence over it through a trust fund and entities linked to his family. The court rejected this argument because the Council had failed to explain Tkach’s specific role in the company. The court also said VEB.RF, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Sberbank had controlled a 75% stake in Prosveshcheniye since 2021.
The court therefore found that the grounds cited in the Council’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions did not justify keeping Tkach on the sanctions list.
Tkach remains on the EU sanctions list under a March 14, 2026, Council decision. He has already filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn that extension, but the court has not yet ruled on the case. The Council’s September 22, 2026, decision lifting sanctions on billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman does not mention Tkach.

articles.title: Is Israel committing genocide in Lebanon? RT reports (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Is Israel committing genocide in Lebanon? RT reports (VIDEO)
Israel is facing accusations of genocide over its military campaign in Lebanon, where thousands have been killed and large areas devastated. RT correspondent Steve Sweeney reports from Nabatieh, a city in the south of the country that has been repeatedly hit by Israeli strikes.
More than 4,300 people, including over 250 children and 130 medical professionals, have been killed since the latest escalation began in March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.
The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention and Doctors Against Genocide have accused Israel of pursuing what they called a “genocidal policy of absolute destruction,” targeting the foundations of life of Lebanon’s Shia communities. The groups said attacks on medical personnel were part of a sustained pattern affecting “the very systems necessary for civilian survival.”
Around 56,000 hectares of agricultural land have been affected, with losses to the sector estimated at more than $1 billion, according to Lebanon’s Agriculture Ministry.
Israel denies that its campaign targets Lebanon’s Shia population, saying its operations are directed against Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has warned, however, that Beirut’s predominantly Shia Dahiya district would “look like Khan Yunis,” referring to a war-devastated city in Gaza.
The latest Israeli campaign in Lebanon began in early March, after Hezbollah attacked Israel following the start of US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Israel responded with airstrikes and later expanded its military operations in Lebanon.
Israeli attacks have continued despite a US-brokered framework agreed upon in June aimed at ending the fighting. The deal calls for a progressive Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon alongside Lebanese Army deployments and the disarmament of armed groups, including Hezbollah, but implementation has stalled.
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. RT looks at whether the destruction and statements accompanying Israel’s campaign could meet that definition.

articles.title: Old American armor, new Ukrainian brain: Skelya regiment nears completion of M1117 unmanned conversion
articles.body:
Ukraine's 425th Separate Assault Regiment Skelya is converting American-made armored vehicles into remotely operated platforms as part of its "remote infantry" concept, head of the regiment's innovation support group Edhar Vinnik wrote in an exclusive column for 24 Kanal. The approach rests on a simple principle: if a machine can do the job, no soldier should risk their life doing it, Vinnik argued. The regiment established an Innovation Center to develop unmanned systems and robotic platforms, Militarnyi reported.
The M1117 is the second vehicle Skelya has converted to unmanned control—after completing the Novator armored car in June—and the regiment's approach won a Defense Ministry DELTA innovation competition on 31 August 2026, earning approximately $33,700. The pattern suggests Ukraine's cheapest path to unmanned ground capability may not run through purpose-built robots but through vehicles already in service, upgraded with off-the-shelf hardware.
M1117 conversion nears completion
The regiment is in the final stages of converting the American M1117 Guardian into a remotely controlled platform. The 4x4 vehicle has been in Ukrainian service since 2023.
"The project of remote control of the American armored wheeled vehicle M1117 is in the final stage," Vinnik said.
This is Skelya's second such conversion. In June, the regiment completed a similar project with the Novator armored car. The Novator received multiple communication channels: Starlink, LTE, and Silvus radio systems. Vinnik argued the conversions prove that remote control can scale to any vehicle in service, if the hardware supports it.
Software ties the system together
Without adequate software, all unmanned platforms would remain isolated machines, Vinnik noted. The regiment's IT Innovation Department develops proprietary software for coordinating unmanned systems. One solution replicates functionality similar to R2D2—a network data-relay infrastructure that enables remote equipment operation. Using off-the-shelf routers cut the cost roughly fourfold.
"Without adequate software, all these drones and ground systems would remain just separate machines," Vinnik said.
The cost reduction matters for scalability, Vinnik argued. A technology that exists in one copy is a demo—one cheap and reliable enough for hundreds of crews is a capability. The regiment measures its progress by one number, he wrote: how many soldiers were not sent where they could be killed or wounded.
Why old armor gets a second life
The M1117 Guardian—built on the Cadillac Gage Commando chassis from the Vietnam War era—exemplifies the trend. The regiment's Innovation Center, established in autumn 2025, won a Defense Ministry DELTA innovation competition on 31 August 2026. Skelya's approach reflects a broader Ukrainian trend of converting existing vehicles into unmanned platforms rather than building robots from scratch. The National Guard's Khartiia Corps earlier converted a 12-ton US-made M113 armored personnel carrier into an unmanned platform for remote demining and logistics, fitting it with anti-drone armor and a mine flail. Ukraine is also rebuilding Soviet BRDM-2 armored scouts into remotely operated robotic platforms, and three units recently received Kaban—a bolt-on kit that turns ordinary vehicles into uncrewed ones.

articles.title: At UNGA, Qatar Emir urges Hormuz reopening to 'avert war'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
At UNGA, Qatar Emir urges Hormuz reopening to 'avert war'
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a return to diplomacy on Tuesday, warning that the Gulf was going through "one of the most dangerous phases" amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, Sheikh Tamim said the regional crisis could still be resolved through diplomatic means and reiterated Qatar's role as a mediator.
"We remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war," he said.
Sheikh Tamim said Qatar was doing "everything in our power to address the conflict in the region through diplomatic means", while stressing that Doha remained steadfast in defending its territory and sovereignty.
He described the war as the cumulative result of years of delaying diplomatic solutions and called for the establishment of a regional collective security system.
"In the absence of such a system, it has become possible for a war to erupt," he said.
His comments came as the conflict increasingly threatens key economic and energy routes across the Gulf, particularly the Strait of Hormuz.
The war began after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February amid negotiations over Tehran's nuclear programme, killing Iran's supreme leader, other senior officials and civilians.
Iran subsequently launched attacks across the Gulf region, including against the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain.
Shortly after Sheikh Tamim's speech, US President Donald Trump revealed that American officials had held a three-hour meeting with an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN gathering, describing the talks as "very good".
Trump's announcement came after he threatened during his own UN address to "annihilate" Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement with Washington.
Sheikh Tamim also used his address to condemn Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, saying they had repercussions for the security of the wider region.
"There can be no talk of a just international order as long as Palestine remains in its plight," he said.
"What has transpired in Gaza is genocide in every sense of the word."
The Qatari leader also reiterated Doha's support for the sovereignty of Lebanon, Sudan and Libya.
On Yemen, he backed UN efforts to reach a comprehensive political settlement based on the outcomes of the UN-facilitated national dialogue, saying any solution should preserve the country's unity and sovereignty and achieve security and stability.

articles.title: Under new deal, U.S. military buys non-standard weapons
articles.body:
- Global Military Products won a spot on a new five-year, $19.5 million USSOCOM contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and protective equipment.
- GMP has historically supplied Soviet-pattern weapons like AK-platform rifles and RPG-7 launchers for training and partner-force support.
Global Military Products has been selected as one of several contractors on a new U.S. Special Operations Command indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and personal protective equipment, the Tampa, Florida-based company said Sept. 21.
The five-year contract has a ceiling of $19.5 million, and GMP will compete against other contract holders for individual delivery orders as the command’s needs arise.
The company has not disclosed which specific weapons this contract will cover. But GMP’s business has long centered on sourcing non-standard, foreign-made military equipment through a separate line of contracts known as Special Ammunition and Weapon Systems, or SAWS, which the company has held with the Army for over a decade. Those items typically include Soviet and former-Eastern-Bloc-pattern hardware not in the standard U.S. arsenal: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles such as the AKM and AK-74, PKM and RPK machine guns, RPG-7 rocket launchers, SVD-pattern sniper rifles, and mortars in non-NATO calibers such as 82mm, along with the ammunition that feeds them. The U.S. military uses this kind of foreign-made equipment to train special operations forces on weapons they may encounter in the field, to equip foreign partner forces already using Soviet-era arms, or for testing.
This is the second consecutive USSOCOM IDIQ contract for weapons and ammunition procurement that GMP has held. The company said its work on the earlier agreement, which involved sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition through its international supplier network, factored into its selection this time.
“Special operations forces require speed, flexibility and dependable access to equipment,” said Austin Gouveia, associate program manager at Global Military Products. “This award reflects Global Military Products’ commitment to providing U.S. and allied forces with reliable access to critical defense equipment and capabilities.”
“This award also reflects our ability to perform under the previous USSOCOM IDIQ contract, where we excelled at sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition while leveraging our global network and supply chain capabilities to respond to evolving operational requirements and support USSOCOM missions,” Gouveia said.
GMP, a subsidiary of Global Ordnance, has built its business around supplying this kind of non-standard hardware to the U.S. military and its allies, including mortar systems, sniper rifles, assault rifles, machine guns, grenade launchers, anti-armor weapons, ammunition, electro-optics, and weapon accessories. The company separately holds a $639.8 million Army contract for 155mm artillery rounds awarded in 2025.

articles.title: Tajani says Iran must 'change tone' after 'very hard' UN speech
articles.body:
Deputy Premier and Foreign Minister
Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticised Iranian President Masoud
Pezeshkian's speech at the United Nations General Assembly, in
which he accused the United States of terrorism and said Tehran
would never "bend at the knee".
                                    
                                       
				Tajani, who is in New York for the General Assembly, described
the speech as "very hard".
                                    
                                       
				"We are working toward a diplomatic solution - Iran must adopt a
different tone and abandon its pursuit of nuclear weapons,"
Tajani added.
                                    
                                       
				"It is necessary to use a less confrontational tone here as
well, even in order to defend one's positions".
